The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.
In this personal lament, the psalmist prays for redemption because of his innocence and the Lord's justice.
For God’s truth to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.
Because of his devotion to the Lord ({{Psalm 26:1-3|Psalm 26:1–3}}), the psalmist separates himself from evil people (see {{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}).

- Ritual purity required the worshiper to wash their hands. This act symbolized separating from evil and evildoers (see {{Psalm 73:13|Psalm 73:13}}). 

- The altar symbolizes God's presence ({{Psalm 43:4|Psalm 43:4}}).
The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the temple.
The sanctuary represented the visible presence of the Lord (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}).
*Do not take my soul away with sinners*: The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.

- The psalmist standing on solid ground represents salvation (compare {{Psalm 143:10|Psalm 143:10}}). 

- *in the congregations*: This means *in the great assembly* at the temple ({{Psalm 26:6-8|Psalms 26:6–8}}; {{Psalm 22:25|22:25}}).

The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life ({{Psalm 27:1|Psalm 27:1}}). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or disrupt his inner peace.

This psalm combines two types—a psalm of confidence ({{Psalm 27:1-6|Psalm 27:1–6}}) and an individual lament ({{Psalm 27:7-14|27:7–14}})—united by the theme of longing for the Lord's presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord, making his own circumstances less important. The psalmist shows strong faith by being open to the Lord's guidance, timing, and priorities.
The psalmist's enemies want to take advantage of him and live off his resources (see study note on Psalm 14:4).
Seeking and enjoying the Lord's presence gives the psalmist confidence and security. He trusts in God's protection and looks forward to giving thanks and praise (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}).
*tent* (or *tabernacle*): This early shrine was where the Israelites worshipped before they built the temple.

- *my head will be held high*: This is a sign of victory. 

- The granting of the request of {{Psalm 27:4|Psalm 27:4}} leads to sacrifices with joyful shouts.

Unlike the wicked ({{Psalm 10:4|Psalm 10:4}}), who only want a temporary advantage ({{Psalm 78:34-36|78:34–36}}), the godly search for the Lord like a thirsty person seeks water in the desert ({{Psalm 63:1|63:1}}; {{Psalm 105:4|105:4}}; {{Psalm 119:2|119:2}}, {{Psalm 119:10|10}}; {{Matthew 6:33|Matthew 6:33}}). They act wisely ({{Psalm 34:10|Psalm 34:10}}, {{Psalm 34:14|14}}) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis ({{Psalm 34:4|34:4}}; {{Psalm 69:6|69:6}}; {{Psalm 77:2|77:2}}; {{Psalm 119:58|119:58}}).
The psalmist asks for the Lord's mercy, presence, and guidance. For the psalmist, God is the greatest good, while enemies and other situations are less important.

The psalmist shows confidence and hope in the Lord's presence. Living in faith means waiting patiently, knowing the Lord is good. This life is not always easy for the faithful ({{Psalm 42:2-3|Psalm 42:2–3}}; {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}), but their future is secure ({{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}; {{Psalm 130:7|130:7}}; see {{Psalm 9:18|9:18}}).
*if You remain silent*: The psalmist asks the Lord to act ({{Psalm 35:22|Psalm 35:22}}; {{Psalm 50:3|50:3}}; {{Psalm 83:1|83:1}}; {{Psalm 109:1|109:1}}).
The psalmist asks the Lord to listen. His urgent request comes from the tension between his close relationship with the Lord and the trouble he is facing.
In this personal lament, the psalmist asks for justice and mercy. He trusts in the Lord's strength and faithfulness and prays for the Lord's people.
People often raised their hands as a sign of devoted prayer ({{Psalm 63:4|Psalms 63:4}}; {{Psalm 134:2|134:2}}).
The psalmist asks God to punish his enemies and prove his innocence.
The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.
The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.
*my strength and my shield*: The Lord protects the psalmist (see {{Psalm 59:9|Psalm 59:9}}, {{Psalm 59:17|17}}).

- The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people. 

- *bless Your inheritance*: See {{Psalm 29:11|Psalms 29:11}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}.

- The psalmist issues a call to honor the Lord for his power (see {{Psalm 96:7-8|Psalm 96:7–8}}). 

- *O heavenly beings*: Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other gods but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.
This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.

The Hebrew word *qol* can mean "voice," "noise" ({{1 Kings 1:45|1 Kings 1:45}}), or "thunder" ({{Joel 3:16|Joel 3:16}}). The Lord's voice is awe-inspiring and overpowers any sounds people might attribute to other gods.
The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their large size and high quality (see {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}).

- Lebanon’s mountains and Sirion (another name for Mount Hermon) are high mountains to the north of Israel. 

- The Lord can make even huge mountains shake when he commands it (see {{Psalm 114:4|Psalm 114:4}}).
The Wilderness of Kadesh was south of Judah. People could hear God's voice across the land, from the north ({{Psalm 29:6|Psalm 29:6}}) to the south.
The image of strong floodwaters relates to the great flood ({{Genesis 6:17|Genesis 6:17}}). The Lord rules as king over all creation. No one challenges his kingdom.
The ruler of nature blesses his people with peace (see {{Psalm 28:8-9|Psalms 28:8–9}}; {{Psalm 37:11|37:11}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}).

- *I will exalt You* is a call to praise and thank the Lord ({{Psalm 34:3|Psalms 34:3}}; {{Psalm 81:1|81:1}}; {{Psalm 99:5|99:5}}, {{Psalm 99:9|9}}; {{Psalm 107:32|107:32}}; {{Psalm 118:28|118:28}}; {{Psalm 145:1|145:1}}; see {{Exodus 15:1|Exodus 15:1}}; {{Isaiah 25:1|Isaiah 25:1}}). 

- *You have lifted me up*: God saved the psalmist from death ({{Psalm 30:3|Psalm 30:3}}).

- God, in his justice and care, did not let the psalmist’s enemies win (see {{Psalm 26:9|Psalms 26:9}}; {{Psalm 27:12|27:12}}; {{Psalm 28:3|28:3}}; {{Psalm 31:8|31:8}}).
The psalmist praises God for his victory over difficult circumstances, comparing it to being saved from death.

This individual thanksgiving psalm begins by praising the Lord for his salvation ({{Psalm 30:1-3|Psalm 30:1–3}}). It then contrasts God's favor with his anger ({{Psalm 30:4-7|Psalm 30:4–7}}) and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing ({{Psalm 30:8-12|30:8–12}}).
Perhaps David wrote this psalm before the dedication of the temple, making his own experience representative of the nation’s.
The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and praise ({{Psalm 33:21|Psalms 33:21}}; {{Psalm 97:12|97:12}}; {{Psalm 103:1|103:1}}; {{Psalm 105:3|105:3}}; {{Psalm 145:21|145:21}}).

- *I will never be shaken*: The psalmist admits his overconfident attitude (compare {{Psalm 32:3-4|Psalm 32:3–4}}). 

- *my mountain stand strong*: In the psalms, this phrase powerfully symbolizes stability and God's control (see {{Psalm 11:1|Psalms 11:1}}; {{Psalm 18:7|18:7}}; {{Psalm 36:6|36:6}}; {{Psalm 46:2|46:2}}; {{Psalm 72:3|72:3}}; {{Psalm 76:4|76:4}}; {{Psalm 83:14|83:14}}; {{Psalm 97:5|97:5}}; {{Psalm 114:4|114:4}}, {{Psalm 114:6|6}}; {{Psalm 125:2|125:2}}). 

- *I was dismayed*: The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (compare {{Psalm 104:27-30|Psalm 104:27–30}}).

The psalmist faced death (also in {{Psalm 30:1-3|Psalm 30:1–3}}), either literally or figuratively. When he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and changed his mourning into joyful dancing. Only God's favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and deep despair.
The Lord provides safety to anyone seeking his protection. The psalmist trusts and submits to the Lord. See also {{Psalm 71:1-3|Psalm 71:1–3}}.

The psalmist urges the faithful to seek safety in the Lord and wait for his salvation. After experiencing something like death, he shares how the Lord remained faithful. This psalm points ahead to the suffering of Jesus ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}).
The psalmist urgently asks the Lord to notice his desperate situation ({{Psalm 71:2|PSalms 71:2}}; {{Psalm 88:2|88:2}}; {{Psalm 102:2|102:2}}).
*Into Your hands I commit my spirit*: The psalmist will trust his Lord, whether he lives or dies. Jesus said these words on the cross before he died ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}).
Trusting the Lord means believing he cares about our well-being.
*in the open*: This means a wide area, unlike a narrow or tight place that causes distress (see {{Psalm 18:19|Psalm 18:19}}).

In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist places a description of his intense suffering and the pain of rejection between two statements of trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 31:6|Psalm 31:6}}, {{Psalm 31:14|14}}).
*my bones are wasting away*: This phrase powerfully describes how despair can harm our physical health.
Hope does not trust weak and unreliable human beings. It trusts only in the Lord. The suffering person places his life in God’s hands while he waits for the Lord to bring justice.
*My times are in Your hands*: To give up control of timing is one way to express submission.
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on Psalm 1:6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution
The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer and rescuing him ({{Psalm 31:1-18|Psalm 31:1–18}}).
*Blessed be the LORD*: The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his struggles, the Lord has cared for him.

Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.

The Lord’s forgiveness brings people back into a relationship with him, removes their guilt, and gives them joy. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone ({{Romans 4:4-8|Romans 4:4–8}}).

This wisdom psalm of confession and thanks urges the godly to learn from the psalmist’s journey through sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. The early church used this psalm as one of the seven penitential psalms (psalms of repentance, see also {{Psalm 6:1-10|Psalms 6}}, {{Psalm 38:1-22|38}}, {{Psalm 51:1-19|51}}, {{Psalm 102:1-28|102}}, {{Psalm 130:1-8|130}}, {{Psalm 143:1-12|143}}).

The psalmist admits his sin (see {{Psalm 19:12-13|Psalms 19:12–13}}; {{Psalm 25:7|25:7}}, {{Psalm 25:11|11}}, {{Psalm 25:15-22|15–22}}) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.
The psalmist believes his suffering comes directly from the Lord's discipline (compare {{Psalm 38:2|Psalms 38:2}}; {{Psalm 39:10|39:10}}).

God has forgiven the guilt and rebellion mentioned in {{Psalm 32:1|Psalm 32:1}}. The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive ({{Psalm 78:38|Psalms 78:38}}; {{Psalm 85:2|85:2}}; {{Psalm 130:4|130:4}}), but he requires people to confess and repent.
The godly will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.
The Lord promises to be a safe place for his people ({{Psalm 31:20|Psalm 31:20}}). Instead of feeling terrified ({{Psalm 31:13|Psalm 31:13}}), the psalmist hears songs of victory all around.
God interrupts the psalmist's teaching with a message inviting the godly to receive the Lord's wisdom (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 23:3|23:3}}; {{Psalm 25:4-6|25:4–6}}).
The foolish person lacks wisdom. Ignoring the Lord’s advice harms life and makes a person like an animal (see {{Isaiah 1:3|Isaiah 1:3}}; {{James 3:3|James 3:3}}).
Difficulties common to all of life will come to the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.
The psalmist urges the godly to praise the Lord with melodies, with a new song, and with skillfully-played music.

This hymn of creation (see also {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalms 8}}, {{Psalm 19:1-14|19}}, {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) might be a continuation of {{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalm 32}}. It urges readers to praise God ({{Psalm 33:1-3|Psalm 33:1–3}}), to recognize the power of his word in creation ({{Psalm 33:4-7|33:4–7}}), and to respect the Creator ({{Psalm 33:8-11|33:8–11}}). It gives hope to forgiven sinners ({{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalm 32}}) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.
God's word shows his character and power.
The nations surrounding Israel thought that the sea had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within boundaries that he set (see {{Psalm 104:8-10|Psalm 104:8–10}}).
The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see Psalm 22; {{Psalm 96:1-3|96:123}}).
Fear of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He frustrates the plans of people who oppose his will.
The plans of powerful people will only succeed if God allows it (see {{Isaiah 8:9-10|Isaiah 8:9210}}).

- God’s word still orders creation and will do so forever.

- God's purposes are wonderful ({{Psalm 40:5|Psalms 40:5}}; {{Psalm 92:5|92:5}}).
People who fear God are chosen as his inheritance (see {{Psalm 33:13-19|Psalm 33:13–19}}). This does not include rebellious people ({{Psalm 78:62|Psalm 78:62}}).
From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see {{Psalm 14:2-3|Psalm 14:2–3}}).
*army …great strength. … horse*: Even military power is under God's control (see {{Psalm 33:10-11|Psalm 33:10–11}}; {{Ecclesiastes 9:11|Ecclesiastes 9:11}}).
God watches over all who live by his counsel ({{Psalm 32:8|Psalm 32:8}}). He protects, rescues, and stays close to them ({{Psalm 34:15-22|Psalm 34:15–22}}).
The faithful see God's power in creation and world events. They respond with trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God's help.
The psalmist uses wordplay to contrast his people's certain hope (Hebrew *yakhal*) in the Lord with the supposed strength (Hebrew *khayil*) of the wicked's horses.
Abimelech is another name for Achish (see {{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.
The psalmist encourages those in need to join him in praise.

This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving song of praise ({{Psalm 34:1-7|Psalm 34:1–7}}) that celebrates the Lord for caring for and protecting godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom ({{Psalm 34:8-14|Psalm 34:8–14}}) and explains wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked ({{Psalm 34:15-22|Psalm 34:15–22}}).
The psalmist describes his experiences of answered prayer.

The *angel of the LORD* showed God's presence during the journey through the wilderness. He protected Israel from Egypt's forces ({{Exodus 14:19-20|Exodus 14:19–20}}), and he will guard all those who are godly ({{Psalm 91:11|Psalm 91:11}}).
The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.
Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Proverbs 9:10|9:10}}).
Anyone who listens, even children, can become wise followers of God.

Wisdom has three parts: 

- fearing the Lord ({{Psalm 34:11|Psalm 34:11}}),

- doing good ({{Psalm 34:14|Psalm 34:14}}), and

- rejecting evil ({{Psalm 34:13|Psalm 34:13}}).
Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living ({{1 Peter 3:10-12|1 Peter 3:10–12}}).
Godly people choose their words carefully. Speaking evil and telling lies is unwise (see {{Psalm 10:7|Psalm 10:7}}; compare {{Psalm 17:1|17:1}}).
The way of peace leads to harmony and order, whereas evil destroys them (see {{Psalm 37:11|Psalm 37:11}}).

The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble ({{Psalm 34:15|Psalm 34:15}}, {{Psalm 34:17-20|17–20}}). However, God destroys the foolish ({{Psalm 34:16|Psalm 34:16}}, {{Psalm 34:21|21}}).

Those who are brokenhearted have a spirit of deep sorrow for sin and a strong dependence on the Lord. God accepts this humble spirit as a proper sacrifice ({{Psalm 51:17|Psalm 51:17}}). The wicked hate people who are brokenhearted ({{Psalm 109:16|Psalm 109:16}}). But the Lord heals them and restores them ({{Psalm 147:3|Psalm 147:3}}; see {{Isaiah 57:15|Isaiah 57:15}}; {{Isaiah 61:1|61:1}}).

The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalms 1:6}}; {{Psalm 34:15-16|34:15–16}}).

- Bones represent a person's whole self (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}). 

- *not one of them will be broken*: John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion ({{John 19:36|John 19:36}}).
In this lament, the Lord's troubled servant asks God to notice his situation and defend him.
The psalmist desires the Lord's salvation. The language may seem harsh, but it comes from a wish for justice and for the Lord to help the needy and oppressed.

- A *dark and slick* path suggests instability and sudden disaster under the Lord's judgment (see {{Psalm 69:23|Psalms 69:23}}; {{Psalm 73:18|73:18}}; {{Psalm 82:5|82:5}}; {{Psalm 107:10|107:10}}; {{Psalm 143:3|143:3}}). 

- The *angel of the LORD* is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.
Nothing in the universe can compare with the Lord (see {{Psalm 86:8|Psalms 86:8}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}, {{Psalm 89:8|8}}; {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}, {{Isaiah 40:25|25}}).
False witnesses want nothing but violence (see {{Psalm 11:4-6|Psalms 11:4–6}}; {{Psalm 54:3|54:3}}).
The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.
The psalmist's attackers *gnashed their teeth* to show their jealousy.
John applied this claim of innocence (see also {{Psalm 69:4|Psalm 69:4}}) to Jesus ({{John 15:25|John 15:25}}).

In this prayer for justice, the psalmist faces a crisis so great that only the Lord can resolve it. The psalmist chooses the right path and believes that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

God’s patience allows the wicked to continue in their evil ways. Because of this, their hearts grow harder and they find reasons to justify their behavior.
*Aha, aha!*: This Hebrew word (*he’akh*) expresses a feeling of joy.
The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.
*no fear of God*: Paul uses this phrase to describe how all people are morally corrupt ({{Romans 3:18|Romans 3:18}}).
Foolish people reject wisdom and goodness while they chase after evil.

This lament contrasts the foolish world made by the wicked with the wise world created and maintained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, while the Lord cares for all creation. He will step in to bring justice to his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will die.
God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.
As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.
All creatures live by God's grace ({{1 Timothy 4:10|1 Timothy 4:10}}).
God invites everyone to a feast in his house (compare {{Proverbs 9:1-6|Proverbs 9:1–6}}).
God's wisdom covers all of creation and protects those who follow him.
The psalmist is sure that the chaos caused by the wicked ({{Psalm 36:1-4|Psalm 36:1–4}}) will stop when they die.
*envy*: The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin ({{Psalm 73:3|Psalm 73:3}}; {{Proverbs 3:31|Proverbs 3:31}}; {{James 1:14-15|James 1:14–15}}; {{James 4:1-2|4:1–2}}).

The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust has five parts:

- Do not become irritated or jealous of those who do evil ({{Psalm 37:1-2|Psalm 37:1–2}}).

- Delight in the Lord ({{Psalm 37:3-4|Psalm 37:3–4}}).

- Submit to the Lord ({{Psalm 37:5-6|Psalm 37:5–6}}).

- Practice patience in hope ({{Psalm 37:7|Psalm 37:7}}).

- Avoid anger ({{Psalm 37:8-9|Psalm 37:8–9}}).

This psalm addresses the issues raised in {{Psalm 36:1-12|Psalm 36}}: 

- How should the godly react to evil? 

- When will the Lord bring justice? 

- Why does he allow the wicked to harm his creation? 

{{Psalm 37:1-40|Psalm 37}} provides clear answers that reduce the tensions of life ({{Psalm 37:1-9|Psalm 37:1–9}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}) and promise that the meek will have a future ({{Psalm 37:10-11|Psalm 37:10–11}}, {{Psalm 37:39-40|39–40}}). 

The contrast between the godly and the wicked highlights the uselessness of foolishness ({{Psalm 37:12-24|Psalm 37:12–24}}, {{Psalm 37:27-33|27–33}}). The psalmist's personal insights add a human element ({{Psalm 37:25-26|Psalm 37:25–26}}, {{Psalm 37:35-38|35–38}}). He encourages viewing the land's inheritance with a long-term perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the humble and godly who trust, hope, and follow him (see {{Psalm 37:9|Psalm 37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:11|11}}, {{Psalm 37:22|22}}, {{Psalm 37:29|29}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}; see also {{Isaiah 57:13|Isaiah 57:13}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}).

Human life is limited and does not last long (see {{Psalm 90:5-6|Psalms 90:5–6}}; {{Psalm 92:7|92:7}}; {{Psalm 102:4|102:4}}, {{Psalm 102:11|11}}; {{Psalm 103:15|103:15}}; {{Psalm 129:6|129:6}}; {{Isaiah 40:7-8|Isaiah 40:7–8}}).
Doing good means developing a commitment to wisdom (see {{Psalm 34:14|Psalm 34:14}}; {{Proverbs 3:5-7|Proverbs 3:5–7}}).
Trusting in the Lord helps reduce irritability and envy ({{Psalm 37:1|Psalm 37:1}}).
To delight in the Lord means to follow the Lord’s ways and find joy in him.
Justice occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue ({{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}; {{Isaiah 51:5-6|51:5–6}}; {{Isaiah 58:8|58:8}}, {{Isaiah 58:10-11|10–11}}).
*Be still*: We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.

Irritability and anger can quickly damage a person’s character.

When someone becomes easily upset or angry, it affects the way that person thinks and acts. Over time, this can weaken good habits and harm relationships.

Learning patience and self-control helps protect and strengthen character.
The wicked will not possess the land; those who trust in the Lord will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.

The Lord creates peace ({{Psalm 85:10|Psalm 85:10}})—he brings peace to a chaotic world ({{Psalm 29:11|Psalm 29:11}}; {{Psalm 37:11|37:11}}; {{Psalm 85:8|85:8}}; {{Psalm 147:14|147:14}}). His wisdom leads the meek to peace ({{Psalm 119:165|Psalm 119:165}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}).

The wicked show their envy by gnashing their teeth (an expression of anger and hostility). They make plans to harm the godly. But the Lord laughs at them because he knows they will fail ({{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}).
The wicked seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.
The wicked prepare weapons, but those weapons will turn against them (compare {{Psalm 7:12-13|Psalm 7:12–13}}).
It is better to be wise with little money than to be rich and evil ({{Proverbs 15:16|Proverbs 15:16}}; {{Proverbs 16:8|16:8}}, {{Proverbs 16:19|19}}; {{Proverbs 17:1|17:1}}; {{Proverbs 28:6|28:6}}).
The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.
*Smoke* represents the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 68:2|Psalm 68:2}}; {{Psalm 102:3|102:3}}).

- To borrow and never repay shows a dishonest way of life.

- Generous givers freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see {{Psalm 111:5|Psalm 111:5}}; {{Psalm 112:5|112:5}}).
The honesty and strength of a godly person's life come from the Lord (see {{Proverbs 4:12|Proverbs 4:12}}; {{Proverbs 14:15|14:15}}; {{Proverbs 16:9|16:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:24|20:24}}).
The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

The godly are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of the land as their inheritance. The wicked might try to ambush the godly, but they will not succeed.
The righteous base their counsel on the Lord’s wisdom.
*The law of his God is in his heart*: The godly accept God’s instruction and live by it (see {{Psalm 119:11|Psalm 119:11}}; {{Jeremiah 24:7|Jeremiah 24:7}}; {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|31:31–34}}).
The wicked might appear to be flourishing like a tree (compare {{Psalm 52:8|Psalm 52:8}}; {{Psalm 92:12-13|92:12–13}}), but they eventually die and are forgotten ({{Psalm 37:2|Psalm 37:2}}).
The Lord provides strength for his people.
The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in {{Psalm 70:1|70:1}}).
The psalmist’s sins brought the Lord’s anger and rage. Because of this, the Lord disciplined and rebuked him, like arrows and blows striking him. As a result, his whole body is sick.
These verses introduce the psalmist's confession ({{Psalm 38:18|Psalm 38:18}}) and describe his miserable state.
This psalm is a lament and a prayer for healing. The psalmist's suffering is linked to his unconfessed sin. He admits his sin and trusts the Lord with his situation.

Sin can lead to sickness and even death ({{1 Corinthians 11:30|1 Corinthians 11:30}}). The psalmist may have felt physically ill, or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional distress. He understood it came from God and endangered his life (see {{Psalm 32:3|Psalms 32:3}}; {{Psalm 39:10|39:10}}).
The psalmist feels burdened because of sin (see {{Psalm 40:12|Psalms 40:12}}; {{Psalm 41:4|41:4}}; compare {{Genesis 4:13|Genesis 4:13}}).
The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.
The psalmist wants to reconnect with God but feels distant. He feels lost and alone as his friends leave him.
The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see {{Isaiah 53:7|Isaiah 53:7}}).
The Lord alone will resolve the conflict ({{Psalm 9:18|Psalms 9:18}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}; {{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}).
The psalmist, unable to bear his suffering and close to collapse (compare {{Psalm 15:5|Psalm 15:5}}), admits his sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).
The psalmist feels more pain because his enemies hate him for no reason.

In the Psalms, people often ask the Lord to act quickly in times of great need ({{Psalm 22:19|Psalms 22:19}}; {{Psalm 31:2|31:2}}; {{Psalm 40:13|40:13}}; {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 70:1|70:1}}; {{Psalm 71:12|71:12}}; {{Psalm 79:8|79:8}}; {{Psalm 102:2|102:2}}; {{Psalm 141:1|141:1}}; {{Psalm 143:7|143:7}}). However, wisdom and experience show that God's people often need to wait for him to act ({{Psalm 27:14|Psalms 27:14}}; {{Psalm 37:7|37:7}}; {{Isaiah 8:17|Isaiah 8:17}}; {{Isaiah 40:31|40:31}}).
Jeduthun was a Levitical singer who was appointed by David, along with Asaph ({{1 Chronicles 9:16|1 Chronicles 9:16}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:38|16:38}}; {{1 Chronicles 25:1|25:1}}).
Suffering in silence makes the psalmist's anguish, pain, and inner distress worse.
This prayer for rescue shows the psalmist's discouragement, which comes from not fully understanding his situation.

*how fleeting my life is*: This perspective comes out of suffering (see {{Psalm 78:39|Psalms 78:39}}; {{Psalm 89:47-48|89:47–48}}; {{Psalm 90:3-10|90:3–10}}). The human lifetime is but a moment to God ({{Psalm 90:4|Psalm 90:4}}), as temporary as a breath (see {{Psalm 39:11|Psalms 39:11}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}).

Due to his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and short (see {{Job 7:7-10|Job 7:7–10}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}). He had expected only a wicked life to be like that (see {{Psalm 37:2|Psalms 37:2}}, {{Psalm 37:20|20}}; {{Psalm 103:15-16|103:15–16}}), but now it seems irrelevant whether a person is godly or not.
The idea that rebellion leads to suffering is a common theme in {{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalms 32}}, {{Psalm 38:1-41:13|38–41}}.
The psalmist links suffering with God’s discipline, assuming that it is punishment for his sin.

The Lord uses discipline to correct his children ({{Psalm 38:1|Psalms 38:1}}, {{Psalm 38:3|3}}, {{Psalm 38:7|7}}; {{Psalm 40:12|40:12}}; see {{Proverbs 3:11-12|Proverbs 3:11–12}}; {{Hebrews 12:5-6|Hebrews 12:5–6}}).
A *foreigner* could not own land (see {{Leviticus 25:23|Leviticus 25:23}}). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan ({{Psalm 105:23|Psalm 105:23}}).
Earlier, the psalmist asked God to stay close to him ({{Psalm 38:21-22|Psalm 8:21–22}}). Now, he wants God to leave him alone. This is similar to how Job felt ({{Job 7:17-19|Job 7:17–19}}).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for rescue and affirms that people can trust God.

This psalm has a thanksgiving song ({{Psalm 40:1-10|Psalm 40:1–10}}) and a lament ({{Psalm 40:11-17|40:11–17}}). The thanksgiving song explains why the psalmist is thankful ({{Psalm 40:1-5|Psalm 40:1–5}}), shows a promise to stay committed ({{Psalm 40:6-8|40:6–8}}), and shares a public testimony about God's character ({{Psalm 40:7-10|40:7–10}}). The lament talks about the psalmist's troubles due to his sins ({{Psalm 40:11-12|Psalm 40:11–12}}) and includes two prayers asking for justice ({{Psalm 40:13-15|40:13–15}}, {{Psalm 40:17|17}}).

- The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person giving an offering more than the offering itself. 

- *my ears You have opened*: The Greek text reads *You have given me a body.* In {{Hebrews 10:5-7|Hebrews 10:5–7}}, the writer quotes from the Greek version of {{Psalm 40:6-8|Psalm 40:6–8}}. He presents these words as something Jesus said when he left heaven and came into the world.
*it is written about me in the scroll*: Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in {{Deuteronomy 17:14-15|Deuteronomy 17:14–15}}.
The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.

- The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own sins and prays for rescue.

- This passage is almost the same as {{Psalm 70:1-5|Psalm 70}}.

The poor who suffer hardship have special protection under God's law ({{Leviticus 14:21|Leviticus 14:21}}; {{Leviticus 19:10|19:10}}). They receive God's justice and guidance ({{Psalm 72:13|Psalms 72:13}}; {{Psalm 82:3-4|82:3–4}}). The word translated as *poor* often means the godly ({{Psalm 113:7|Psalm 113:7}}; see {{Zephaniah 3:12|Zephaniah 3:12}}).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist: 

- asks for healing ({{Psalm 41:4|Psalm 41:4}}, {{Psalm 41:10|10}}),

- laments his distress ({{Psalm 41:5-9|Psalm 41:5–9}}), and

- expresses confidence in the Lord's blessing ({{Psalm 41:1-3|Psalm 41:1–3}}, {{Psalm 41:11-12|11–12}}).
*on his bed of illness*: This illness might be physical or spiritual (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; {{Psalm 38:1-22|Psalm 38}}).

The psalmist applies the blessing to himself ({{Psalm 41:12|Psalm 41:12}}). He has helped the poor ({{Psalm 41:1|Psalm 41:1}}), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. In his pain, he asks for healing and admits his sin. Only the Lord can provide the restoration that brings true joy ({{Psalm 30:2|Psalm 30:2}}; {{Psalm 107:20-21|107:20–21}}).
*When will he die*: The psalmist's enemies see his suffering as a judgment from God (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).
The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.

*the one who shared my bread*: Eating together was a sign of unity ({{Acts 2:42|Acts 2:42}}). Refusing to eat with someone was a sign of hostility ({{1 Corinthians 5:11|1 Corinthians 5:11}}). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal ({{John 13:1|John 13:1}}, {{John 13:18|18}}).
The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.
This doxology (song of praise) ends Book One ({{Psalm 1:1-41:13|Psalms 1–41}}). Compare with {{Psalm 106:48|Psalm 106:48}}.

The sons of Korah were members of a Levitical choir. They were chosen by David to serve as singers in the temple (see {{1 Chronicles 6:22-38|1 Chronicles 6:22–38}}; {{1 Chronicles 9:19-34|9:19–34}}; {{2 Chronicles 20:19|2 Chronicles 20:19}}). Their ancestor Korah was the rebel who opposed Moses and was swallowed by the earth ({{Exodus 6:24|Exodus 6:24}}; {{Numbers 16:1-50|Numbers 16}}).

- The psalmist's deep desire for God arises from being far away from the temple as he remembers the past. 

- The verb translated as "longs" appears only here and in {{Joel 1:20|Joel 1:20}} (meaning "cry out"). In both instances, it describes extreme thirst in a dry desert (see {{Psalm 63:1|Psalms 63:1}}; {{Psalm 143:6|143:6}}; see also {{Psalm 84:2|84:2}}).

These psalms, like {{Psalm 9:1-20|Psalms 9}} and {{Psalm 10:1-18|10}}, form a unit with a lament and a bittersweet refrain of hope ({{Psalm 42:5|Psalm 42:5}}, {{Psalm 42:11|11}}; {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}). Many Hebrew manuscripts combine these two psalms into one. 

The historical context is unclear; these psalms might represent God's people in exile, expressing loyalty to God while he punishes them for their ongoing disobedience. 

The psalmist longs for the fellowship with God he had in Jerusalem ({{Psalm 42:4|Psalm 42:4}}); his memories only deepen his discouragement. As the psalmist cries out to God, he remembers God's love and faithfulness ({{Psalm 42:8|Psalm 42:8}}), which leads him to ask for vindication ({{Psalm 43:1-4|43:1–4}}).

- Crying so much that tears become food shows deep sadness ({{Psalm 80:5|Psalms 80:5}}; {{Psalm 102:9|102:9}}; see {{Psalm 6:6|6:6}}; {{Psalm 56:8|56:8}}; {{Psalm 119:136|119:136}}; {{Psalm 126:5|126:5}}). 

- The wicked try to impose their timing on God and deny his power to intervene.
The psalmist remembers leading a large procession as part of the Levitical choir, possibly during the important holy days.
The psalmist feels sad, but he can still function. He remembers that the living God is his Savior. This verse appears again in {{Psalm 42:11|Psalms 42:11}} and {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}.
The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.

- Mount Hermon is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The source of the Jordan is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon.

- Mount Mizar might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.
The raging seas, waves, and surging tides bring to mind God's anger (see {{Psalm 88:7|Psalm 88:7}}).
The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life focused on God includes joyful songs and prayers for justice and vindication ({{Psalm 42:9-10|Psalm 42:9–10}}; {{Psalm 43:1-4|43:1–4}}).
The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.
The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.

*rejected me*: Other psalms also ask if God has rejected his people ({{Psalm 44:9|Psalm 44:9}}, {{Psalm 44:23|23}}; {{Psalm 60:1|60:1}}, {{Psalm 60:10|10}}; {{Psalm 74:1|74:1}}; {{Psalm 77:7|77:7}}; {{Psalm 88:14|88:14}}; {{Psalm 89:38|89:38}}; {{Psalm 108:11|108:11}}).

- This prayer for God's redemption sees light and truth as guides (see {{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalms 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 27:1|27:1}}; {{Psalm 85:10-13|85:10–13}}; {{Psalm 89:14-18|89:14–18}}; see also {{Psalm 119:105|119:105}}; {{John 3:19|John 3:19}}; {{Ephesians 5:8|Ephesians 5:8}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:5-7|1 Thessalonians 5:5–7}}). 

- The temple on the mountain in Jerusalem symbolized God's holy presence among his people ({{Psalm 15:1|Psalms 15:1}}; {{Psalm 43:3|43:3}}; {{Psalm 99:5|99:5}}, {{Psalm 99:9|9}}; {{Psalm 132:7|132:7}}).
This verse is repeated in {{Psalm 42:5|Psalm 42:5}} and {{Psalm 42:11|11}}.

*We have heard … the work You did*: The story of redemption includes God's favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see {{Psalm 78:1-4|Psalm 78:1–4}}; see also {{Psalm 105:1-106:48|Psalms 105–106}}).

This national lament after a defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms. It reflects on an unspecified moment in Israel's history and calls on God for salvation. The people: 

- recite God's past acts of rescue ({{Psalm 44:1-3|Psalm 44:1–3}}),

- recognize God's power to save ({{Psalm 44:4-8|Psalm 44:4–8}}),

- describe their humiliation in exile ({{Psalm 44:9-16|Psalm 44:9–16}}),

- claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation ({{Psalm 44:17-22|Psalm 44:17–22}}), and

- cry for vindication ({{Psalm 44:23-26|Psalm 44:23–26}}).
God drove out the pagan nations during the conquests recorded in Joshua.

Though the Israelites used swords and other weapons ({{Psalm 44:6|Psalm 44:6}}), they would have lost their battles without the light of the Lord’s favor (see {{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalms 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 27:1|27:1}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}).
God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.
The people have experienced defeat ({{Psalm 44:9-12|Psalm 44:9–12}}), so they understand suffering and shame ({{Psalm 44:13-16|44:13–16}}).
*scattered us among the nations*: This likely refers to the exile (see {{Psalm 51:18-19|Psalms 51:18–19}}; {{Psalm 89:38-51|89:38–51}}; {{Psalm 106:40-47|106:40–47}}; {{Psalm 137:1-9|137}}).
Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love ({{Romans 8:36|Romans 8:36}}).
*Wake up*: Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis ({{Psalm 35:23|Psalms 35:23}}; {{Psalm 44:23|44:23}}; {{Psalm 73:20|73:20}}; {{Psalm 80:2|80:2}}; {{Mark 4:38|Mark 4:38}}).
In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.
*To the tune of "The Lilies"* is no longer known (see also {{Psalm 69:1-36|Psalm 69}}).

This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).

This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his enduring legacy ({{Psalm 45:16|Psalm 45:16}}). The Lord’s blessing and the charge to reflect God’s attributes are symbolized by his handsome appearance and gracious speech.
Glory and majesty belong to the Lord ({{Psalm 96:6|Psalms 96:6}}; {{Psalm 111:3|111:3}}).
The psalmist describes the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.

As God's representative of truth, humility, and justice (see {{Psalm 72:1-2|Psalm 72:1–2}}, {{Psalm 72:4|4}}, {{Psalm 72:7|7}}), the king can perform impressive deeds ({{Psalm 65:5|65:5}}; {{Psalm 96:4|96:4}}).
Justice characterizes God’s rule, as it should characterize the king’s administration.

- The king is like a god among humans. God anointed him, gave him a powerful throne, and he delivers justice as he rules eternally. 

- The writer of Hebrews uses {{Psalm 45:6-7|Psalm 45:6–7}} to describe Jesus, arguing that the Son is greater than the angels ({{Hebrews 1:8-9|Hebrews 1:8–9}}).

- Fine spices mixed with oil create unique perfumes. 

- The king's palaces had wood panels with ivory inlays (see {{Psalm 6:4|Psalm 6:4}}; {{Amos 3:15|Amos 3:15}}).
Royal marriages often confirmed diplomatic alliances between kings, and the women became part of the royal harem (see {{1 Kings 11:1-3|1 Kings 11:1–3}}).

The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.
*The Daughter of Tyre*: Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The city's most noble woman brings a wedding gift to the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.
*According to Alamoth* (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chronicles 15:20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.
Even during natural disasters, the citizens of Zion show no fear.

This psalm of Zion celebrates God's special presence in Jerusalem (see also {{Psalm 48:1-14|Psalms 48}}, {{Psalm 76:1-12|76}}, {{Psalm 87:1-7|87}}, {{Psalm 122:1-9|122}}). It encourages trust in the Lord because the people of Zion have his protection.

This river provides life, renewal, and healing like the streams flowing through Eden ({{Psalm 36:8-9|Psalm 36:8–9}}; see {{Genesis 2:10|Genesis 2:10}}; {{Ezekiel 47:1-23|Ezekiel 47}}; {{Revelation 22:2|Revelation 22:2}}).

The strong city, where God lives, protects its people. They enjoy the river flowing within the city. This river is calm, unlike the turbulent waters (representing the powers of the nations) outside the city.
*when morning dawns*: In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day. Even in dangerous times, the Lord will protect the place where his name is.

People and nations live in chaos. They take every chance to benefit themselves ({{Psalm 83:2|Psalm 83:2}}), stay busy with many things ({{Psalm 39:6|39:6}}), and fill the world with noise. They are unstable and can fall apart, unlike the city of God (compare {{Psalm 15:5|Psalm 15:5}}). But when the godly are troubled, they cry out to God for help ({{Psalm 42:5|Psalm 42:5}}, {{Psalm 42:11|11}}; {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}; {{Psalm 55:17|55:17}}).

- This refrain reminds us who the God of Zion is. 

- *with us*: Hebrew *'immanu,* part of the name Immanuel, meaning “God with us” ({{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}; {{Isaiah 8:8|8:8}}; {{Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23}}).

Israel witnessed the Lord's amazing works in the wilderness ({{Psalm 107:24|Psalms 107:24}}; {{Psalm 111:2|111:2}}), but the wicked, who do not care about them ({{Psalm 28:5|28:5}}), end up desolate ({{Psalm 73:19|73:19}}).
This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.

- A message directly from the Lord confirms the truth of the psalmist’s vision (see also {{Psalm 12:5-6|Psalms 12:5–6}}; {{Psalm 32:8|32:8}}). 

- *know that I am God*: The Lord will fulfill his promises ({{Isaiah 45:3|Isaiah 45:3}}; {{Isaiah 49:23|49:23}}; {{Isaiah 60:16|60:16}}). 

- God will be honored ({{Psalm 47:1-9|Psalm 47}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}); he will judge the nations and save his people (see {{Psalm 57:11|Psalms 57:11}}; {{Psalm 89:13|89:13}}; {{Psalm 108:5-6|108:5–6}}; {{Psalm 118:16|118:16}}).
People clap their hands in praise and recognition of wonderful deeds ({{Psalm 47:3-4|Psalm 47:3–4}}; see {{Psalm 98:8|98:8}}; {{Isaiah 55:12|Isaiah 55:12}}; compare {{Nahum 3:19|Nahum 3:19}}).
As the ruler of all nations, God deserves praise.

This psalm praises God's rule as king over the entire earth. It describes God's victory with Israel and other nations. Both Israel ({{Psalm 47:3-4|Psalm 47:3–4}}) and the nations ({{Psalm 47:9|47:9}}) are part of God's kingdom.
The Lord gave Israel victory, especially under David (see {{Psalm 18:40-50|Psalm 18:40–50}}). God's powerful acts of redemption show his love for Israel.

- *pride of Jacob*: Jacob was the father of all Israelites ({{Genesis 32:28|Genesis 32:28}}). The name *Jacob* often represents the nation of Israel. 

- God loves and commits himself to Jacob (see {{Psalm 78:68|Psalms 78:68}}; {{Psalm 127:2|127:2}}; see {{Romans 11:28|Romans 11:28}}).

*horn*: Or *rams’ horns* (see {{Psalm 81:3|Psalm 81:3}}). People sometimes blew rams’ horns during celebrations ({{Psalm 98:5-6|Psalm 98:5–6}}; {{2 Kings 11:14|2 Kings 11:14}}; {{1 Chronicles 15:28|1 Chronicles 15:28}}).
The psalmist describes the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a description of his descent, see {{Psalm 18:9-16|Psalm 18:9–16}}.
People from all over the world (see {{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}) will worship God.

This song of Zion (see also {{Psalm 46:1-11|Psalms 46}}, {{Psalm 76:1-12|76}}, {{Psalm 87:1-7|87}}, {{Psalm 122:1-9|122}}) clearly describes Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King, where the godly find protection ({{Psalm 48:1-3|48:1–3}}). God rules from Zion with faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, inspiring his people with confidence and joy ({{Psalm 48:9-11|Psalm 48:9–11}}). They dedicate themselves to witnessing Zion's glory so they can share it with the next generation ({{Psalm 48:8|Psalm 48:8}}, {{Psalm 48:12-14|12–14}}).
God lives in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see {{Psalm 46:5|Psalm 46:5}}).

The ships of Tarshish were built for long voyages and represent human achievement (see also {{2 Chronicles 9:21|2 Chronicles 9:21}}; {{Isaiah 2:16|Isaiah 2:16}}). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in {{1 Kings 22:48|1 Kings 22:48}}.
The psalmist happily celebrates the Lord's presence with the community, thinking about God's faithful, righteous, and just rule.
*towers … ramparts … citadel*: These structures show Zion's strength.

No one is like God ({{Psalm 35:10|Psalms 35:10}}; {{Psalm 71:19|71:19}}; {{Psalm 86:8|86:8}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}, {{Psalm 89:8|8}}; {{Psalm 113:5|113:5}}; see {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}, {{Isaiah 40:25|25}}). He is the shepherd King ({{Psalm 95:7|Psalm 95:7}}) who will guide (see {{Psalm 5:8|5:8}}; {{Psalm 23:2|23:2}}) the sheep of his flock ({{Psalm 77:20|77:20}}).
Anyone who will listen can gain wisdom ({{Proverbs 1:5|Proverbs 1:5}}, {{Proverbs 1:8|8}}, {{Proverbs 1:33|33}}).
The wisdom teacher invites everyone to come and learn wisdom. He promises to teach them through a proverb and a riddle.

In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns about enemies who live richly and care only for themselves ({{Psalm 49:5-9|Psalm 49:5–9}}). They cannot save anyone, not even themselves, from death or being forgotten ({{Psalm 49:10-12|Psalm 49:10–12}}). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter ({{Psalm 49:14-20|Psalm 49:14–20}}).
The teacher used proverbs and riddles to teach wisdom (see {{Proverbs 1:5-6|Proverbs 1:5–6}}).
If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
The teacher uses irony to teach wisdom. Everyone dies, and even those who give their names to lands or estates will be forgotten.
The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
The wicked might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.
The whole universe must pay attention when God approaches to bring justice into the world.
God appears as judge. He reminds both the godly and the ungodly that sacrifices and reciting the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.

The Lord is coming to bring justice. This hope encourages his faithful people. However, those who have been unfaithful will not receive blessings when the heavens and earth testify against them (see {{Deuteronomy 30:19|Deuteronomy 30:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:28|31:28}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:1|32:1}}; {{Isaiah 1:2|Isaiah 1:2}}). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 22:31|22:31}}; {{Psalm 33:5|33:5}}; {{Psalm 40:9|40:9}}; {{Psalm 50:6|50:6}}; {{Psalm 71:16|71:16}}; {{Psalm 97:6|97:6}}).
The psalmist warns against valuing sacrificial rituals more than having the right attitude in your heart.
Unlike pagan gods, God does not need food. Instead, he wants his people to serve him with sincere hearts ({{Psalm 50:14-15|Psalm 50:14–15}}).
*the cattle on a thousand hills*: God has no needs because he owns everything.

- Thankfulness involves recognizing and appreciating God's blessings beyond personal gain (see {{Psalm 51:15-17|Psalms 51:15–17}}; {{Psalm 54:6|54:6}}). 

- True sacrifice means dedicating oneself to honor God ({{Psalm 50:23|Psalm 50:23}}; {{Romans 12:1-2|Romans 12:1–2}}).
God’s response to his people’s cry is to rescue them.
This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
*My instruction … My words*: The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (compare {{Matthew 23:23-24|Matthew 23:23–24}}).
Because he is patient, God remained silent.
God will destroy the wicked like a lion tearing its prey ({{Isaiah 5:29|Isaiah 5:29}}; {{Isaiah 31:4|31:4}}; {{Ezekiel 19:3|Ezekiel 19:3}}; compare {{Psalm 7:2|Psalms 7:2}}; {{Psalm 22:13|22:13}}).
The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.

A prayer for God's mercy and kindness is a type of lament. Sometimes, the psalmist asks for mercy because he recognizes his own weakness and sin (see also {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; {{Psalm 9:13|9:13}}; {{Psalm 25:16|25:16}}; {{Psalm 31:9|31:9}}; {{Psalm 41:4|41:4}}, {{Psalm 41:10|10}}). Other times, the plea comes from the psalmist's dedication to the Lord (see {{Psalm 26:11|Psalm 26:11}}; {{Psalm 27:7|27:7}}; {{Psalm 119:29|119:29}}, {{Psalm 119:58|58}}, {{Psalm 119:132|132}}). In every situation, God's mercy leads to inner renewal.
The person who regrets their wrongdoing cannot offer anything to God. They need God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing to experience renewal and restoration.

Psalm 51 is a poem about admitting sin. David’s sins against Bathsheba and Uriah show how serious and hurtful sin is.

Sins committed against other people are also committed against God. This is because God made everyone and he has tender and faithful love for them. The Israelites understood that sin made them unclean. It kept them from being in God’s presence. This was like being sent away from God and having the Holy Spirit taken from them.

God provided several ways for the Israelites to be made clean and pure. One way was to dip a hyssop plant into special water. Then the water would be sprinkled on someone to wash them (Numbers 19). Another way was to make sin offerings or burnt offerings.

Being washed and making sacrifices were important parts of how the Israelites worshipped God. But they only showed what happened on the outside of a person’s body. They didn’t show what happened inside the person’s heart. In their heart is where people can feel truly sorry for their sin.

God cares deeply about people’s hearts. When people sin, they must make themselves humble before God. They must be completely honest and recognise all that they have done wrong. This is what it means to have a broken spirit. The spirit is the spiritual part of a person. People offer their broken spirit to God. They ask him to have mercy and to forgive them.

Only God can take away a person’s guilt. He can make a person able to say no to sin. He can make people able to be faithful to him.

This heartfelt prayer for restoration seeks God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. With a broken spirit, the psalmist admits his sin and takes responsibility ({{Psalm 51:3-6|Psalm 51:3–6}}). He then asks God to remove his guilt and renew him internally ({{Psalm 51:7-12|Psalm 51:7–12}}). The psalmist commits again to living wisely and joyfully while serving God and others ({{Psalm 51:13-17|Psalm 51:13–17}}).
See {{2 Samuel 11:1-27|2 Samuel 11:1–27}}. The psalm does not directly mention this event.

These psalms of David share a common theme. They reflect on the experience of evil. In {{Psalm 51:1-19|Psalm 51}}, the psalmist admits his wrongdoing and asks for God's forgiveness. {{Psalm 52:1-64:10|Psalms 52–64}} express sorrow over specific evils David faced. A song of praise ({{Psalm 65:1-13|Psalm 65}}) brings David's laments to an end.

*Wash me … cleanse me*: The psalmist asks for cleansing and freedom from the guilt of his sin ({{Psalm 51:7|Psalm 51:7}}; see {{Psalm 26:6|26:6}}; {{Isaiah 1:16|Isaiah 1:16}}, {{Isaiah 1:18|18}}; {{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}).
The psalmist accepts the results of his sin against God. He understands that he has no goodness without God's renewal.

*Against You, You only*: This is an exaggeration. The psalmist knows he also sinned against people ({{2 Samuel 11:2-4|2 Samuel 11:2–4}}, {{2 Samuel 11:15-17|15–17}}), but his sin against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God gives (see {{Romans 3:4|Romans 3:4}}).
*I was brought forth in iniquity*: The psalmist is not making excuses but is admitting how deep his sinfulness is. From the time we are conceived, we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.

*Purify me with hyssop* (literally *Purify me with the hyssop branch*; see {{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Leviticus 14:4|Leviticus 14:4}}; {{John 19:29|John 19:29}}; {{Hebrews 9:19|Hebrews 9:19}}): The psalmist relies on God to cleanse and renew him (see {{Isaiah 1:18|Isaiah 1:18}}).

- Regaining joy is a gracious gift from God. 

- *You have crushed*: The psalmist feels completely broken ({{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; compare {{Psalm 34:20|34:20}}).
A loyal spirit produces inner strength. It helps a person remain faithful and continue even during difficulty.
God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
*Your Holy Spirit*: Only the Holy Spirit can change a person's will to make it "right" ({{Psalm 51:10|Psalm 51:10}}) and "willing" to obey ({{Psalm 51:12|51:12}}).
As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to teach others.

*bloodguilt*: This expression refers to any injustice, not only killing someone ({{Psalm 9:12|Psalm 9:12}}; {{Psalm 58:10|58:10}}; see {{2 Samuel 11:14-26|2 Samuel 11:14–26}}; compare {{Isaiah 1:15-17|Isaiah 1:15–17}}).

*build up the walls of Jerusalem*: These verses were likely added as a prayer for national restoration after the exile (see {{Psalm 42:1-43:5|Psalms 42–43}}). The entire community in exile shared the feelings expressed in this psalm.

Sacrifices made with the right intentions come from a heart that is right with God and others (see {{Psalm 15:2-5|Psalms 15:2–5}}; {{Psalm 24:3-6|24:3–6}}; {{Psalm 50:14|50:14}}; {{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}).
The accuser, Doeg the Edomite, is an example of a person who chose to do evil.

Liars deceive themselves by thinking they can be heroes with their words. They see themselves as innocent, even though they love evil and cause harm. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and lies ({{Psalm 31:18|Psalms 31:18}}; {{Psalm 34:13|34:13}}; {{Psalm 59:7|59:7}}, {{Psalm 59:12|12}}; {{Psalm 120:2-3|120:2–3}}; {{Psalm 140:3|140:3}}, {{Psalm 140:9|9}}) create chaos, isolation, and destruction ({{James 3:5|James 3:5}}). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers ({{Psalm 55:21|Psalms 55:21}}; {{Psalm 57:4|57:4}}; {{Psalm 64:3|64:3}}), the fangs of a snake ({{Psalm 140:3|140:3}}), or a razor.

Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words ({{Psalm 52:1-4|Psalm 52:1–4}}), but their downfall comes suddenly ({{Psalm 52:5-7|52:5–7}}). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord ({{Psalm 52:8-9|Psalm 52:8–9}}) and find security in their future with him.
Dishonest speech can change a person's character.
God will strike the wicked down like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel ({{Exodus 34:13|Exodus 34:13}}; {{Leviticus 11:35|Leviticus 11:35}}; {{2 Kings 10:27|2 Kings 10:27}}).
God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
*see and fear*: In Hebrew, these words sound almost alike.

- The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord.

- An olive tree can live a long time with proper care ({{Psalm 1:3|Psalms 1:3}}; {{Psalm 128:3|128:3}}). The psalmist wants to be near the Lord, who is his Savior and the source of his blessings ({{Psalm 18:6|Psalms 18:6}}; {{Psalm 23:6|23:6}}).
Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage to describe the moral corruption of all people ({{Romans 3:10-12|Romans 3:10–12}}).
This psalm is similar to {{Psalm 14:1-7|Psalm 14}}, with differences only in verse 5.

*scattered the bones*: Israel's enemies would face a shameful defeat and would not have the peaceful rest of a proper burial (compare {{Psalm 141:7|Psalm 141:7}}; {{2 Kings 9:10|2 Kings 9:10}}; {{Jeremiah 8:1-2|Jeremiah 8:1–2}}; {{Ezekiel 6:5|Ezekiel 6:5}}).
The Ziphites intended to use violence.

This personal lament was caused by violent and godless people ({{Psalm 54:3|Psalm 54:3}}). The psalmist prays to God and focuses on God's help ({{Psalm 54:4|54:4}}). He asks God to save him from evil and judge his enemies ({{Psalm 54:5|Psalm 54:5}}, {{Psalm 54:7|7}}).

- The strangers were excluded from the covenant community (see {{Psalm 109:11|Psalm 109:11}}; {{Proverbs 5:10|Proverbs 5:10}}). 

- Proud and violent people do not respect God or others (see {{Psalm 35:11|Psalms 35:11}}, {{Psalm 35:25|25}}; {{Psalm 86:14|86:14}}; {{Proverbs 11:16|Proverbs 11:16}}).
A voluntary offering is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see {{Psalm 50:14-15|Psalm 50:14–15}}, {{Psalm 50:23|23}}).
In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from sorrow to thanksgiving.
The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.

The psalmist faces enemies led by a former friend ({{Psalm 55:12-14|Psalm 55:12–14}}). This causes him great distress. He prays to the Lord and trusts him for justice ({{Psalm 55:22-23|Psalm 55:22–23}}). 

Jesus went through similar pain when Judas, his friend, betrayed him. He also experienced the psalmist’s prayer being answered: 

- by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their punishment ({{Isaiah 53:7-9|Isaiah 53:7–9}}), and

- by trusting the Father, who saved ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}) and rewarded him ({{Isaiah 53:10-12|Isaiah 53:10–12}}).
In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
The psalmist's enemy used to be a friend. Remembering their close relationship causes him pain (see {{Psalm 31:11|Psalm 31:11}}).
God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
The psalmist commits all his cares to the Lord.
To die young means missing out on God's full blessings (compare {{Proverbs 3:2|Proverbs 3:2}}, {{Proverbs 3:16|16}}).

- *A Miktam*: This may be a literary or musical term.

- David was *seized* by *Philistines* concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish ({{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}).
In this lament, the psalmist first asks for help and then expresses confidence in God. This pattern occurs two times ({{Psalm 56:1-4|Psalm 56:1–4}}, {{Psalm 56:5-13|5–13}}).
*man*: Or *mere flesh,* in contrast to God, who is immortal and much more powerful (see {{Isaiah 2:22|Isaiah 2:22}}).
The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to end.
The psalmist uses wordplay with two similar Hebrew words: *wanderings* (*nod*) and *bottle* (*no’d*).

*man* (Hebrew *’adam*): The psalm also uses two other words for man: 

- *’enosh* (meaning “people,” {{Psalm 56:1|Psalm 56:1}}) and

- *basar* (meaning “mere mortals,” {{Psalm 56:4|Psalm 56:4}}).

All these words point to the short and limited nature of human life.
The light of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of death (see {{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalms 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 27:1|27:1}}).
*shadow of Your wings*: Like a bird protects its young, God protects those who trust in him (see {{Psalm 17:8|Psalm 17:8}}).

The psalmist asks for mercy and protection, then expresses trust and confidence in the Lord ({{Psalm 57:1-4|Psalm 57:1–4}}). When the wicked fall into their own traps ({{Psalm 57:6|Psalm 57:6}}), the psalmist will praise the Lord ({{Psalm 57:7-10|57:7–10}}).

- *God Most High* (Hebrew *Elohim-Elyon*) is a common title for God. He is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see {{Psalm 91:1|Psalms 91:1}}; {{Psalm 97:9|97:9}}; {{Genesis 14:18-22|Genesis 14:18–22}}). 

- *who fulfills His purpose for me*: Or *who will end my [trouble]*, or *who deals kindly with me*.

These verses are a prayer for rescue from strong enemies. The metaphor of fierce lions describes human foes. The psalmist feels unable to escape them without God's help (see also {{Psalm 35:11-21|Psalms 35:11–21}}; {{Psalm 124:6|124:6}}).

- This verse appears again in {{Psalm 57:11|Psalm 57:11}} and {{Psalm 108:5|108:5}}. 

- God's glory, which is his visible presence that keeps out all evil ({{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}), will fill the entire creation ({{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}}).
The psalmist is sure that God will stop the night of evil (compare {{Psalm 56:13|Psalm 56:13}}).
This section is repeated with a few changes in {{Psalm 108:1-5|Psalm 108:1–5}}.
God's glory reaches the entire universe, and people will praise his constant love and faithfulness.

*rulers* (or *gods*): People used this term for high officials and administrators of justice ({{Psalm 82:1|Psalm 82:1}}, {{Psalm 82:6|6}}). In other contexts, it might refer to angelic creatures ({{Psalm 89:7|Psalm 89:7}}) or the gods of other nations ({{Psalm 82:1|82:1}}; {{Daniel 11:36|Daniel 11:36}}).
The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.

All humans are born with a tendency to sin (see {{Psalm 51:5|Psalm 51:5}}). However, the wicked follow their sinful desires, while the godly struggle against them ({{Romans 7:19-23|Romans 7:19–23}}; {{James 4:1-10|James 4:1–10}}).
The psalmist calls on God to break the destructive power of the wicked.
When moving over dry ground, slugs dry up.
God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.
Being shown to be right is the reward for those who live for God.
*protect me* (or *lift me up high*): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
The psalmist asks God not to show mercy to the treacherous, deceptive, and wicked traitors (see {{Psalm 25:2|Psalm 25:2}}).
The wicked threaten like aggressive dogs, but the Lord shows that he does not fear them.
The psalmist prays that the wicked will suffer the same pain they have caused others.
The wicked will remain unsatisfied, but the psalmist will praise the Lord's strength and loving devotion.

- This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. 

- *When*: See {{2 Samuel 8:13-14|2 Samuel 8:13–14}}. 

- *Aram-naharaim* and *Aram-zobah* refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Genesis 24:10). 

- The tune *“Lily of the Testimony”* is unknown today.
When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.
The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.

*we are staggered from the wine: Yayin*, the Hebrew word for "wine," is often associated with drunkenness ({{2 Samuel 13:28|2 Samuel 13:28}}; {{Isaiah 5:11|Isaiah 5:11}}; {{Isaiah 28:7-8|28:7–8}}; see also {{Psalm 104:15|Psalm 104:15}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:26|Deuteronomy 14:26}}; {{Isaiah 55:1|Isaiah 55:1}}). It symbolized God's judgment on the wicked ({{Psalm 75:8|Psalm 75:8}}; {{Jeremiah 51:7|Jeremiah 51:7}}).

- God raised a banner over his people to serve as a rallying point and as a source of pride and confidence. 

- The fear of God that leads to wisdom ({{Psalm 111:10|Psalm 111:10}}) is not weakness. It gives the perspective and strength needed to do what is right.
The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.

Shechem and Succoth represent the heartland of Israel.

These places were located in the central region of the land. Because of this, they can represent the center of Israel’s life and strength.
The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.
Destroying the capital (*the fortified city*) of a defeated invader would help prevent future attacks. Edom's capital was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant victory.
The psalmist asks God to protect him and guide him into his presence ({{Psalm 61:4-5|Psalm 61:4–5}}). He prays for God to extend and protect the king's rule and promises to praise God.
In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.

- *the ends of the earth*: This phrase suggests a cry that comes from a place far away from God. 

- The psalmist feels deep sorrow and distress.

- The poet desires God's presence and seeks entry into God's earthly home for protection and care. Being welcomed into God's sanctuary (*tent*) is the greatest blessing (see {{Psalm 15:1|Psalms 15:1}}; {{Psalm 23:6|23:6}}; {{Psalm 24:3-6|24:3–6}}). The Hebrew word for *tent *refers to the tabernacle and the tent David built for the ark ({{1 Chronicles 15:1|1 Chronicles 15:1}}). See also study note on John 1:14. 

- The shelter of your wings represents God's protection and care (see {{Psalm 9:9|Psalms 9:9}}; {{Psalm 17:8|17:8}}).

- *You have heard my vows*: The psalmist's vows might be part of ceremonial sacrifices ({{Psalm 66:13-15|Psalms 66:13–15}}; {{Psalm 76:11|76:11}}; {{Psalm 116:14|116:14}}, {{Psalm 116:18|18}}). He praises and thanks God for rescuing him. 

- The inheritance refers to the promise of the land (see {{Psalm 60:1-12|Psalm 60}}), the sacredness of the temple, the joy of God's presence ({{Psalm 119:111|Psalm 119:111}}), or any similar reward ({{Psalm 16:6|Psalms 16:6}}; {{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:11|11}}, {{Psalm 37:18|18}}, {{Psalm 37:22|22}}, {{Psalm 37:29|29}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}; {{Psalm 127:3|127:3}}).
See {{1 Chronicles 25:1|1 Chronicles 25:1}}; also in {{Psalm 39:1-13|Psalms 39}} and {{Psalm 77:1-20|77}}.

This psalm expresses trust in the king and includes a prayer for him. The king relies on God even during tough times. 

His tricky and strong enemies challenge him, but he stays strong. He urges himself and his people to trust God. 

He wants them to view their human enemies from God's perspective, where they seem weak, temporary, and deceitful ({{Psalm 62:9|Psalm 62:9}}).
The enemies want to overthrow the king using lies and tricks.
*his lofty perch:* This means the royal throne.
The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
*are but a lie*: People often try to appear stronger and better than they truly are.
Humans are temporary, unlike God. Even when successful, their prosperity does not last long.
*Extortion* involves using threats to force someone to give up their belongings. *Stealing* means taking what belongs to someone else.
Only God balances power and loving devotion. He cares for his people by removing those who do evil from the world (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).

- Together, *soul* and *body* refer to a person's entire being. 

- *dry and weary land*: When David lived in the desert, he felt spiritually empty, away from God's people and the sanctuary.

The king deeply desires God's presence. He experiences God's goodness in everything he does. Despite being tired and troubled by the wicked, the king finds strength in God and praises him. God is his source of life ({{Psalm 63:3|Psalm 63:3}}), while the wicked face destruction ({{Psalm 63:9|63:9}}).
The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his sanctuary (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}; {{Psalm 61:4|61:4}}; {{Psalm 62:5|62:5}}, {{Psalm 62:11-12|11–12}}).
*better than life*: The best life comes from a relationship with God (see {{Psalm 4:7|Psalms 4:7}}; {{Psalm 63:5|63:5}}; {{Proverbs 16:8|Proverbs 16:8}}).
Meditating on God requires focus, concentration, thought, and reflection (see {{Psalm 1:2|Psalm 1:2}}).

The psalmist thinks about and feels God's presence during the night. When it is dark, God is the light. The quiet night and the wait for morning offer time to reflect on the true meaning of life with the Lord.

- The wicked planned to ruin the psalmist's life with lies and deceit, but they would fail. 

- *the depths of the earth*: This refers to the place of the dead.

Wild foxes and jackals are often associated with places that are ruined and abandoned ({{Isaiah 13:20-22|Isaiah 13:20–22}}; {{Isaiah 34:10-15|34:10–15}}; {{Jeremiah 9:11|Jeremiah 9:11}}; {{Jeremiah 49:33|49:33}}; {{Jeremiah 51:37|51:37}}; {{Lamentations 5:18|Lamentations 5:18}}; {{Malachi 1:3|Malachi 1:3}}). The wicked will not receive honor in death. Scavenging animals will consume their bodies ({{Ecclesiastes 6:3|Ecclesiastes 6:3}}; {{Jeremiah 22:18-19|Jeremiah 22:18–19}}; {{Jeremiah 36:29-30|36:29–30}}).
These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.

This lament speaks against the destructive plans and arrogant attitude of the wicked ({{Psalm 64:1-6|Psalm 64:1–6}}). The psalmist prays to God and finds comfort in God's justice because the righteous judge will undo the wicked's actions. The godly will rejoice and gain wisdom as they think about God's powerful deeds.
*their tongues … bitter words*: Liars use their words to harm others. This description might also refer to practicing magic.

- The enemies make a plan to harm the innocent without getting caught. 

- Human beings can act with extreme evil through words, actions, or plans ({{Psalm 83:3|Psalm 83:3}}; see {{Jeremiah 17:9|Jeremiah 17:9}}).
God acts righteously. God stops wickedness and gives the wicked what they intended for others.
God alone deserves praise and is worthy to have vows made to him.
Praise is the right response to God's great acts in redemption ({{Psalm 65:3-5|Psalm 65:3–5}}) and in nature ({{Psalm 65:5-13|65:5–13}}).
This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
*You atone*: God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).

- *the one You choose and bring near*: This includes people from Israel and other nations. 

- Only those God sees as blameless live in his holy courts ({{Psalm 15:1-5|Psalms 15}} and {{Psalm 24:1-10|24}}). 

- At the temple, God's earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God's holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see {{Revelation 21:22|Revelation 21:22}}).

- God brought order to the mountains, the roaring oceans, and the pounding waves (see {{Psalm 95:4-5|Psalms 95:4–5}}; {{Psalm 104:6-9|104:6–9}}). 

- The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the nations (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalms 2:1–12}}; {{Psalm 33:6-11|33:6–11}}; {{Psalm 46:6|46:6}}).
All over the world ({{Job 38:13|Job 38:13}}; see {{Psalm 50:1-3|Psalm 50:1–3}}), people should stand in awe of the Lord.

The *streams of God* and all rivers show God's power and goodness through nature's order and the regularity of the harvests (see {{Psalm 1:3|Psalms 1:3}}; {{Psalm 36:8|36:8}}; {{Psalm 46:4|46:4}}; {{Ezekiel 47:6-12|Ezekiel 47:6–12}}; {{Zechariah 14:8|Zechariah 14:8}}; {{Revelation 22:1|Revelation 22:1}}).
The created world clearly shows God's power ({{Psalm 65:6-8|Psalm 65:6–8}}). He shows his love by taking care of nature. Everything praises the Lord as all parts work together smoothly.
The psalmist urges nature to join a powerful song to praise God's glory, name, and power.
This anonymous psalm includes two hymns ({{Psalm 66:1-12|Psalm 66:1–12}}, {{Psalm 66:13-20|13–20}}) that praise God for saving his people.
The glory of his name represents the perfection of God’s character.

The story of the exodus and God's victory over the sea causes the people to be amazed ({{Psalm 66:5|Psalm 66:5}}) and to worship ({{Psalm 66:6|66:6}}). God performs miracles to redeem people for himself.
God's power brings redemption. The same word appears in {{Psalm 65:6|Psalm 65:6}} to describe God's power in creation (see also {{Psalm 80:2|Psalm 80:2}}).
The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
God guides his people into wisdom and away from foolishness ({{Psalm 17:5|Psalms 17:5}}; {{Psalm 37:31|37:31}}; {{Psalm 121:3|121:3}}).
*For You, O God, have tested us*: Like a silversmith heats silver to remove impurities, God's discipline removes sin from his people (see {{Psalm 12:6|Psalm 12:6}}).
God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
*You let men ride over our heads*: Or *You made people rule over us.* This likely refers to a foreign ruler who controlled the Israelites.
Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including burnt offerings (see {{Psalm 20:3|Psalms 20:3}}; {{Psalm 40:6|40:6}}; {{Psalm 50:8|50:8}}; {{Psalm 51:19|51:19}}).
The private testimony at the end of the psalm matches the public praise at the beginning ({{Psalm 66:1-4|Psalm 66:1–4}}).
This prayer is inspired by the priestly blessing in {{Numbers 6:24-26|Numbers 6:24–26}}. God's kindness to Israel influences his reputation among other nations (see {{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}).

This anonymous prayer asks for God's blessing. The psalmist speaks about knowing and worshiping God among all nations (compare {{Psalm 64:9|Psalms 64:9}}; {{Psalm 65:8|65:8}}). The prayer asks for God's name to remain holy and that his kingdom come (compare {{Matthew 6:9-13|Matthew 6:9–13}}).

- God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the nations (see {{Psalm 138:4|Psalm 138:4}}). Their chaos and rebellion will stop when they join Israel in praising God. 

- One God rules over everyone, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see {{Psalm 67:4|Psalm 67:4}}).
God delivers the ultimate justice that people seek ({{Psalm 96:10|Psalms 96:10}}; {{Psalm 98:9|98:9}}).

- Large harvests show God’s blessing ({{Genesis 26:12|Genesis 26:12}}; {{Isaiah 30:23|Isaiah 30:23}}). 

- *all the ends of the earth*: See {{Psalm 2:8|Psalms 2:8}}; {{Psalm 96:1-3|96:1–3}}. 

- People from every nation will join Israel in acknowledging the God of Israel.
These verses form a prayer for God to rise and scatter his enemies, like when Israel entered the promised land (compare {{Numbers 10:35-36|Numbers 10:35–36}}; {{Joshua 6:1-12:24|Joshua 6–12}}).

This prayer for God's victorious rule describes God's journey from Sinai to Zion ({{Psalm 68:7|Psalm 68:7}}, {{Psalm 68:16-18|16–18}}, {{Psalm 68:24|24}}). He saved Israel from Egypt, led them through the wilderness, brought them to the promised land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature does not change. Therefore, the faithful hope and rejoice in the promise of God's universal rule.
Both *smoke* and *wax* represent a temporary existence ({{Psalm 22:12-18|Psalms 22:12–18}}; {{Psalm 37:20|37:20}}; {{Psalm 102:3|102:3}}).
The fate of the godly is different from that of the wicked (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).

*Him who rides on the clouds*: This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite god. The psalmist uses it to describe the Lord as the true God "who rides upon the highest heavens" (see {{Psalm 68:33|Psalms 68:33}}; {{Psalm 104:3|104:3}}). God has power over the clouds and the rain.
The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

- God, the Father of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see {{Psalm 10:14|Psalms 10:14}}, {{Psalm 10:18|18}}; {{Psalm 69:33|69:33}}; {{Psalm 82:3|82:3}}). 

- Like his dwelling, the Lord is holy. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.

- God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt ({{Exodus 20:2|Exodus 20:2}}; see {{Psalm 69:33|Psalm 69:33}}), and he continues to free prisoners today. 

- The* sun-scorched land* represents being far from God and separated from blessing.

- The *earth shook* as it does during an earthquake (see {{Exodus 19:18|Exodus 19:18}}). 

- *the heavens poured down rain*: Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan provided plenty of water.
*a great company of women proclaim it*: A large group of women singers celebrates the victory in song (see {{Psalm 68:25|Psalm 68:25}}; {{Exodus 15:20|Exodus 15:20}}).
The people who cared for flocks and moved from place to place were surprised to receive silver and gold ornaments from the battle.

- The Almighty (Hebrew *Shaddai*) is an ancient name for God (see {{Psalm 91:1|Psalm 91:1}}; {{Genesis 17:1|Genesis 17:1}}). 

- The exact location of Mount Zalmon is unknown; it might have been a mountain in Bashan (see {{Psalm 68:15|Psalm 68:15}}).

Bashan is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee. It was famous for its forests and pastureland (see {{Psalm 22:12|Psalm 22:12}}; {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}). The mountains might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, possibly Jebel ed-Druze to the east.
*Why do you gaze in envy*: Bashan is more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the Lord's home. Only Mount Zion had the honor of being God's dwelling place.
Chariots were the top weapon of the military in the psalmist’s time. They represent the Lord’s power to give victory ({{Psalm 20:7|Psalms 20:7}}; {{Psalm 44:3|44:3}}).

- *You have ascended on high*: The Most High victoriously established his reign in Zion. 

- *captives … gifts*: This image shows a victorious ruler leading a victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ ({{Ephesians 4:8-13|Ephesians 4:8–13}}).
Like a caring father or a shepherd, God carries his people in his arms (see {{Psalm 55:22|Psalm 55:22}}; {{Psalm 68:5-6|68:5–6}}).
God cares for his people like a shepherd, and the people praise him.
*God will crush the heads of His enemies*: Compare {{Genesis 3:15|Genesis 3:15}}.
God will deal with all enemies, whether from high places (represented by *Bashan*) or low (*the depths of the sea*).
A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
The people pray for God's help and victory over enemy nations ({{Psalm 68:1-3|Psalm 68:1–3}}).
The conquered kings will bring gifts to the Lord.
Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see {{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}).
The phrase *kingdoms of the earth* refers to all nations and power structures.
The psalmist urges the people to praise God, who triumphs over his enemies.
When the Lord shows his power, majesty, and strength to the nations, he makes his people stronger (see {{Psalm 96:4-6|Psalm 96:4–6}}).

{{Psalm 45:1-17|Psalm 45}} also mentions this tune, but {{Psalm 45:1-17|Psalm 45}} praises the glory of kingship. In contrast, {{Psalm 69:1-36|Psalm 69}} is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.

The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and his sense of separation from God (see {{Psalm 42:7|Psalm 42:7}}; {{Psalm 69:14|69:14}}, {{Psalm 69:15|15}}; {{Isaiah 8:8|Isaiah 8:8}}).
In this personal lament, the poet shares his vulnerability, humiliation, and deep pain. He asks God to defend him for the sake of the righteous.
