These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the earlier psalms that describe God’s mighty acts in creation and redemption, ending with God’s march to Zion ({{Psalm 65:1-68:35|Psalms 65–68}}). {{Psalm 69:1-71:24|Psalms 69–71}} describe the king's suffering, and {{Psalm 72:1-20|Psalm 72}} responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
John applied this lament to Jesus ({{John 15:25|John 15:25}}).
The psalmist confesses his sins and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist seeks comfort, relief ({{Psalm 69:13-18|Psalm 69:13–18}}), and justice ({{Psalm 69:22-28|69:22–28}}) from the Lord.

The psalmist is devoted to God and what is holy, yet people repay him with insults. Later, this verse was applied to the anger of Jesus at the temple’s money changers ({{John 2:17|John 2:17}}) and his undeserved suffering ({{Romans 15:3|Romans 15:3}}).
When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
The psalmist can only pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
The psalmist feels alone and misunderstood. He cannot bear his doubts, and his troubles overwhelm him.
*vinegar to quench my thirst*: This description applies to the suffering of Jesus ({{Matthew 27:34|Matthew 27:34}}, {{Matthew 27:48|48}}; {{Luke 23:36|Luke 23:36}}; {{John 19:28-29|John 19:28–29}}).
The psalmist asks God to give his suffering ({{Psalm 69:3|Psalm 69:3}}) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day ({{Romans 11:9-10|Romans 11:9–10}}).
Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot ({{Acts 1:20|Acts 1:20}}).
*May they be blotted out of the Book of Life*: Compare {{Psalm 1:5-6|Psalm 1:5–6}}; {{Psalm 9:5|9:5}}; {{Revelation 3:5|Revelation 3:5}}; {{Revelation 20:15|20:15}}; {{Revelation 21:22-27|21:22–27}}.
The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.
Making a vow often included a sacrifice ({{Psalm 20:3|Psalms 20:3}}; {{Psalm 51:19|51:19}}; compare {{Psalm 50:13-14|50:13–14}}; {{Psalm 51:16|51:16}}).

The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer ({{Psalm 69:1-33|Psalm 69:1–33}}) to the desperate condition of Judah (see {{Psalm 51:18-19|51:18–19}}).
God’s people will inherit the land because the wicked will perish (see {{Psalm 37:8-9|Psalm 37:8–9}}).
*To bring remembrance*: The meaning of this phrase is not known (also found in {{Psalm 38:1|Psalm 38:1}}).

This psalm is almost exactly the same as {{Psalm 40:13-17|Psalm 40:13–17}}. It has an urgent tone ({{Psalm 70:1|Psalm 70:1}}, {{Psalm 70:5|5}}) that matches the nearby psalms (compare {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 71:12|71:12}}).
The poet recognizes God as a dependable protector who will act justly towards him and his oppressors. See also {{Psalm 31:1-3|Psalm 31:1–3}}.

This untitled lament by an aging believer is more a confession of confidence and hope than a cry of abandonment by God. The psalmist experienced God's power and protection in his youth ({{Psalm 71:5-8|Psalm 71:5–8}}) and now prays for rescue from enemies who pursue him in his old age ({{Psalm 71:9-13|Psalm 71:9–13}}). 

Even in danger, he continues to speak of God's past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to sharing with the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
The psalmist has trusted God throughout his life (see {{Psalm 22:9|Psalm 22:9}}).

The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see {{Psalm 9:10|Psalm 9:10}}; {{Psalm 51:11|51:11}}). In his weakness, the poet needs the Lord's strength even more (see {{Psalm 143:7|Psalm 143:7}}).

The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.
The psalmist's enemies plan and scheme together ({{Psalm 2:2|Psalms 2:2}}; {{Psalm 21:11|21:11}}; {{Psalm 31:13|31:13}}; {{Psalm 35:4|35:4}}; {{Psalm 63:9-10|63:9–10}}).
The psalmist compares his goodness to his enemies' evil. He focuses on the Lord, even in difficult times (see {{Psalm 9:17-18|Psalms 9:17–18}}; {{Psalm 27:13-14|27:13–14}}).
God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.
*You will bring me back up*: The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly life. This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.

Knowing God provides comfort also assures the poet of God's presence, care, and goodness ({{Psalm 23:4|Psalms 23:4}}, {{Psalm 23:6|6}}; {{Psalm 86:17|86:17}}). God's comfort increases the psalmist's sense of being alive (see {{Psalm 119:50|Psalm 119:50}}).
As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.
*justice … righteousness*: In the ancient Near East, kings were expected to represent justice. For Israel's kings, the standard was higher because they followed the Lord's example.
Justice brings balance to nature, leading to harmony, prosperity, and fertility.

This royal psalm concludes Book Two, with {{Psalm 72:18-20|Psalm 72:18–20}} serving as an epilogue for the entire book. The psalmist considers the future of David's royal line and Zion (see {{Psalm 46:1-11|Psalms 46}}, {{Psalm 48:1-14|48}}). He prays that Israel's kings will be good and successful, spreading the Lord's blessing to all people worldwide. The exceptional righteousness and rule desired in this prayer hint at the future arrival of Jesus, the Son of David.
Justice makes the world fruitful, abundant, harmonious, and good (see {{Isaiah 32:16-17|Isaiah 32:16–17}}).
A just ruler will defend the poor against injustice, rescue them from violence, and bring their oppressors to account for their wrongdoing.

*May they fear him*: In Hebrew, this phrase appears to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads *May they endure,* which makes this a prayer for long life ({{Psalm 21:4|Psalm 21:4}}; {{Psalm 72:15|72:15}}, {{Psalm 72:17|17}}).

- The administration of justice is refreshing like spring rain, allowing the godly to thrive (see {{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}) like flowers. 

- *until the moon is no more*: This phrase means forever (see {{Psalm 89:36-37|Psalm 89:36–37}}).

- *from sea to sea*: This phrase represents the entire world. 

- Solomon's kingdom stretched from the Euphrates River in the east to the Philistine territory in the west ({{1 Kings 4:21|1 Kings 4:21}}; see {{Psalm 80:8-11|Psalms 80:8–11}}; {{Psalm 89:19-25|89:19–25}}), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at the ends of the earth (see {{Psalm 2:8|2:8}}). 

Everyone will bow before this king, including desert nomads ({{Psalm 72:9|Psalm 72:9}}), his enemies, and all the world's kings (see {{Micah 7:17|Micah 7:17}}).

The anointed king will rule the entire world. Even enemy nations will obey him. In the ancient Near East, giving gifts to the king showed his success and reputation (see {{1 Kings 10:1-29|1 Kings 10}}).

- The western kings of Tarshish came from a major colony in the western Mediterranean. The eastern kings of Sheba came from southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba ({{1 Kings 10:1-29|1 Kings 10}}). 

- Seba was likely south of Egypt, possibly on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba. 

- The gifts given to the king were a tribute and a sign of submission.

All kings and nations must submit to the messianic king (God's chosen leader). The hope in {{Psalm 2:10-11|Psalm 2:10–11}} will come true (see {{Psalm 96:1-3|96:1–3}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25}}) when other leaders and peoples bow and serve this king.
To *deliver the needy *means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.
The anointed king will help those in need. He is both a judge and a father to the poor ({{Psalm 10:14|Psalms 10:14}}, {{Psalm 10:17|17}}; {{Psalm 68:5|68:5}}).
Like a father, the king feels pity for those in need (see {{Malachi 3:17|Malachi 3:17}}).
The people will bless him, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham ({{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}; see {{Psalm 133:3|Psalm 133:3}}).
The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.
*the forests of Lebanon*: Lebanon was famous for its wood (see study note on 2 Chronicles 2:8).
This doxology (song of praise) ends Book Two of the Psalms.

This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of prayers of David. Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David ({{Psalm 86:1-17|Psalms 86}}, {{Psalm 101:1-8|101}}, {{Psalm 103:1-22|103}}, {{Psalm 108:1-110:7|108–110}}, {{Psalm 122:1-9|122}}, {{Psalm 124:1-8|124}}, {{Psalm 131:1-3|131}}, {{Psalm 133:1-3|133}}, {{Psalm 138:1-145:21|138–145}}).

People with pure hearts (people who are sincere and devoted to God) are renewed by God’s Spirit ({{Psalm 51:10|Psalm 51:10}}). They choose to live in a godly way, turn away from sin, and enjoy God’s presence (see {{Psalm 24:3-4|Psalm 24:3–4}}).

Psalm 73 is about learning to trust in God. In verse 1 the speaker says something that is true about God. God is good to people who have pure hearts. For the Israelites, to have a pure heart meant worshipping and obeying God faithfully.

But the speaker hadn’t always believed this was true about God. This is because the speaker was in pain. The speaker had a pure heart but was suffering. It seemed to the speaker that God punished people with pure hearts. It seemed like God blessed people who were proud and sinful. It seemed like proud and sinful people were always rich and healthy. It seemed like they were never punished for the evil things they did. This was unfair. It went against the pattern described by parts of the Law of Moses. It also went against the pattern described by many proverbs. Proverbs 11:8 taught that trouble comes on those who do wrong.

Job noticed the same things about sinful people that the speaker of Psalm 73 noticed. Job noticed that they didn’t have problems like most other people had (Job 21:6–18). The speaker in Psalm 73 felt jealous, confused and troubled about all of this. But the speaker’s mind, heart and spirit changed in the temple. In the temple the speaker came to understand something important. God will bring justice. God will stop everything that is unfair and evil. He will destroy everyone who refuses to obey him.

This hadn’t happened yet for the speaker in Psalm 73. But the speaker became completely sure that it would happen in the future. So the speaker fully trusted God. They didn’t have anyone in heaven but God. This means that the speaker didn’t ask false gods for help. The speaker didn’t want anything on earth besides God. This means that they didn’t trust in anything or anyone but God to rescue them. The speaker was still in pain and was still waiting for God to bring justice. But while they waited, they knew that God was with them. The speaker described this like God holding their hand. Being close to God made the speaker sure that God is truly good.

This wisdom psalm looks at the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist states that God is good to the godly, but his own experience is different ({{Psalm 73:2-12|Psalm 73:2–12}}). 

Almost overwhelmed by doubt ({{Psalm 73:13-16|Psalm 73:13–16}}), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary. This meeting gives him a broader view and renews his trust in God ({{Psalm 73:17-26|Psalm 73:17–26}}). His troubling doubts lead to a stronger desire for truth. He knows he can trust God and that God will save him ({{Psalm 73:27-28|Psalm 73:27–28}}).

Asaph was a Levitical singer appointed by David ({{1 Chronicles 6:39|1 Chronicles 6:39}}). His descendants were singers and instrumentalists ({{1 Chronicles 15:16-17|1 Chronicles 15:16–17}}). Many of the Psalms of Asaph ({{Psalm 50:1-23|Psalms 50}}, {{Psalm 73:1-83:18|73–83}}) were likely written by Asaph’s descendants later in Israel’s history (for example, {{Psalm 74:1-23|Psalm 74}}).

The seeming success of the wicked ({{Psalm 73:1-28|Psalm 73}}) and God's apparent rejection of his people ({{Psalm 74:1-23|Psalm 74}}) raise questions about his justice. God rules the entire world and decides when to judge ({{Psalm 75:1-10|Psalm 75}}).

- The poet thinks it is unfair that wicked people prosper (see {{Psalm 72:7|Psalm 72:7}}) and feels upset about it. 

- The psalmist almost strayed from the path of wisdom and godliness (see {{Psalm 17:5|Psalm 17:5}}; {{Psalm 37:31|37:31}}), but God prevented him from completely losing his way ({{Psalm 38:16|38:16}}; {{Psalm 66:9|66:9}}; {{Psalm 94:18|94:18}}; {{Psalm 121:3|121:3}}). 

- *when I saw the prosperity of the wicked*: Compare {{Psalm 72:3|Psalm 72:3}}, {{Psalm 72:7|7}}.
The psalmist gives an exaggerated picture of the happiness of the wicked (compare {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}}).
Proud people choose pride and cruelty over wisdom ({{Proverbs 1:9|Proverbs 1:9}}).
The proud boast, claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see {{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}).

- These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” as an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see {{Malachi 3:14-15|Malachi 3:14–15}}). 

- *my heart*: This refers to his whole being. 

- The psalmist’s pain comes from discipline and rebuke ({{Psalm 39:11|Psalm 39:11}}; {{Proverbs 1:23|Proverbs 1:23}}, {{Proverbs 1:25|25}}; {{Proverbs 12:1|12:1}}).
When the psalmist sees the effect of his discouragement and doubt, he turns to the Lord and gains new understanding.

If the psalmist had spoken about his doubts regarding the value of living a godly life, he might have discouraged God's people and given God's enemies a chance to speak against God (compare {{John 13:20|John 13:20}}). Instead, the psalmist keeps the problem to himself and thinks about it.

- During this period, God's sanctuary was the temple in Jerusalem. In God's presence, the psalmist receives special insight (compare {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}). 

- God deals with the wicked over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent ({{Ezekiel 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11}}; {{2 Peter 3:9|2 Peter 3:9}}). Those who do not repent will get what they deserve.
The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a bitter spirit.
The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.
Nothing in heaven or on earth is better than being near God.

- God rejected his people because their sin made him angry ({{Psalm 106:34-46|Psalm 106:34–46}}). 

- Like a caring shepherd, God looks after his people, the sheep of his pasture ({{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalms 23}}; {{Psalm 100:3|100:3}}).
In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.

The psalmist laments the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. This happened in 586 BC. The psalmist uses vivid imagery, asks questions, recalls fresh memories, and directly asks the Lord to act ({{Psalm 74:19-23|Psalm 74:19–23}}).

- The Lord chose and redeemed Israel from Egypt in the exodus (compare {{Exodus 15:13|Exodus 15:13}}). 

- *Your congregation*: This is another expression for "your people" ({{Psalm 28:9|Psalms 28:9}}; {{Psalm 78:62|78:62}}; {{Psalm 94:14|94:14}}; {{Psalm 106:40|106:40}}).
Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
*my King from ancient times*: The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel ({{Psalm 5:2|Psalms 5:2}}; {{Psalm 44:4|44:4}}; {{Psalm 84:3|84:3}}).

*Leviathan*: See {{Psalm 104:26|Psalm 104:26}}; {{Job 3:8|Job 3:8}}; {{Job 41:1|41:1}}, {{Job 41:12|12}}, {{Job 41:22|22}}, {{Job 41:31|31}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}. Here, the creature’s multiple heads suggest a mythical monster.

*ever-flowing rivers*: God gave water in the desert to his people (see {{Psalm 68:8-9|Psalm 68:8–9}}; {{Exodus 17:6|Exodus 17:6}}). He dried up the Red Sea ({{Exodus 14:21|Exodus 14:21}}) and the Jordan River ({{Joshua 3:17|Joshua 3:17}}).
The poet urges God to act.

This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that assure us of his justice ({{Psalm 75:2-3|Psalm 75:2–3}}, {{Psalm 75:10|10}}). The Lord warns arrogant people who defy him, promising to humble them by force ({{Psalm 75:4-8|Psalm 75:4–8}}). Together, the community and the psalmist give thanks for God's character ({{Psalm 75:1|Psalm 75:1}}, {{Psalm 75:9|9}}).
The Lord will bring justice in his own time.
The wicked proudly defy heaven, where God lives. By boasting, they claim that they are wiser than God.
No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.
The Lord alone is the Judge. He has the power to raise people up or bring them down (see {{1 Samuel 2:7|1 Samuel 2:7}}; {{Luke 1:52|Luke 1:52}}).
*A song*: The Greek version reads *for the Assyrian.*
God's victory over Zion's enemies hints at his future victory over all his enemies worldwide.

This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on {{Psalm 76:1|76:1}}; see also {{Isaiah 37:1-38|Isaiah 37}}). Or, it might be remembering God's great acts of rescue in the past.
God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see {{Psalm 46:9|Psalm 46:9}}).
The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order ({{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 29:4|29:4}}; {{Psalm 111:3|111:3}}).
The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his glorious majesty.
*feared*: The Hebrew word *nora’* sounds like the Hebrew word *na’or*, translated "resplendent," in {{Psalm 76:4|Psalm 76:4}}.
The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.

The night provides a special opportunity for prayer and meditation ({{Psalm 77:6|Psalms 77:6}}, {{Psalm 77:11|11}}; see {{Psalm 6:6|6:6}}; {{Psalm 16:7|16:7}}; {{Psalm 17:3|17:3}}; {{Psalm 30:5|30:5}}; {{Psalm 63:6|63:6}}; {{Psalm 119:55|119:55}}, {{Psalm 119:62|62}}, {{Psalm 119:148|148}}).

The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation ({{Psalm 77:3|Psalm 77:3}}, {{Psalm 77:6|6}}, {{Psalm 77:12|12}}) and finds hope (see {{Psalm 25:5|25:5}}) in remembering God's past actions ({{Psalm 77:11|77:11}}).

- *I remembered You, O God*: God's people often face hard times. Remembering God's powerful actions at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God's commitment.

- Feeling overwhelmed, the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis ({{Psalm 142:3|Psalms 142:3}}; {{Psalm 143:4|143:4}}).
As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.
Feeling rejected (see {{Psalm 43:2|Psalm 43:2}}), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.
The psalmist questions his status before God.

The psalmist is afraid that God's hand of protection ({{Psalm 44:3|Psalm 44:3}}; {{Psalm 77:15|77:15}}; {{Exodus 6:6|Exodus 6:6}}) and favor ({{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalms 16:7–8}}; {{Psalm 110:1|110:1}}) are now against him for no clear reason.
The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.
This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.
*the waters saw You and swirled: *The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.
The introduction is an invitation to learn wisdom.
This wisdom psalm urges people to learn wisdom and share it faithfully.

- The psalmist tells Israel’s story ({{Psalm 78:5-72|Psalm 78:5–72}}) as a parable to teach wisdom and insight.

- Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables ({{Matthew 13:35|Matthew 13:35}}).
This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see {{Deuteronomy 6:20-25|Deuteronomy 6:20–25}}; {{Proverbs 4:1-4|Proverbs 4:1–4}}).
The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he commanded ({{Deuteronomy 6:4-9|Deuteronomy 6:4–9}}).

God holds each generation responsible for its own actions. They should maintain faith and hope (see {{Psalm 9:18|Psalm 9:18}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}) and avoid being stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful (see {{Deuteronomy 9:6-7|Deuteronomy 9:6–7}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:16|10:16}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:6|30:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:27|31:27}}).

Ephraim was the second son of Joseph. He received a special blessing from Jacob ({{Genesis 48:15-20|Genesis 48:15–20}}; {{Genesis 49:22-26|49:22–26}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:13-17|Deuteronomy 33:13–17}}). His descendants inherited land with fertile valleys and important roads ({{Judges 8:2|Judges 8:2}}). However, the people of Ephraim did not follow God's covenant.
The *wonders* are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity ({{Exodus 7:1-12:51|Exodus 7–12}}).
The focus shifts from Ephraim ({{Psalm 78:9-11|Psalm 78:9–11}}) to all of Israel. The psalmist thinks about God's power in Egypt (see {{Psalm 81:4-7|Psalm 81:4–7}}) and in the wilderness.
God *split the sea* when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see {{Exodus 14:1-15:27|Exodus 14–15}}).
God used *a cloud *and *a light of fire* to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness ({{Exodus 13:21-22|Exodus 13:21–22}}).
Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.

- Abundance comes through the doors of heaven ({{Genesis 8:2|Genesis 8:2}}; {{2 Kings 7:2|2 Kings 7:2}}; {{Malachi 3:10|Malachi 3:10}}). 

- The Israelites ate manna for 40 years in the wilderness ({{Exodus 16:31-36|Exodus 16:31–36}}; {{John 6:31|John 6:31}}).
God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.
Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.
An entire generation died in the wilderness ({{Numbers 14:22-23|Numbers 14:22–23}}, {{Numbers 14:28-35|28–35}}).
*they repented*: This strong show of effort was not sincere.
Israel continued to exist because of God's compassion, despite the people's rebellion and lack of belief ({{Psalm 78:7-8|Psalm 78:7–8}}).

The Israelites remembered the correct teaching about God ({{Psalm 9:9|Psalms 9:9}}; {{Psalm 91:1|91:1}}), but they did not let God change the way they thought and lived ({{Leviticus 26:41|Leviticus 26:41}}).
The Israelites rebelled even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.

Israel’s rebellion defiled the promised land. During the time of the judges, the people built shrines to false gods and worshiped idols ({{Psalm 78:58|Psalm 78:58}}; see also {{Judges 2:11|Judges 2:11}}; {{Judges 3:7|3:7}}, {{Judges 3:17-18|17–18}}).
God abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh because of the people’s idol worship ({{1 Samuel 4:11|1 Samuel 4:11}}; {{Jeremiah 7:12|Jeremiah 7:12}}).
The tribe of Ephraim was not completely rejected, but God favored Judah ({{Psalm 78:68|Psalm 78:68}}).
In the choice of Mount Zion instead of Shiloh as God’s sanctuary on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see {{Psalm 69:1-36|Psalm 69}}).

The God who had turned against his own people ({{Psalm 78:62|Psalm 78:62}}) chose David, a shepherd ({{Genesis 46:34|Genesis 46:34}}; {{1 Samuel 16:10-11|1 Samuel 16:10–11}}), to lead them as their shepherd ({{Psalm 78:52|Psalm 78:52}}; compare {{Psalm 23:1|23:1}}).
*Your inheritance*: This phrase might refer to the land, the temple (see {{Psalm 61:5|Psalm 61:5}}), or the people (see {{Psalm 79:2|79:2}}; {{Psalm 78:71|78:71}}).
The poet laments the defilement of the temple and the success of the enemy.

This lament describes the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Israel’s early history of rebellion, described in {{Psalm 78:1-72|Psalm 78}}, angered God. As a result, Zion was destroyed. The temple was defiled, and the bodies of the dead lay across the land. 

The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue ({{Psalm 79:8-9|Psalm 79:8–9}}) and asks God to repay the nation's enemies ({{Psalm 79:12-13|Psalm 79:12–13}}). Other psalms lamenting the exile include {{Psalm 42:1-44:26|Psalms 42–44}}, {{Psalm 102:1-28|102}}, {{Psalm 107:1-43|107}}, {{Psalm 126:1-6|126}}, and {{Psalm 137:1-9|137}}.

The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verse {{Psalm 6:1-7:17|6–7}} are nearly identical to {{Jeremiah 10:25|Jeremiah 10:25}}.
The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.

The people’s many sins in the past helped lead to the exile ({{2 Kings 17:7-23|2 Kings 17:7–23}}; {{2 Kings 24:3-4|24:3–4}}). However, each person also suffered because of his or her own sin ({{Jeremiah 31:30|Jeremiah 31:30}}; {{Ezekiel 18:20|Ezekiel 18:20}}).
The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the pagan nations must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.

- The exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord. 

- *Pay back*: See {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}; {{Psalm 94:2|94:2}}; {{Jeremiah 32:18|Jeremiah 32:18}}. 

- The phrase *sevenfold* means something is complete. 

- Israel's neighbors included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see {{Psalm 137:7|Psalm 137:7}}; {{2 Kings 24:2|2 Kings 24:2}}; {{Obadiah 1-21|Obadiah 1}}).
The tune of “The Lilies of the Covenant” is unknown today.

- *O Shepherd of Israel*: See also {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}; {{Psalm 28:9|28:9}}; {{Psalm 78:52-53|78:52–53}}.

- *shine forth … mighty power*: These expressions ({{Psalm 145:11|Psalm 145:11}}) refer to God's visible presence.
The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.

This psalm of lament may come from the remnant (the small group that survived) of the northern kingdom after it fell in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Hosts (a title that describes God as the ruler over the armies of heaven). They hope that he will return to them and restore them.

They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord. The psalm ends with a promise of renewed commitment to him ({{Psalm 80:18|Psalm 80:18}}).
This verse is repeated (with a growing intensity) in {{Psalm 80:7|Psalm 80:7}} and {{Psalm 80:19|19}}.
The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.

Israel had been like a fruitful grapevine ({{Genesis 1:28|Genesis 1:28}}; {{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}) that God transplanted to Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil ({{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}; {{Hosea 10:1|Hosea 10:1}}).
Israel has a glorious past that began when God rescued the people from Egypt.
Solomon’s kingdom had extended west to the Mediterranean Sea and east to the Euphrates River (see {{Psalm 72:8-9|Psalms 72:8–9}}; {{Psalm 89:25|89:25}}; {{1 Kings 4:21|1 Kings 4:21}}).
*broken down its walls*: God no longer defended Israel ({{Isaiah 5:5|Isaiah 5:5}}).
The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a wild boar or vicious wild animals.
Israel was the son that God had brought out of Egypt (see {{Hosea 11:1|Hosea 11:1}}) and *planted* him in the Holy Land.
The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.
The son God chose was probably the northern kingdom of Israel. But it may also refer to the king from David’s line ({{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}).
Before giving a warning, the psalmist calls Israel to think about their God through song and dance.
This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.

- An Israelite tambourine was a hand drum with a round frame and skin cover. People used it as a percussion instrument during celebrations, often to accompany dancing ({{Psalm 68:25|Psalms 68:25}}; {{Psalm 149:3|149:3}}; {{Psalm 150:4|150:4}}). 

- The *sweet-sounding harp and lyre*, both stringed instruments, are the most frequently mentioned instruments in the psalms (for example, {{Psalm 33:2|Psalms 33:2}}; {{Psalm 57:8|57:8}}; {{Psalm 71:22|71:22}}; {{Psalm 150:3|150:3}}).

- The* ram’s horn* gathered armies and announced special holy days ({{Psalm 47:5|Psalms 47:5}}; {{Psalm 98:6|98:6}}). 

- *New Moon*: The first day of each lunar month was a festival.
The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
*for Joseph*: The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.

- God emphasizes that he and no one else rescued Israel.

- The nation should eagerly accept God's word (compare {{Deuteronomy 8:3|Deuteronomy 8:3}}; {{Ezekiel 3:1|Ezekiel 3:1}}).
The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.

- God wants to give his goodness to his children, but they must listen ({{Isaiah 1:18-19|Isaiah 1:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 28:12|28:12}}; {{Isaiah 48:18-19|48:18–19}}; see {{Deuteronomy 6:3|Deuteronomy 6:3}}). 

- God promises to defeat the enemies ({{Deuteronomy 9:3|Deuteronomy 9:3}}) of those who follow the paths of obedience and loyalty. He will also provide abundantly for his people ({{Isaiah 1:19|Isaiah 1:19}}).

- God is ready to give judgment (see {{Isaiah 3:13|Isaiah 3:13}}). 

- *divine assembly*: See {{Job 1:6|Job 1:6}}.
God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.

Because justice defines God’s rule ({{Psalm 89:4|Psalm 89:4}}), he does not support the wicked. The psalmist is confused by this situation and cries out to God to bring justice ({{Psalm 82:3-4|Psalm 82:3–4}}, {{Psalm 82:8|8}}).
Unjust oppressors cannot bring or restore order. They wander about in darkness, unmoved by circumstances, even when the whole world order falls apart around them (compare {{Psalm 11:3|Psalm 11:3}}).
The gods (see study notes on Psalm 29:1–2; 58:1), like mere humans, cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in {{John 10:34|John 10:34}}.
The nations belong to God. He will take over the realms formerly ruled by local gods and give them to his people, just as he did with the promised land.
The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.

This community lament asks God to rescue his people and give them victory. The short and direct poetry suggests a time of great trouble. A strong group of nations plans to destroy Israel ({{Psalm 83:1-4|Psalm 83:1–4}}) and joins together against God ({{Psalm 83:5-8|83:5–8}}). 

The psalmist remembers what happened to other enemies who attacked Israel in the past ({{Psalm 83:9-12|Psalm 83:9–12}}). He prays that the same thing will happen to these enemies ({{Psalm 83:13-16|83:13–16}}), so that they will recognize God’s power and give him honor ({{Psalm 83:17-18|83:17–18}}). 

It is not clear whether this psalm refers to one specific historical event or whether it gathers together several nations as a poetic picture of Israel’s enemies.
*they form an alliance*: The allies agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations named in this alliance lived around Israel and Judah.

- The Edomites were descendants of Esau. They lived southeast of Judah (see {{Genesis 25:30|Genesis 25:30}}; {{Genesis 32:3|32:3}}; {{Genesis 36:1-8|36:1–8}}). 

- The Ishmaelites were descendants of Hagar. They lived in the desert. 

- The Moabites and Ammonites were descendants of Lot. They lived east of Israel and Judah. 

- The Hagrites might have lived north of the Ammonites ({{1 Chronicles 5:10|1 Chronicles 5:10}}).

- Gebal, also known as Byblos, was on the coast of Lebanon. 

- The Amalekites lived south of Israel in the Negev desert. 

- Philistia was southwest of Judah, near the Mediterranean Sea. 

- Tyre was a port city on the Mediterranean Sea, northwest of Israel.

- Assyria was located northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. 

- Lot's descendants were the Moabites and the Ammonites ({{Psalm 83:6-7|Psalm 83:6–7}}).

The Midianites, led by Oreb and Zeeb and ruled by Zebah and Zalmunna, were Israel's enemies during Gideon's time ({{Judges 7:1-8:5|Judges 7:1–8:5}}). Barak's alliance defeated Sisera and Jabin ({{Judges 4:1-24|Judges 4}}).
The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.
The coalition wanted to destroy Israel to take over the land (see {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}).
*tumbleweed … chaff*: This dry plant material blows away easily (see {{Isaiah 17:13|Isaiah 17:13}}).
*fire … flame … tempest*: These images describe how God appears when he brings judgment (see {{Isaiah 29:6|Isaiah 29:6}}).
The psalmist is far from the temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.

The psalmist deeply longs for God's presence. He feels weak with longing as he thinks about the temple and the pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem ({{Psalm 84:1-7|Psalm 84:1–7}}). He prays for himself and the community ({{Psalm 84:8-9|Psalm 84:8–9}}). 

The end of the psalm ({{Psalm 84:10-12|Psalm 84:10–12}}) shows that the temple represents God. The psalmist truly desires God's presence. He understands that God's goodness is better than life and that only God can grant his people favor and honor ({{Psalm 84:10-11|Psalm 84:10–11}}).
The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the temple.
The priests and those who worked in the temple also lived there.
Travelers needed strength to meet the challenges of pilgrimage by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.

The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reminded people of the exodus, when God provided for his people in a wonderful way (see {{Psalm 78:15-16|Psalm 78:15–16}}; {{Psalm 105:41|105:41}}). The psalmist describes how the hardships of the journey turn into joy when the travelers arrive.

- The *Valley of Baca* is also called the Valley of Weeping or the Valley of Tears. It likely symbolizes the sadness that lonely pilgrims felt (see {{Psalm 23:4|Psalm 23:4}}), rather than a real place. 

- *spring … autumn rain*: Even when pilgrims feel completely worn out, the hope of getting closer to the Lord encourages them (compare {{Isaiah 35:6-10|Isaiah 35:6–10}}; {{Isaiah 41:18-20|41:18–20}}; {{Isaiah 43:17-20|43:17–20}}; {{Isaiah 49:10|49:10}}).

Both kings and priests were anointed to dedicate them for service (see {{Psalm 132:17|Psalm 132:17}}; {{Exodus 28:41|Exodus 28:41}}; {{1 Samuel 9:16|1 Samuel 9:16}}; {{1 Samuel 16:1-13|16:1–13}}; compare {{Isaiah 61:1|Isaiah 61:1}}; {{Acts 10:38|Acts 10:38}}).
The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much better than being anywhere else.
Some people worshiped the sun as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.
God brought Israel back from exile and restored its fortunes (see {{Psalm 14:7|Psalm 14:7}}; {{Psalm 126:1|126:1}}).
Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.

The psalmist leads the community that returned from exile in a lament and a prayer for complete restoration:

- He remembers how God rescued Israel from exile ({{Psalm 85:1-3|Psalm 85:1–3}}), 

- asks for clearer signs of God’s goodness, and

- leads the people in prayer for full renewal ({{Psalm 85:4-7|Psalm 85:4–7}}).

God answers with a message of peace ({{Psalm 85:8-9|Psalm 85:8–9}}). The psalm ends with a poetic description of the greatness of God’s salvation ({{Psalm 85:10-13|85:10–13}}).
When God forgave the guilt of their sins, he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).
This prayer for renewal is based on God’s unfailing love for his people.

- When God speaks, his faithful people listen. He promises them peace, meaning wholeness and well-being (see {{Psalm 37:11|Psalm 37:11}}). They respect the Lord and know that he and his salvation are near. 

- The Lord does not tolerate foolish ways, such as those that resulted in the exile.

In the renewed world of salvation, all the qualities of God’s care (love, truth, righteousness, and peace) come together. They transform creation and make it new (see {{Isaiah 32:15-20|Isaiah 32:15–20}}).
Righteousness is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people ({{Psalm 85:4-7|Psalms 85:4–7}}; {{Psalm 89:14|89:14}}).
This is the only Psalm connected to David in the third book.
God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.

The psalmist cries out to God for help and praises God’s character while facing evil ({{Psalm 86:14|Psalm 86:14}}, {{Psalm 86:17|17}}). He says that all nations will one day worship the gracious and powerful God ({{Psalm 86:8-10|Psalm 86:8–10}}). Because of this hope, the psalmist commits himself to live in a right and honest way ({{Psalm 86:11|Psalm 86:11}}) and to praise the Lord ({{Psalm 86:12-13|86:12–13}}). 

The final section contrasts the behavior of evil people with the character of the Lord ({{Psalm 86:14-17|Psalm 86:14–17}}).

The psalmist lists God's perfect qualities ({{Exodus 34:6-7|Exodus 34:6–7}}), especially God's readiness to forgive sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalms 32:5}}; {{Psalm 85:2|85:2}}; {{Psalm 145:7-10|145:7–10}}).
The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.
All the nations must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him ({{Psalm 45:17|Psalms 45:17}}; {{Psalm 117:1|117:1}}; {{Psalm 148:7-11|148:7–11}}).

- The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the truth. 

- A person with an *undivided heart *has integrity and wholeness (see {{Psalm 73:1|Psalm 73:1}}).
In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
Arrogant people exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks God to show his character. God is so great that even a small glimpse of his goodness will silence the wicked.

God shows mercy to his people ({{Psalm 51:1|Psalm 51:1}}). God is compassionate ({{Psalm 25:6|Psalm 25:6}}). God is slow to become angry ({{Psalm 103:8|Psalms 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}). God is full of loving devotion and faithfulness (Hebrew *khesed* and *’emeth*; {{Psalm 143:1|Psalm 143:1}})

This verse repeats a theme first expressed in {{Exodus 34:7|Exodus 34:7}}; {{Numbers 14:18|Numbers 14:18}} (compare {{Psalm 103:8|Psalms 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}; {{Nehemiah 9:17|Nehemiah 9:17}}; {{Joel 2:13|Joel 2:13}}; {{Jonah 4:2|Jonah 4:2}}).
Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the temple, God’s earthly palace (see {{Psalm 84:1-12|Psalm 84}}).
This psalm presents Jerusalem as the city of God, where people from all nations are counted as citizens.

- Zion is great, but it will be even greater as an international city where believers from all nations are citizens. 

- God keeps a record of everyone who confesses him as their Lord ({{Daniel 7:10|Daniel 7:10}}; {{Revelation 13:8|Revelation 13:8}}).
Jerusalem becomes the international city where all God’s children are citizens.

- *A Maskil:* This may be a literary or musical term.

- *Heman the Ezrahite*: Heman might have been:

- a wise person from the time of King Solomon ({{1 Kings 4:31|1 Kings 4:31}}), 

- a descendant of Judah ({{1 Chronicles 2:6|1 Chronicles 2:6}}), or 

- a member of the Levite family responsible for singing at the temple ({{1 Chronicles 15:17|1 Chronicles 15:17}}; {{2 Chronicles 5:12|2 Chronicles 5:12}}).
The psalmist calls on the Lord for salvation.

In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God ({{Psalm 88:6-7|Psalm 88:6–7}}, {{Psalm 88:8-12|8–12}}, {{Psalm 88:13-17|13–17}}).

- In his first complaint, the psalmist blames the Lord for his suffering. God’s overwhelming anger does not make sense to him.

- The phrase *the darkest of the depths* might refer to:

- the place of the dead ({{Psalm 143:3|Psalm 143:3}}; see {{Lamentations 3:6|Lamentations 3:6}}), or 

- the deep sea ({{Psalm 68:22|Psalms 68:22}}; {{Psalm 69:1-2|69:1–2}}).

In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (compare {{Psalm 31:11|Psalms 31:11}}; {{Psalm 38:11|38:11}}). In that culture, loneliness was a curse because relationships mattered more than personal success.
In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.
The psalmist restates his second and first charges.
God’s* loving devotion* gives reason to celebrate forever.

Book Three ({{Psalm 73:1-89:52|Psalms 73–89}}) starts and ends with serious questions. {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}} begins with praise for how the Lord established David’s throne and kingdom ({{Psalm 89:1-37|89:1–37}}). But later the psalmist protests that the Lord seems to have rejected his covenant with David ({{Psalm 89:38-51|Psalm 89:38–51}}; see {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}).
Ethan the Ezrahite was a wise man ({{1 Kings 4:31|1 Kings 4:31}}; compare {{Psalm 88:1|Psalm 88:1}}).
The Lord has sworn by his own holiness ({{Psalm 89:35|Psalm 89:35}}; see {{Psalm 110:4|110:4}}).
The psalmist repeats God's covenant with David (see also {{Psalm 89:19-37|Psalm 89:19–37}}).
Those in heaven praise God's greatness (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}) because they witness his faithfulness.
God is the absolute standard of faithfulness, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
*heavenly beings*: Literally *son of God* (see study note on Psalm 29:1–2).

- The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. 

- *You scattered Your enemies*: The Lord will defeat ({{Luke 1:51|Luke 1:51}}) evil forces that oppose him ({{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}). 

- *with Your mighty arm*: This phrase represents God’s strength ({{Psalm 89:13|Psalm 89:13}}).
In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s complete and powerful rule over nature.
Mount Tabor was in northern Israel. Mount Hermon formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of righteousness, justice, and faithfulness fit the description of a wise ruler. The happy people who live under his rule enjoy his protection.
Those who are wise worship God, walk in his light, rejoice in their relationship with him, and delight in his character.
The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
The Lord chose David as his son and king of Israel (see {{Psalm 2:4-6|Psalm 2:4–6}}; {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}) to protect his people.
*I have anointed him*: This is the verb from which comes *anointed one* (Hebrew *mashiakh*, which means “messiah”).

The Lord adopted David as his son, appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him forever. Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise ({{2 Samuel 22:47|2 Samuel 22:47}}).
David would become the greatest of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated *highest* is the same word used for God as “Most High” (*‘elyon*).

The Lord displays his faithfulness in the heavens, across his whole creation (see {{Psalm 89:2|Psalm 89:2}}). In the same way, he confirms his commitment to the kings that would come from David's family.

The Lord disciplines his children when they go astray, but he does not reject them. He knows they will break their trust and will need correction, yet he remains committed to keep his covenant. His faithfulness to David is like his faithfulness to the created world.

*holiness*: The Lord is completely different from the created world ({{Psalm 22:3|Psalm 22:3}}). His character is entirely pure. He acts according to his will ({{Psalm 115:3|Psalm 115:3}}) and chooses to be faithful ({{Psalm 89:1|89:1}}; {{Psalm 115:1|115:1}}). Therefore, he cannot lie.
*You are enraged*: The psalmist is confused by the severity of God's anger.
*broken down all his walls*: The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he has made David’s enemies strong
The psalmist wonders whether he will live long enough to see the Lord’s anger end. Human life is short and passes quickly before the Lord ({{Psalm 90:4|Psalm 90:4}}, {{Psalm 90:10|10}}).
The phrase *Your servants *refers to the community loyal to the Lord.

This doxology (a short praise to God) ends Book Three of the Psalms ({{Psalm 73:1-89:52|Psalms 73–89}}). It was not meant to be read as part of {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}. Its words of praise stand in strong contrast to the pain and questions expressed in {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}. Compare {{Psalm 41:13|Psalm 41:13}}; {{Psalm 106:48|106:48}}.

- Moses led God's people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai. There, he received the law and established God's covenant with Israel. 

- *the man of God*: Moses had a special relationship with God ({{Deuteronomy 33:1|Deuteronomy 33:1}}).

The Lord is the* dwelling place* for the godly. He has provided shelter for many generations. The word translated as *dwelling place* is rare in the Psalms. It describes a safe place where the Lord meets and cares for those in need ({{Psalm 68:5|Psalms 68:5}}; {{Psalm 71:3|71:3}}).

Although the Lord’s people have lived in him for many generations, their sin creates distance between them and their eternal Lord. The Lord’s anger against human sin can seem to last a lifetime. Even then, it is only a small sign of his full displeasure with sin. This sad situation leads the community to seek the Lord’s light.

The first step is to ask the Lord to restore them because of his compassion and faithful love ({{Psalm 90:13-14|Psalm 90:13–14}}). He alone can make his servants glad. He alone can bless the generations that come after them ({{Psalm 90:16-17|Psalm 90:16–17}}).

- The Lord is the eternal God. 

- The Lord created the earth.
Unlike God, humans are mortal and temporary.
Sinners cannot escape God’s anger against sin because the Lord sees their sins. Their lives pass quickly and are full of suffering.

- A groan of sorrow ({{Ezekiel 2:10|Ezekiel 2:10}}) represents a life facing the consequences of sin. 

- Humans create trouble (see {{Psalm 10:6|Psalm 10:6}}) and receive pain as a result.

In the search for wisdom, no one can fully understand the Lord (see {{Isaiah 40:13|Isaiah 40:13}}). The right human response to the Lord is godly fear (see {{Psalm 60:4|Psalm 60:4}}). The Lord alone can teach humans to follow the path of wisdom ({{Psalm 25:4-6|Psalm 25:4–6}}).
The phrase *Your servants* refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.
The psalmist calls upon the Lord to give the people gladness to replace their mourning (see {{Psalm 92:4-5|Psalm 92:4–5}}).
The *children* represent future generations in contrast to the generations past ({{Psalm 90:1|Psalm 90:1}}).
Humans waste their efforts unless the Lord makes them successful ({{Psalm 44:3|Psalm 44:3}}).
The *Most High* is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see {{Genesis 14:19|Genesis 14:19}}).
The Lord is an ancient shelter (see {{Psalm 90:1|Psalm 90:1}}), open to those who seek refuge in him.

This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
God protects the godly from deadly disease and even a destructive word.
The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
The *shield* might refer to a large shield that covers the body. The *rampart* likely refers to a smaller shield, though the exact meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.
The godly should not be afraid, because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
The word *pestilence* here means any kind of suffering or trouble.
The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.

*He will command His angels*: Satan quoted these words when he tempted Jesus ({{Matthew 4:6|Matthew 4:6}}; {{Luke 4:10-11|Luke 4:10–11}}). However, God makes this promise for those who obey him ({{Psalm 91:14|Psalm 91:14}}), not for those who arrogantly test him ({{Matthew 4:4|Matthew 4:4}}, {{Matthew 4:7|7}}).

Those who love the Lord will follow his commands ({{Deuteronomy 30:20|Deuteronomy 30:20}}; {{1 John 5:3|1 John 5:3}}) and look for his protection ({{Psalm 91:1|Psalms 91:1}}; {{Psalm 145:18|145:18}}).
The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.

- The Lord promises to answer the prayers of his people. 

- The Psalms often mention people honoring the Lord ({{Psalm 50:15|Psalm 50:15}}). Here, God promises to honor the faithful who risk everything for him ({{Psalm 62:7|Psalms 62:7}}; {{Psalm 71:21|71:21}}; {{Psalm 84:11|84:11}}).
A long life on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).

In Jewish tradition, each day of the week has an assigned psalm: 

- Sunday ({{Psalm 24:1-10|Psalm 24}})

- Monday ({{Psalm 48:1-14|Psalm 48}})

- Tuesday ({{Psalm 82:1-8|Psalm 82}})

- Wednesday ({{Psalm 94:1-23|Psalm 94}})

- Thursday ({{Psalm 81:1-16|Psalm 81}})

- Friday ({{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}})

- Saturday, which is the Sabbath ({{Psalm 92:1-15|Psalm 92}})

This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s loving devotion and faithfulness.

This psalm begins with thanksgiving and praise. The Lord, the Most High, is fair and just in judging the godly and the wicked. The godly will have a bright and strong future, while the wicked will die. 

Wise people see and understand the Lord's actions, which show his justice ({{Psalm 92:6-7|Psalm 92:6–7}}, {{Psalm 92:11|11}}, {{Psalm 92:15|15}}). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed ({{Psalm 92:7-10|Psalm 92:7–10}}).
The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise ({{Psalm 92:4|Psalm 92:4}}). God’s actions come from his thoughts ({{Psalm 92:5|Psalm 92:5}}).
Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s great works and his eternal plans.
The Lord’s thoughts confuse those who lack understanding or act foolishly, and those who do not seek wisdom ({{Proverbs 1:22|Proverbs 1:22}}; {{Proverbs 10:23|10:23}}).
Even when the ungodly appear to thrive ({{Psalm 73:3-5|Psalm 73:3–5}}), they have no future ({{Psalm 92:9|92:9}}; see {{Psalm 1:6|1:6}}; {{Psalm 90:5-6|90:5–6}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}).

The Lord is above the world of human experience. From this exalted place, he rules and judges ({{Psalm 7:7|Psalm 7:7}}). From there, he:

- celebrates his victories ({{Psalm 68:18|Psalm 68:18}}; see {{Psalm 47:1-9|47}}), 

- comes to rescue the needy ({{Psalm 102:19|Psalm 102:19}}), 

- brings an end to the wicked ({{Psalm 92:7-8|Psalm 92:7–8}}), and 

- receives praise ({{Psalm 148:1|Psalm 148:1}}).
The glory of the Lord is the reason the poet receives new strength and honor. It is also the reason the enemy will soon be defeated.
*like that of a wild ox*: The Lord allows the psalmist to express his joy ({{Psalm 92:8|Psalm 92:8}}). Because of this, the psalmist is strong and will overcome his enemies.
The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

Carvings of palm trees ({{1 Kings 6:29|1 Kings 6:29}}, {{1 Kings 6:32|32}}, {{1 Kings 6:35|35}}; {{1 Kings 7:36|7:36}}) decorated the temple. Builders used many cedars ({{1 Kings 5:6|1 Kings 5:6}}). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the temple.
The temple area consisted of the Lord’s own house and the courts that surrounded it.
*in Him there is no unrighteousness*: The Lord is always just. He rightly judges everyone (see {{Zephaniah 3:5|Zephaniah 3:5}}).
*robed in majesty*: The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see {{Psalm 45:3|Psalm 45:3}}).
The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (see {{Psalm 47:1-9|Psalms 47}}, {{Psalm 99:1-100:5|99–100}}).

These psalms challenge the doubts created by the exile (see {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}) and answer the questions asked in {{Psalm 90:11|Psalm 90:11}}, {{Psalm 90:13|13}}. The Lord has established a kingdom ({{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}}) that is characterized by: 

- punishment of the wicked ({{Psalm 94:1-23|Psalm 94}}),

- respectful obedience among his people ({{Psalm 95:1-11|Psalm 95}}),

- justice for the poor ({{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalm 96}}),

- celebration in Zion ({{Psalm 97:1-12|Psalm 97}}),

- salvation for Israel ({{Psalm 98:1-9|Psalm 98}}),

- holiness ({{Psalm 99:1-9|Psalm 99}}), and

- praise ({{Psalm 100:1-5|Psalm 100}}).
God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (compare {{Jeremiah 46:8|Jeremiah 46:8}}; {{Jeremiah 47:2|47:2}}).

- Through his stable rule and royal laws, the Lord orders the world.

- *Your house*: The *house* from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly temple.
After the community suffers at the hands of the wicked ({{Psalm 94:5-7|Psalm 94:5–7}}), they pray for the Lord to bring justice (see {{Psalm 7:11|Psalm 7:11}}; {{Psalm 9:12|9:12}}).

This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of sorrow ({{Psalm 94:1-7|Psalm 94:1–7}}, {{Psalm 94:16-23|16–23}}). The psalmist speaks about the pain and suffering caused by the wicked. He also describes the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their foolishness ({{Psalm 94:8-11|Psalm 94:8–11}}), and speaks a blessing on the wise ({{Psalm 94:12-15|94:12–15}}).
When the Lord's enemies rise against him and his people ({{Psalm 3:7|Psalm 3:7}}; {{Psalm 93:3|93:3}}), he must rise and punish the enemy (see {{Psalm 79:12|79:12}}; {{Isaiah 65:6|Isaiah 65:6}}).
*widow … foreigner … fatherless*: The Lord’s law protects those in need ({{Deuteronomy 24:17|Deuteronomy 24:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|27:19}}), but they remain vulnerable in society.
The wicked think that they can get away with their evil acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God is not looking or does not care.
The writer of the psalm corrects people for acting foolishly.
It makes no sense for people who have ears and eyes to think that their Creator is deaf and blind.

*discipline*: This word can also mean "admonished" ({{Psalm 2:10|Psalm 2:10}}), "discipline" ({{Psalm 6:1|6:1}}; {{Psalm 94:12|94:12}}), or "instructs" ({{Psalm 16:7|16:7}}). The Lord disciplines his people to improve their character ({{Proverbs 3:11-12|Proverbs 3:11–12}}; {{Hebrews 12:6-11|Hebrews 12:6–11}}). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}; {{Romans 6:23|Romans 6:23}}).
While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, people’s thoughts are worthless (compare {{Psalm 92:5|Psalm 92:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:20|1 Corinthians 3:20}}).
Because the Lord is faithful to his character, he rewards those who live by his wise instruction. He makes them happy, just as he promised.
God’s relief includes his comfort and rescue.
Even when it seems that he has, the Lord will not reject his people.
Only God has the power to stand up to the wicked (see {{Psalm 2:2|Psalm 2:2}}).
The psalmist resumes their prayer (see {{Psalm 94:1-7|Psalm 94:1–7}}) with a desperate plea for the Lord's justice. It ends with the hope that evil will cease.
The psalmist feels like he is slipping, but God promises to stand with him ({{Psalm 94:12-13|Psalm 94:12–13}}; see {{Psalm 15:5|15:5}}; {{Psalm 93:1|93:1}}).

This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the promised land.
*above all gods*: The psalmist argues against idol worship and pagan beliefs ({{Psalm 96:4-6|Psalms 96:4–6}}; {{Psalm 135:15-18|135:15–18}}; see also {{Isaiah 46:5-7|Isaiah 46:5–7}}).
The Lord is the great King over the whole universe.
All creation exists because of the Lord alone, not because of many gods.

- The great King cares for his people like a shepherd cares for sheep ({{Isaiah 40:11|Isaiah 40:11}}). 

- The Lord, our Maker, the Creator of heaven and earth, also created a people for himself ({{Isaiah 45:9-12|Isaiah 45:9–12}}; {{Isaiah 51:12-16|51:12–16}}).

To *harden your hearts* means to be stubborn and resist the Lord's grace (see {{Numbers 20:2-13|Numbers 20:2–13}}; see also {{Matthew 13:3-23|Matthew 13:3–23}}; {{John 12:37-43|John 12:37–43}}; {{Ephesians 4:17-32|Ephesians 4:17–32}}; {{Hebrews 3:6-19|Hebrews 3:6–19}}; {{Hebrews 4:6-11|4:6–11}}).
If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see {{Hebrews 3:7-4:11|Hebrews 3:7–4:11}}).
Israel's ancestors saw the Lord's wonders but did not understand their importance (see {{Psalm 92:5-6|Psalm 92:5–6}}).

- The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for 40 years did not enter the place of rest that Israel enjoyed after conquering the land ({{1 Kings 8:56|1 Kings 8:56}}; see {{Deuteronomy 12:9|Deuteronomy 12:9}}). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them ({{Isaiah 28:12|Isaiah 28:12}}), but they did not obey him ({{Isaiah 28:1|Isaiah 28:1}}). This warning reminds every generation of the need to obey with faith. 

- The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection ({{Psalm 132:14-18|Psalm 132:14–18}}). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ ({{Hebrews 3:7-4:13|Hebrews 3:7–4:13}}).

Three psalms begin by urging people to sing a new song ({{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalms 96}}, {{Psalm 98:1-9|98}}, {{Psalm 149:1-9|149}}). The song celebrates the Lord's universal kingship (see {{Psalm 33:3|Psalm 33:3}}).

- This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see {{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}}) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness to the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord ({{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}), the glorious Creator of the earth ({{Psalm 96:4-6|96:4–6}}), because only he deserves worship ({{Psalm 96:7-9|96:7–9}}). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order ({{Psalm 96:10-13|Psalm 96:10–13}}). 

- This psalm (along with {{Psalm 105:1-15|Psalm 105:1–15}}; {{Psalm 106:1|106:1}}, {{Psalm 106:47-48|47–48}}) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16:1–43}}.

*great is the LORD … greatly to be praised*: The poet praises the Lord above all gods ({{Psalm 95:3|Psalm 95:3}}) and nations ({{Psalm 99:2|99:2}}). The Lord inspires more awe than anyone or anything else ({{Psalm 76:7|Psalm 76:7}}, {{Psalm 76:12|12}}; {{Psalm 89:7|89:7}}; {{Psalm 99:3|99:3}}; {{Psalm 111:9|111:9}}). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.
The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and awesome Creator of the earth.
The Lord made the heavens, an even greater task than creating the earth. The idols, made by human hands ({{Psalm 115:4|Psalm 115:4}}), created nothing.

*Splendor and majesty*: The Lord is glorious ({{Psalm 96:6|Psalm 96:6}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}; {{Psalm 148:13|148:13}}), and so are his works in nature ({{Psalm 8:1|8:1}}) and in redemption ({{Psalm 111:3|111:3}}; {{Psalm 145:5|145:5}}).

- *families of the nations*: Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see {{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}). 

- The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory ({{Psalm 8:1|Psalms 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}).

The courts of God’s sanctuary were usually not open to non-Jewish people. In this psalm, the nations of the world (people who are not Jews) are invited to come in ({{Psalm 65:4|Psalm 65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:2|84:2}}, {{Psalm 84:10|10}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 116:19|116:19}}; {{Psalm 135:2|135:2}}; {{Isaiah 1:12|Isaiah 1:12}}).

Worshipers should tremble in awe ({{Psalm 96:4|Psalm 96:4}}; see {{Psalm 18:7-15|18:7–15}}; {{Psalm 97:4|97:4}}) at the splendor of the Lord’s great power and holiness ({{Hebrews 12:25|Hebrews 12:25}}).

- The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly ({{Psalm 9:8|Psalm 9:8}}; {{Psalm 96:13|96:13}}; {{Psalm 98:9|98:9}}). He brings a time of peace and order like the world has not known since Adam and Eve lived in the garden of Eden.

- The Lord’s rule over the world stands on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” ({{Psalm 89:14|Psalm 89:14}}), so it cannot be shaken (compare {{Psalm 11:3|11:3}}).
The psalmist urges all of creation to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Compare a similar theme in {{Psalm 98:7-9|Psalm 98:7–9}}.

All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence ({{Psalm 65:13|Psalms 65:13}}; {{Psalm 72:6|72:6}}, {{Psalm 72:16|16}}; {{Isaiah 44:23|Isaiah 44:23}}; {{Isaiah 55:12|55:12}}; {{Romans 8:21-22|Romans 8:21–22}}).
The *distant shores* represent the most remote parts of the world.

God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
*Clouds … Fire … lightning*: This language shows that the Lord is coming to judge.
All creation responds to the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.

- When the Lord comes into the world, the heavens announce his righteousness ({{Psalm 50:6|Psalm 50:6}}). 

- Every nation will see the clear display of the Lord’s glory (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4a}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}; {{Isaiah 40:5|Isaiah 40:5}}).
At the Lord’s coming, when every god must bow to him, those who worship other gods will face their own foolishness (see {{Psalm 95:3-5|Psalm 95:3–5}}).
Jerusalem rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the *upright of heart*.

Godly people who live with integrity (see {{Proverbs 2:7|Proverbs 2:7}}, {{Proverbs 2:21|21}}; {{Proverbs 3:32|3:32}}; {{Proverbs 11:6|11:6}}, {{Proverbs 11:11|11}}; {{Proverbs 14:2|14:2}}) have hearts that are right before the Lord. They maintain a relationship with the Lord and live rightly with others ({{Psalm 94:15|Psalms 94:15}}; {{Psalm 125:4|125:4}}). 

The wicked plan to destroy the godly ({{Psalm 11:2|Psalm 11:2}}), but the Lord rescues them ({{Psalm 11:1|11:1}}; {{Psalm 36:10|36:10}}). Then the sorrows of the godly turn into joy and praise ({{Psalm 32:11|Psalms 32:11}}; {{Psalm 64:10|64:10}}; {{Psalm 111:1|111:1}}; {{Psalm 119:7|119:7}}).

This psalm celebrates the Lord as King. The Lord is the true King of Israel, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song to celebrate his victory and his faithfulness to them.

The Lord shows his righteous rule to all the nations of the earth. One day, this will lead to a worldwide kingdom of justice ({{Psalm 98:2|Psalm 98:2}}, {{Psalm 98:9|9}}). Because of this, all the earth should worship and rejoice together, for the Lord is coming ({{Psalm 98:4-6|Psalm 98:4–6}}).
The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also {{Isaiah 52:10|Isaiah 52:10}}).
The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see {{Psalm 96:1|Psalm 96:1}}).
The temple musicians played trumpets to gather people for meetings (compare {{Psalm 81:3|Psalm 81:3}}).
The psalm speaks as if all creation rejoices when the righteous Judge comes (see {{Psalm 93:3-4|Psalms 83:3–4}}; {{Psalm 96:11-13|96:11–13}}).

- It is appropriate to tremble and quake in response to the Lord’s holiness (see {{Psalm 96:9|Psalm 96:9}}). 

- The throne between the cherubim refers to the cover of the ark of the Testimony ({{Exodus 25:17-22|Exodus 25:17–22}}).

The Lord is the holy and righteous King ({{Isaiah 6:1-5|Isaiah 6:1–5}}). Mount Zion, where the temple of the Lord is located, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}; {{Isaiah 2:2|Isaiah 2:2}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|6:1}}). From this high place, the "great King" ({{Psalm 47:2|Psalm 47:2}}) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.

The qualities of the Lord’s rule include: 

- strength,

- justice,

- love,

- fairness, and

- righteousness (see {{Psalm 93:4|Psalms 93:4}}; {{Psalm 97:2|97:2}}, {{Psalm 97:6-7|6–7}}, {{Psalm 97:12|12}}; {{Psalm 98:2-3|98:2–3}}, {{Psalm 98:9|9}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}).
Moses and Samuel were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people ({{Exodus 32:31-32|Exodus 32:31–32}}; {{1 Samuel 12:23|1 Samuel 12:23}}).
God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from *the pillar of cloud* ({{Exodus 33:9|Exodus 33:9}}; {{Numbers 12:5-6|Numbers 12:5–6}}). For a while, the people responded to the revelation.
This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.

- The Lord is the one who determines who his people are.

- *the sheep of His pasture*: God will guide and protect his people ({{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}, {{Psalm 23:4|4}}).
Gates and courts were part of the temple in Jerusalem.
This song of praise expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

- *in my house*: This commitment to integrity might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters see *my house* as the king’s palace. The commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. 

- Living with integrity means choosing a wise lifestyle.

- The psalmist hates what the Lord hates ({{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; see {{Psalm 5:5|Psalms 5:5}}; {{Psalm 11:4-5|11:4–5}}). 

- Perverse ideas come from corrupt human hearts (compare {{Psalm 18:26|Psalm 18:26}}).
The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity ({{Psalm 101:2|Psalm 101:2}}).
The psalmist promises to remove all evil from his house and the city of the Lord, which represents the entire kingdom.
The psalmist asks the Lord not to turn away (or *hide your face*). Israel experienced God turning his face away when they were exiled.
A weak and suffering person prays for the Lord's mercy on Jerusalem and for his presence with its people.

- *Smoke* is an image of the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 37:20|Psalms 37:20}}; {{Psalm 68:2|68:2}}). 

- The psalmist’s *bones* represent his whole being (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalms 6:2}}; {{Psalm 34:19-22|34:19–22}}).
Like *withered grass,* the psalmist senses his life fading away.
*skin hangs on my bones*: The psalmist has become very thin due to his deep sorrow (see {{Psalm 102:9|Psalm 102:9}}; {{Psalm 109:24|109:24}}).
Owls often live in deserted places, such as ruined cities. Because of this, the Bible sometimes uses the owl as a sign of ruin and desolation ({{Isaiah 34:11|Isaiah 34:11}}, {{Isaiah 34:15|15}}).
The psalmist cannot sleep (see {{Psalm 63:6-8|Psalm 63:6–8}}). Like* a lone bird on a housetop,* he feels alone and separated from both friends (see {{Psalm 88:8|Psalm 88:8}}) and enemies.
The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
The psalmist feels that life is empty and short ({{Psalm 102:4|Psalms 102:4}}; {{Psalm 109:23|109:23}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}).
*forever … to all generations*: Human life is short and fragile ({{Psalm 102:3-11|Psalm 102:3–11}}). In contrast, the Lord remains forever and rules through every generation.
The topic changes from the psalmist’s troubles to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
Now is the time for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see {{Psalm 75:2|Psalm 75:2}}; {{Jeremiah 29:10|Jeremiah 29:10}}; {{Daniel 9:1-19|Daniel 9:1–19}}).

When the Lord arises ({{Psalm 102:13|Psalm 102:13}}), the nations will tremble with fear because they will see his glory (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4a}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}). Rebuilding Zion and the temple shows God's glory and fulfills this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem ({{Revelation 21:1-27|Revelation 21}}).
The people of Israel were very poor and vulnerable (*destitute*) during the exile.
*Let this be written*: The written record serves as a reminder of the Lord's goodness.
The Lord will show mercy. Both Jews and Gentiles will worship him.
*His sanctuary* refers to God's holy place in heaven (see {{Psalm 92:8-10|Psalm 92:8–10}}).

Many people (both Jews and non-Jews) will worship the Lord together (see {{Psalm 96:7|Psalm 96:7}}, {{Psalm 96:9|9}}; {{Psalm 106:48|106:48}}; {{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}; {{Isaiah 43:10-13|43:10–13}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}; {{Isaiah 60:3-7|60:3–7}}).
Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
The psalmist compares his short life ({{Psalm 102:23|Psalm 102:23}}) to God's eternal existence (compare {{Psalm 90:4|90:4}}).

- *wear out like a garment*: Unlike the eternal Creator, the created world will wear out like a piece of clothing (see {{Isaiah 40:28|Isaiah 40:28}}). 

- The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son ({{Hebrews 1:10-12|Hebrews 1:10–12}}).
The Lord’s presence provides the basis for the security and happiness of his people ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).

*all that is within me, bless His holy name*: {{Psalm 103:1-22|Psalms 103}} and {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}} both start and end with this promise ({{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}, {{Psalm 104:35|35}}; see also {{Psalm 146:1|146:1}}).
The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
The Lord revealed himself to Moses in special ways to strengthen his relationship with his people (see {{Exodus 34:6-7|Exodus 34:6–7}}; {{Numbers 14:18|Numbers 14:18}}).
If the Lord were to constantly accuse or remain angry forever, no one would be left (see {{Isaiah 54:7-8|Isaiah 54:7–8}}; {{Isaiah 57:16|57:16}}).
God’s love and forgiveness have no limits and are complete.

The Lord is like a father to his children. This idea is central to the teachings of Jesus about God's fatherhood (see {{Matthew 5:43-48|Matthew 5:43–48}}; {{Matthew 6:1|6:1}}; {{Matthew 10:19-20|10:19–20}}; {{Matthew 12:50|12:50}}; {{Luke 6:36|Luke 6:36}}; {{Luke 12:29-32|12:29–32}}; {{John 8:31-59|John 8:31–59}}; {{John 15:1-8|15:1–8}}; see also {{2 Samuel 7:14|2 Samuel 7:14}}; {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}; {{Jeremiah 31:9|31:9}}; {{Malachi 1:6|Malachi 1:6}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:16-18|2 Corinthians 6:16–18}}).
The Lord compassionately cares for weak humans (see {{Psalm 37:2|Psalm 37:2}}; {{Psalm 90:5|90:5}}; {{Psalm 92:7|92:7}}; {{Psalm 102:4|102:4}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}).
*from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends*: The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
To obey God means to be faithful and loyal to him.
The psalmist urges the Lord's angels, servants, and messengers to praise the Lord.

- God's kingdom extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. 

- The last phrase is similar to {{Psalm 103:1-2|Psalm 103:1–2}}.

- *Bless the LORD, O my soul!*: {{Psalm 103:1-22|Psalms 103}} and {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}} both begin and end with this commitment to praise ({{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}, {{Psalm 104:35|35}}). 

- *You are very great*: These words praise God for rescuing his people (see also {{Psalm 35:27|Psalms 35:27}}; {{Psalm 40:16|40:16}}; {{Psalm 70:4|70:4}}).

This creation hymn (see also {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalms 8}}, {{Psalm 33:1-22|33}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) praises God's goodness and greatness. The psalmist thinks about the current world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He views both creations as wonderfully and wisely made (compare {{Psalm 139:14|Psalm 139:14}}), as the work of the Lord's Spirit ({{Psalm 104:30|104:30}}; {{Genesis 1:2|Genesis 1:2}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:6|2 Corinthians 3:6}}).
The psalmist refers to two days of creation (see {{Genesis 1:1-8|Genesis 1:1–8}}), when God created the heavens and the light.
This poetic description pictures the clouds as *beams* that support the heavens.

- Wind and lightning (*flames of fire*) are described as God’s messengers. The Lord controls the wind, rain, and storms and uses them as he desires ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalm 77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 78:26|78:26}}; {{Psalm 135:7|135:7}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}). 

- The psalmist refers to the third day of creation ({{Genesis 1:9-13|Genesis 1:9–13}}). The Lord is master of water and earth.
At first, water covered the earth.
The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation ({{Genesis 1:9-13|Genesis 1:9–13}}).
The earth was made because God willed it.

The Lord set a firm boundary for the seas to protect the land. This shows that the Lord rules both the sea and the land. This idea also challenged the beliefs of the Canaanites, who celebrated Baal as the god who defeated the sea (see {{Psalm 29:1-11|Psalm 29}}).

The Lord rules over all waters, including seas, rivers, and springs on the land. He brought order to the waters that were once chaotic. As a result, the earth became a rich place for animals and people. Water refreshes the ground and provides life for birds and other animals.
The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it ({{Genesis 1:9-30|Genesis 1:9–30}}).
*for man to cultivate*: People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
Both wine and olive oil can be misused (compare {{Proverbs 21:17|Proverbs 21:17}}), but the Lord gives them as gifts to improve life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by bread.

- The storks migrated from northern Europe and stayed in Palestine during the winter. 

- *rock badgers*: These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky areas.

- *the moon to mark the seasons*: Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon.

- *the sun knows when to set*: This poetic description reflects what people normally see. The sun goes down at a regular time each evening.
The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation ({{Genesis 1:14-19|Genesis 1:14–19}}). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.
Cycles of darkness and dawn mark the days on earth.
The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together (land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures). The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
*teeming with creatures beyond number*: The ocean is full of all kinds of life (see {{Genesis 1:20-21|Genesis 1:20–21}}). This shows the Lord's creative work.

- *ships pass*: Commercial ships used for sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see {{Isaiah 2:16|Isaiah 2:16}}; {{Isaiah 23:1|23:1}}, {{Isaiah 23:3|3}}). 

- *Leviathan*: The psalmist describes this feared sea creature as something the Lord created and controls.
All living things depend on the Lord, who provides what they need and who has power over life and death (compare {{Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11}}).

*When You send Your Spirit*: Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew *ruakh*, which means "breath, wind, or spirit"). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal ({{Isaiah 32:15-20|Isaiah 32:15–20}}).
The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalms 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}) and delights in his new creation (see {{Isaiah 65:19|Isaiah 65:19}}).
The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.
The trembling earth and the smoking mountains represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see {{Psalm 18:7-15|Psalm 18:7–15}}).

- The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. 

- The final phrase returns to the opening words of {{Psalm 104:1|Psalm 104:1}} (see also {{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 146:1|146:1}}).

The poet begins with a call to give thanks (see also {{Psalm 106:1|Psalms 106:1}}; {{Psalm 107:1|107:1}}; {{Psalm 118:1|118:1}}; {{Psalm 136:1|136:1}}). The other psalms continue with the refrain "for He is good!" The rest of {{Psalm 105:1-45|Psalm 105}} tells of God's goodness.

- This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys:

- from Ur to Canaan ({{Psalm 105:12|Psalm 105:12}}),

- to Egypt ({{Psalm 105:17|Psalm 105:17}}, {{Psalm 105:23|23}}),

- through the wilderness ({{Psalm 105:37|Psalm 105:37}}, {{Psalm 105:41|41}}), and

- back to Canaan ({{Psalm 105:44|Psalm 105:44}}).

These events fulfilled the Lord's promise to Abraham ({{Psalm 105:9|Psalm 105:9}}, {{Psalm 105:42|42}}), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering turned into glory, serves as a model of encouragement for Israel ({{Psalm 105:16-25|Psalm 105:16–25}}). 

- {{Psalm 105:1-15|Psalm 105:1–15}} (along with {{Psalm 96:1-13|96}}; {{Psalm 106:1|106:1}}, {{Psalm 106:47-48|47–48}}) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16}}.

Psalms 105 and 106 praise God for his faithful love. Psalm 105 does this by reminding the Israelites of the wonderful things God has done. Psalm 106 does this in a different way. It reminds the Jews how God was faithful even when they forgot about him.

The events mentioned in these psalms are recorded in other books of the Bible. Those in Psalm 105 are recorded in the books from Genesis through to Joshua. Those in Psalm 106 are recorded in the books from Exodus through to 2 Chronicles.

In Psalm 105, remembering God’s covenants, miracles and laws led the Israelites to praise him. Talking about what God had done was one way to teach their children about God.

Psalm 105 ends by reminding God’s people why God allowed them to live in Canaan. They were to obey him and live as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. But they didn’t do that. They disobeyed God over and over again. They followed the practices of the nations around them instead of following the Mount Sinai covenant.
