Psalm 106 tells this history. Verse 47 shows that the speakers of this psalm were living in exile. They had been forced to live far away from their land. This was God’s judgement against them for their sins and the sins of their people.

They talked about the evil things they had done for a reason. It helped them understand why God had brought judgement against them. It also helped them understand something about God. God had always remained faithful to his people. Time after time God’s people had forgotten about him. But God always remembered his covenant. He forgave his people and saved them when they cried out to him. This helped the speakers be bold enough to ask God to save them again. The speaker at the beginning of Psalm 106 was sure that God would save them. God’s people would celebrate, give thanks and praise him when he rescued them.

The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David ({{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
The covenant is the Lord’s unbreakable promise to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see {{Genesis 12:1-9|Genesis 12:1–9}}; {{Genesis 15:1-21|15:1–21}}).

God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham's descendants as their special possession. They could live there as God's people ({{Psalm 105:44-45|Psalm 105:44–45}}; {{Genesis 12:7|Genesis 12:7}}; {{Genesis 15:7-21|15:7–21}}).
The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs, the early fathers of the nation.
Abraham was one of the nation's prophets ({{Genesis 20:7|Genesis 20:7}}).
These verses tell the story of Joseph (see {{Genesis 37:1-41:57|Genesis 37–41}}).

- *his prediction*: Literally, *his word*.

- *the word of the LORD proved him right*: See {{Genesis 39:6-12|Genesis 39:6–12}}.
Egypt (Hebrew *Mitsrayim*) is called the land of Ham.
These verses describe Israel's suffering in Egypt (see {{Exodus 1:1-14|Exodus 1:1–14}}).
The psalmist tells the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (see {{Exodus 7:20-12:30|Exodus 7:20–12:30}}).
*none … stumbled*: The Lord protected all of his people (compare {{Psalm 9:3|Psalm 9:3}}).

The exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God's promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob ({{Psalm 105:9-10|Psalm 105:9–10}}). Unlike {{Psalm 78:1-72|Psalm 78}}, the poet describes the Lord's goodness without mentioning Israel's history of rebellion (compare {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalm 106}}).
The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a fire in the darkness ({{Exodus 13:22|Exodus 13:22}}).
The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.

Canaan was a land of pagan nations (see {{Psalm 111:6|Psalm 111:6}}). The psalmist might also be thinking about God's promise to Abraham ({{Genesis 24:60|Genesis 24:60}}) regarding the lands given to Isaac ({{Genesis 26:3|Genesis 26:3}}).
The Lord planned for Israel to show who he is by obeying him. Israel was to be his example among the nations.

- The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own past sins. From their humble state in exile, they asked for redemption and restoration. They hoped to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his anger. 

The psalm ends with a memory of the Lord’s past mercy and hope for renewed mercy ({{Psalm 106:44-48|Psalm 106:44–48}}). Israel failed, but the Lord remains constant. 

- Verses 1, {{Psalm 47:1-48:14|47–48}} (along with {{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalms 96}}; {{Psalm 105:1-15|105:1–15}}) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16:1–43}}.
Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.

The story of Israel's redemption includes their sinful actions from the time of their ancestors to now ({{Psalm 106:43|Psalm 106:43}}). The themes of sin and God's anger towards sin start and end Book Four ({{Psalm 90:1-9|Psalms 90:1–9}}; {{Psalm 106:6|106:6}}, {{Psalm 106:23|23}}, {{Psalm 106:43|43}}).
The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.

*they … failed to wait*: God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (for example, see {{Exodus 15:24|Exodus 15:24}}; {{Exodus 16:2-3|16:2–3}}; {{Exodus 17:1-3|17:1–3}}; {{Numbers 14:26-45|Numbers 14:26–45}}; {{Numbers 21:4-9|21:4–9}}).
*He … sent a wasting disease*: See {{Exodus 32:35|Exodus 32:35}} and {{Numbers 11:33|Numbers 11:33}}.

- The people became jealous because they wanted the same role as the priests God had chosen (see {{Numbers 16:1-35|Numbers 16:1–35}}). 

- *The earth opened up*: See {{Numbers 16:28-33|Numbers 16:28–33}}.
*they … worshiped a molten image*: The people forgot their Savior and worshiped idols (see {{Exodus 32:1-6|Exodus 32:1–6}}).
*the land of Ham*: This means Egypt ({{Psalm 106:21|Psalm 106:21}}).

- The people disobeyed God’s command when they refused to enter the* pleasant land* (the promised land (see {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}). 

- *they did not believe His promise*: See {{Numbers 13:25-14:12|Numbers 13:25–14:12}}.

God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile ({{Numbers 14:26-30|Numbers 14:26–30}}). These judgments came because the people rejected God’s word ({{Psalm 106:24-25|Psalm 106:24–25}}) and provoked the Lord's anger ({{Psalm 106:28-46|106:28–46}}).
*they yoked themselves to Baal of Peor*: See {{Numbers 25:3|Numbers 25:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:3|Deuteronomy 4:3}}.
When the Israelites entered the land, they brought their idol worship with them. Their behavior stayed the same, and they angered the Lord with their actions.

Phinehas killed an Israelite man who openly turned away from the Lord ({{Numbers 25:3-8|Numbers 25:3–8}}). Because his action stopped the plague, the psalm credits him with righteousness. In this psalm he is presented as a stronger example of zeal for the Lord than Moses, who failed at Meribah ({{Numbers 20:11-13|Numbers 20:11–13}}).

Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the promised land. Instead of destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their customs (see {{Judges 2:1-3|Judges 2:1–3}}, {{Judges 2:11-15|11–15}}; {{Judges 3:5-6|3:5–6}}).
The gods of other nations were really demons (see {{Deuteronomy 32:17|Deuteronomy 32:17}}).
Idolatry is like adultery. Both make God’s people unclean before the Lord (see {{Leviticus 18:24|Leviticus 18:24}}; {{Hosea 5:3|Hosea 5:3}}).
God hated Israel's sin, just as he hates all sin.

The psalmist again talks about the Babylonian exile ({{Psalm 106:26-27|Psalm 106:26–27}}). The Lord judged Israel harshly, but he also restrained his anger, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
When Israel fell, the destruction was not complete. The Lord had compassion on his people and left a remnant (a small group of people who remained).
*He remembered … and relented*: Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his covenant ({{Psalm 105:8|Psalm 105:8}}).
Even though the exile was harsh, the Lord still protected his people (see {{2 Kings 25:27-29|2 Kings 25:27–29}}).

*gather us*: The community prays for God to bring them back from exile (see {{Psalm 102:19-22|Psalms 102:19–22}}; {{Psalm 107:3|107:3}}; see also {{Isaiah 11:12|Isaiah 11:12}}; {{Isaiah 40:11|40:11}}; {{Isaiah 43:5|43:5}}; {{Isaiah 54:7|54:7}}; {{Isaiah 56:8|56:8}}; {{Isaiah 66:18|66:18}}).

- This doxology (a short song of praise) ends Book Four (compare {{Psalm 41:13|Psalms 41:13}}; {{Psalm 89:52|89:52}}). 

- *from everlasting to everlasting*: The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four ({{Psalm 90:1-2|Psalm 90:1–2}}). 

- *Let all the people say, “Amen!”*: The Hebrew word *’amen* means “It is true.” The faithful accept the Lord’s will during exile and his promise to be their God.

This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. The psalmist begins by urging the redeemed to praise God for his goodness ({{Psalm 107:1-3|Psalm 107:1–3}}). The psalmist then presents four examples of people whom the Lord saved from trouble ({{Psalm 107:4-32|Psalm 107:4–32}}). He summarizes the Lord’s control over everything ({{Psalm 107:33-42|Psalm 107:33–42}}) and ends with an invitation to recognize God’s loving devotion in all parts of life ({{Psalm 107:43|107:43}}).
The redeemed might be all who came out of exile.
People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.

Those who were lost in the *desert wastelands* thank God for his rescue. The* desert wastelands* might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom ({{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}; {{Proverbs 4:10-15|Proverbs 4:10–15}}).
The psalmist does not say what caused his trouble and distress. Because the problem is not specific, people in many different situations can identify with the laments.

- God led them like a shepherd (see {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}). 

- Verse 8 is repeated in {{Psalm 107:15|Psalm 107:15}}, {{Psalm 107:21|21}}, {{Psalm 107:31|31}}.
The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
God’s counsel includes his instruction and will.

Exhausted from their hard work ({{Lamentations 5:13|Lamentations 5:13}}), the people *stumbled*. While this might be expected of the wicked ({{Psalm 9:3|Psalms 9:3}}; {{Psalm 27:2|27:2}}), it was different from the Israelites' escape from Egypt ({{Psalm 105:37|105:37}}).
Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.

The Lord creates ({{Genesis 1:3|Genesis 1:3}}) and sustains the universe ({{Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3}}) simply by speaking ({{Psalm 147:18|Psalm 147:18}}). When God speaks, people are also healed ({{Matthew 8:8|Matthew 8:8}}).
Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (compare {{Jonah 1:4|Jonah 1:4}}; {{Matthew 8:26|Matthew 8:26}}).
This call for public praise expands on the repeated phrases in {{Psalm 107:21-22|Psalms 107:21–22}} and {{Psalm 107:31|107:31}}.
The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren ({{Psalm 74:15|Psalm 74:15}}; {{Isaiah 35:6-7|Isaiah 35:6–7}}).
These two sections ({{Psalm 107:33-38|Psalm 107:33–38}}, {{Psalm 107:39-42|39–42}}) expand the theme of the Lord’s complete authority and power over things that humans cannot control.
God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s families and herds ({{Psalm 127:3|Psalms 127:3}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}; compare {{Psalm 109:8|109:8}}).
People often become poor when their leaders are oppressive.
The Lord rejects human rulers who act unjustly. He corrects their wrongdoing and brings justice on the earth.
The large families of the poor are evidence of God’s blessing.
Justice wins in God’s world ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}), and Israel’s history shows God’s loving devotion.
This psalm combines two parts from David's other psalms (compare {{Psalm 57:5|Psalms 57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:7-11|7–11}}; {{Psalm 60:5-12|60:5–12}}).
The psalmist finds no evidence that God cares (see {{Psalm 28:1|Psalm 28:1}}).

The psalmist starts this lament by accusing his accusers of repaying good with evil ({{Psalm 109:1-5|Psalm 109:1–5}}). At the end of the psalm, he prays to the Lord, seeking protection ({{Psalm 109:21-25|Psalm 109:21–25}}) and vengeance ({{Psalm 109:26-31|109:26–31}}).
The psalmist shows kindness and godliness (see {{Psalm 35:12-14|Psalm 35:12–14}}), but faces stubborn opposition and hatred.
The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks They say, which makes it unclear who is speaking.
The wicked person apparently held a position of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot ({{Acts 1:20-26|Acts 1:20–26}}).

Family members of people guilty of capital crimes sometimes died with the offender ({{Numbers 16:1-33|Numbers 16:1–33}}; {{Joshua 7:1-25|Joshua 7:1–25}}) or had their property taken away ({{1 Kings 21:13-16|1 Kings 21:13–16}}).
If one’s family name was blotted out, it meant there was no offspring to continue the family name or remember its history (see {{Proverbs 10:7|Proverbs 10:7}}).

Children share in the sinful condition of their parents ({{Psalm 51:5|Psalm 51:5}}; {{Exodus 20:5|Exodus 20:5}}; {{Ephesians 2:3|Ephesians 2:3}}). The speaker asks the Lord to punish this guilty person also for the sins of his family who lived before him (compare {{Matthew 23:35-36|Matthew 23:35–36}}).
The defendant committed very serious crimes that carried the death penalty and did not show even basic decency.
Cursing is the accused person’s whole way of life.
The psalmist asks God to act fairly and give people what they deserve (see {{Psalm 94:23|Psalm 94:23}}).
The Lord's reputation is important. If the wicked win, people might think the Lord is also wicked and be tempted to act wickedly ({{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}).
Feeling vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist asks his Lord for help. The accusations have crushed his spirit and drained his physical strength.
A *lengthening shadow* suggests a temporary, empty life ({{Psalm 102:11|Psalms 102:11}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}). A single *locust* can be easily brushed off clothing.
These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.
The Lord’s servant demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
The psalmist was accused of being *clothed with disgrace* ({{Psalm 109:18|Psalm 109:18}}). Now, he asks that his accusers *wear their shame* like a piece of clothing.

- The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}; {{1 Chronicles 22:10|1 Chronicles 22:10}}), but he failed ({{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}). This decree restores and elevates his position. 

- *The LORD*: This title represents the Hebrew name *Yahweh,* which is God’s personal name (see {{Exodus 3:6-14|Exodus 3:6–14}}; {{Exodus 6:2-8|6:2–8}}; {{Exodus 20:2|20:2}}). 

- *my Lord:* The Hebrew word *’adoni* means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist understood God’s messianic ruler (the king chosen by God) to be greater than himself. The New Testament often quotes this psalm to show that Jesus is the Messiah ({{Matthew 22:44-45|Matthew 22:44–45}}; {{Mark 12:36-37|Mark 12:36–37}}; {{Luke 20:42-44|Luke 20:42–44}}; {{Acts 2:34-35|Acts 2:34–35}}; {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}). 

- The Lord’s *right hand *represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him ({{Psalm 80:17|Psalm 80:17}}). 

Jesus claimed this position for himself ({{Matthew 26:64|Matthew 26:64}}; {{Mark 14:62|Mark 14:62}}; {{Mark 16:19|16:19}}; {{Luke 22:69|Luke 22:69}}), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having gone up to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father ({{Acts 2:33|Acts 2:33}}; {{Acts 5:31|5:31}}; {{Acts 7:55-56|7:55–56}}; {{Romans 8:34|Romans 8:34}}; {{Ephesians 1:20|Ephesians 1:20}}; {{Colossians 3:1|Colossians 3:1}}; {{Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3}}; {{Hebrews 8:1|8:1}}; {{Hebrews 10:12|10:12}}; {{Hebrews 12:2|12:2}}). 

- Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes shown placing their feet on the backs of their defeated enemies as on a footstool (see {{Hebrews 10:12-13|Hebrews 10:12–13}}).

Psalm 110 is one of the psalms that isn’t a prayer from someone to God. Instead, it announced God’s promises for a certain king from David’s family line. God would let this lord and king sit at his right hand. This meant that God gave him authority and a place of honour.

This king would be a priest forever like Melchizedek. David was lord and king. But the lord and king here was not David. No king of Israel served as a priest. Priests were from the family line of Levi. But they couldn’t serve forever because they died.

Many years later, Zechariah prophesied about someone who was a priest and a king. This person would combine the positions of king and priest in himself (Zechariah 6:13). Many Jews came to understand something about this person. They understood that Psalm 110 and Zechariah were talking about the messiah.

Jesus used words from Psalm 110 to show something. Jesus showed that he is the lord that the psalm talked about (Matthew 22:41–46). New Testament writers understood this as well (Acts 2:33–36). Jesus is the priest and king God made the promises of Psalm 110 about. The writer of Hebrews showed how this was true (Hebrews 6:20 – 7:28).

Jesus and the apostles quote this psalm to explain the unique role and authority of Jesus as the Messiah ({{Matthew 22:43-45|Matthew 22:43–45}}; {{Acts 2:32-36|Acts 2:32–36}}). The psalm also confirms God’s covenant with David. It gives hope that God will fulfill his promise in the future (see {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}).
The kingdom will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.

- God had made an unbreakable oath and covenant with David. When the exile seemed to end the line of kings from David's family ({{Psalm 89:38|Psalm 89:38}}), it created a crisis for God’s people. The placement of {{Psalm 110:1-7|Psalm 110}} in Book Five points again to the future of David’s line. David’s descendant must live according to God’s standard of integrity ({{Psalm 101:1-8|Psalm 101}}). His rule will also be shaped by God’s kingship ({{Psalm 93:1-100:5|Psalms 93–100}}). 

- *You are a priest forever*: The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The kings from David’s family had a limited priestly role. They supported and organized the worship of the temple. For example, David brought the ark to Jerusalem ({{2 Samuel 6:15|2 Samuel 6:15}}) and organized temple services ({{1 Chronicles 6:31-48|1 Chronicles 6:31–48}}; {{1 Chronicles 15:11-26|15:11–26}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:4-42|16:4–42}}; {{1 Chronicles 23:4-32|23:4–32}}; {{1 Chronicles 25:1|25:1}}). Solomon oversaw the construction of the temple ({{1 Kings 5:1-7:51|1 Kings 5:1–7:51}}). 

Even so, the offices of king and priest were separate in Israel. In the messianic kingdom, the king will also serve as a priest. He will be like Melchizedek, the king of Salem who was also a priest ({{Genesis 14:18|Genesis 14:18}}). The New Testament explains that Jesus Christ fulfills this new order of priesthood (see {{Hebrews 5:6-10|Hebrews 5:6–10}}; {{Hebrews 6:20-7:25|6:20–7:25}}).

- *at Your right hand*: This position brings help and protection (see {{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalms 16:7–8}}; {{Psalm 108:13|108:13}}). 

- The Lord will strike down rebellious kings. Rebellion against the Lord leads to death ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}; {{Romans 6:23|Romans 6:23}}).

The new priestly role of David's descendant does not cancel his old role as a conquering ruler. He still needs to bring the nations under his rule ({{Psalm 110:2-3|Psalm 110:2–3}}; see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).
God’s messianic ruler wins victory with renewed strength, like a traveler who drinks from streams along the way ({{Psalm 110:3|Psalm 110:3}}).

The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see {{Psalm 116:5-7|Psalm 116:5–7}}). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.

This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is:

- righteous,

- gracious,

- compassionate,

- faithful,

- just,

- trustworthy,

- upright,

- holy, and

- awe-inspiring ({{Psalm 111:3|Psalm 111:3}}, {{Psalm 111:4|4}}, {{Psalm 111:7|7}}, {{Psalm 111:8|8}}, {{Psalm 111:9|9}}).

God's character gives hope in the covenant relationship ({{Psalm 111:5|Psalm 111:5}}). God rescued Israel from Egypt ({{Psalm 111:9|Psalm 111:9}}). God gave them the land ({{Psalm 111:6|111:6}}). God provides for his people ({{Psalm 111:5|111:5}}). However, God expects those in this relationship to also be righteous and have integrity.
The word *Hallelujah!* is repeated throughout this group of psalms.
God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing food. He remembers his covenant with Abraham (see {{Psalm 105:8-11|Psalm 105:8–11}}).

Giving Israel the land of other nations was just and good. The Lord was judging those nations and showing grace to Israel. However, if the Israelites do not live faithfully and with integrity, they will also lose the land. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.
The people of the exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.

True wisdom is the source of life ({{Proverbs 3:18|Proverbs 3:18}}; {{Proverbs 9:11|9:11}}; {{Ecclesiastes 7:12|Ecclesiastes 7:12}}). It starts with the fear of the Lord ({{Proverbs 9:10|Proverbs 9:10}}).

The fear of the Lord leads to a wise life that honors God and brings blessing to the family and the community. The godly follow God with joy. Their obedience does not come from fear like a slave obeying a master.

This psalm repeats the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord ({{Psalm 111:1-10|Psalm 111}}). Wise people have reasons to be happy ({{Psalm 112:1-5|Psalm 112:1–5}}) and strong ({{Psalm 112:6-10|112:6–10}}).

*blessed*: Everyone will recognize the children of godly people (see {{Psalm 127:4|Psalm 127:4}}) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see {{Psalm 1:3|1:3}}; compare {{Matthew 6:20|Matthew 6:20}}).

Godly people imitate God by being generous, compassionate, and righteous ({{Psalm 51:1|Psalms 51:1}}; {{Psalm 111:1-10|111:1–10}}; {{2 Corinthians 9:9|2 Corinthians 9:9}}). They lend money to the poor without charging interest ({{Psalm 15:5|Psalms 15:5}}; {{Psalm 112:9|112:9}}; {{Exodus 22:25|Exodus 22:25}}).

The wise avoid mistakes because they are honest and compassionate ({{Psalm 15:5|Psalms 15:5}}; {{Psalm 37:23-24|37:23–24}}). People will remember them for a long time ({{Proverbs 10:7|Proverbs 10:7}}).
Because the godly trust that God will rescue them and give them victory, they face their enemies with confidence ({{Psalm 59:10|Psalms 59:10}}; {{Psalm 112:4|112:4}}; {{Psalm 118:7|118:7}}).
Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving ({{2 Corinthians 9:9|2 Corinthians 9:9}}).

- The wicked *gnash their teeth* in anger due to their bitter envy ({{Psalm 35:16|Psalms 35:16}}; {{Psalm 37:12|37:12}}). The strength and reputation of the godly create conflict with those who wish them harm. 

- The wicked will retreat in fear and shame.

*the name of the LORD*: God's personal name (Hebrew *Yahweh;* see {{Exodus 3:15|Exodus 3:15}}) reveals who he is (his nature, character, and reputation). He is exalted at all times (now and forever) and in every place (from east to west).

This song of praise celebrates the greatness of the Lord's name and glory. God is exalted and glorious in heaven ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}). He also stoops down to care for the lowly and needy on earth ({{Psalm 113:5-9|Psalm 113:5–9}}).

These psalms are called the Egyptian Hallel. *Hallel* means “praise.” Jewish people use these psalms during Passover, which began when God brought Israel out of Egypt in the exodus. The people recite {{Psalm 113:1-114:8|Psalms 113–114}} before the Passover meal, and {{Psalm 115:1-118:29|Psalms 115–118}} are recited afterward.

The Lord’s glory extends to the heavens ({{Psalm 57:5|Psalms 57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:11|11}}; {{Psalm 99:2|99:2}}; {{Psalm 108:5|108:5}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}) and throughout the world of human relationships.
The Lord is unlike anyone else, yet he personally cares for people on earth.
The Lord humbles himself to connect directly with his people (see {{Psalm 138:6|Psalm 138:6}}; {{Philippians 2:6-8|Philippians 2:6–8}}).
These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise ({{1 Samuel 2:8-9|1 Samuel 2:8–9a}}).

- People in this culture often treated a woman without children with shame or contempt ({{Genesis 16:4|Genesis 16:4}}). But the Lord has the power to make her a happy mother. For example: 

- Sarah ({{Genesis 21:2|Genesis 21:2}}),

- Rebekah ({{Genesis 25:21|Genesis 25:21}}),

- Rachel ({{Genesis 30:23|Genesis 30:23}}), and

- Hannah ({{1 Samuel 1:20|1 Samuel 1:20}}).

- God's greatness and goodness give people many reasons to praise him.

- At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the promised land, Israel was one holy kingdom ({{Exodus 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5–6}}). 

- The mention of Judah and Israel as separate lands shows the psalm was written after the kingdom was divided ({{1 Kings 12:16-17|1 Kings 12:16–17}}; compare {{1 Samuel 11:8|1 Samuel 11:8}}; {{1 Kings 1:35|1 Kings 1:35}}), and probably after the exile. Judah became God's sanctuary because the people worshiped God there. His tabernacle, and later his temple, were located there.

This song celebrates the Lord's power in nature. It remembers Israel's start as a nation during the exodus ({{Psalm 114:1-2|Psalm 114:1–2}}) and their entry into the promised land ({{Psalm 114:3-6|114:3–6}}). It encourages respect for the God of Jacob ({{Psalm 114:7-8|Psalm 114:7–8}}).

- *fled*: God parted the waters so that Israel could escape Egypt ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalm 77:17–18}}; {{Exodus 14:1-31|Exodus 14}}). 

- The Jordan River *turned back* when Israel arrived to cross it (see {{Joshua 3:1-17|Joshua 3}}). 

- *skipped like rams*: God's presence made the mountains quake ({{Exodus 19:16-20|Exodus 19:16–20}}).
The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the exodus.
The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

This is a song of thanksgiving for God's blessings. The community gives all glory to the Lord, the true source of hope and blessing. Those who trust in idols feel great disappointment. The Creator's blessing extends to future generations ({{Psalm 115:14|Psalm 115:14}}), especially to the priests ({{Psalm 115:12|115:12}}).

*Where is their God?*: People question God's presence or power when he does not act as they expect (compare {{Psalm 14:1|Psalms 14:1}}; {{Psalm 42:3|42:3}}, {{Psalm 42:10|10}}). However, God is in the heavens. He has all power, authority, and knowledge. He does as he wishes, not what people think he should do. He carries out his plans according to his will ({{Ephesians 1:11|Ephesians 1:11}}) and acts in his own time and ways.

- This entire section is repeated in {{Psalm 135:15-20|Psalm 135:15–20}}. 

- Unlike the Lord ({{Psalm 95:3-5|Psalm 95:3–5}}), idols cannot do anything. They are useless.
Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those who trust in them ({{Isaiah 44:20|Isaiah 44:20}}).

*Israel … O house of Aaron … You who fear the LORD*: The psalmist urges everyone in the God-fearing community to trust in the living God. This threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true helper and shield (compare {{Psalm 118:2-4|Psalm 118:2–4}}).
The groups mentioned in {{Psalm 115:9-11|Psalm 115:9–11}} receive assurance of the Lord's blessing, no matter their social status (see {{Psalm 113:8|113:8}}).

- The psalmist blesses ({{Psalm 107:37-38|Psalm 107:37–38}}, {{Psalm 107:41|41}}) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. 

- *the Maker of heaven and earth*: This phrase speaks about how the Lord created everything and has power over all creation.

- *The highest heavens belong to the LORD*: God's exaltation starts in heaven ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}), far above the gods of other nations. The earth also belongs to him ({{Psalm 47:9|Psalm 47:9}}; {{Psalm 95:4|95:4}}). 

- The dead cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living praise God in thanksgiving for his blessings ({{Psalm 79:13|Psalm 79:13}}).
*I love the LORD*: This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see {{Psalm 18:1|Psalm 18:1}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:5|Deuteronomy 6:5}}) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.

Psalm 116 is a poem that gives thanks to God. The speaker explains why they love God. It’s because God heard their cry for help and took action to save them.

This psalm has many things in common with Psalm 22. First, the speaker recognises things that are true about God. This includes God being full of tender love. Second, the speaker describes how they felt when they were suffering. They were sad, terrified and in great pain. Third, the speaker trusted in God even when they were facing danger.

What is different from Psalm 22 is that God has already rescued the speaker. That is why they are thanking God. They show that they are thankful in many ways. They worship God and offer a sacrifice. They tell others what God has done for them. They keep their promises to God and serve him faithfully.

This song of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death ({{Psalm 116:1-11|Psalm 116:1–11}}). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly ({{Psalm 116:12-19|Psalm 116:12–19}}).
Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people({{Psalm 107:41|Psalm 107:41}}; {{Psalm 113:6-8|113:6–8}}), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
It is not clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s name (which represents God's reputation).
The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see {{Psalm 111:1-5|Psalm 111:1–5}}) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
People with childlike faith readily receive God's wisdom and instruction ({{Psalm 19:7-11|Psalm 19:7–11}}; {{Matthew 18:3-4|Matthew 18:3–4}}).
The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had suffered, the Lord was faithful. However, people are all liars.

*I will walk before the LORD*: The psalmist lived with integrity. After experiencing deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see {{Psalm 56:13|Psalm 56:13}}; compare {{Job 42:5|Job 42:5}}).
*I believed*: Paul quotes this phrase in {{2 Corinthians 4:13|2 Corinthians 4:13}}.

- The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude.

- All he has done for the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life.

- The *cup of salvation* overflows with God’s blessings ({{Psalm 23:5|Psalm 23:5}}), unlike the cup of judgment ({{Psalm 75:8|75:8}}). 

- The psalmist makes *vows* ({{Psalm 116:18|Psalm 116:18}}) to praise the Lord publicly ({{Psalm 116:17-18|116:17–18}}).
No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.
Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel ({{Romans 15:11|Romans 15:11}}).
This psalm is the shortest in the Psalter. It invites all people of the earth to praise the Lord for his *loving devotion and faithfulness.*

The psalmist joyfully thanks the Lord for his goodness and urges others to trust in his *loving devotion* ({{Psalm 118:1-4|Psalm 118:1–4}}, {{Psalm 118:29|29}}). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel ({{Psalm 113:1-118:29|Psalms 113–118}}).
*Israel … the house of Aaron … those who fear the LORD*: These three groups represent the entire covenant community (compare {{Psalm 115:9-11|Psalms 115:9–11}}; {{Psalm 135:19-20|135:19–20}}).
The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.

- *The LORD is on my side*: Compare {{Romans 8:31|Romans 8:31;}} {{Hebrews 13:6|Hebrews 13:6}}. 

- God's presence removes the need to fear people ({{Psalm 56:11|Psalm 56:11}}). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue ({{Psalm 59:10|Psalm 59:10}}; {{Psalm 112:8|Psalm 112:8}}).
Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders ({{Psalm 118:6|Psalms 118:6}}; {{Psalm 146:3|146:3}}).

- Strength comes from *the name of the LORD*. This is shown by the threefold repetition of the attackers, the *name of the LORD*, and the victory he gives.

- Even when hostile people surrounded the psalmist, the Lord *extinguished them like burning thorns* (see {{Isaiah 9:18|Isaiah 9:18}}; {{Isaiah 10:17|10:17}}).
The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s strong *right hand,* which kept him from death.
God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (see {{Psalm 116:6|Psalm 116:6}}, {{Psalm 116:12-19|12–19}}).

The *cornerstone* shapes and supports a building or arch. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord selects and places this stone for his sanctuary ({{Isaiah 28:16|Isaiah 28:16}}). 

Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone ({{Matthew 21:42|Matthew 21:42}}; {{Mark 12:10-11|Mark 12:10–11}}; {{Luke 20:17|Luke 20:17}}; see {{Acts 4:11|Acts 4:11}}; {{Ephesians 2:20|Ephesians 2:20}}; {{1 Peter 2:6-7|1 Peter 2:6–7}}).
The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.
*This is the day that the LORD has made*: The Lord's victory has begun, but it will be completed on another day ({{Psalm 118:25|Psalm 118:25}}).
The psalmist ends with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

- The one who comes in the name of the Lord brings the Lord’s complete victory (see {{Psalm 118:10-12|Psalm 118:10–12}}). 

- When Jesus triumphantly entered Jerusalem, the crowds shouted blessings. They used phrases from this verse ({{Matthew 21:9|Matthew 21:9}}; {{Mark 11:9|Mark 11:9}}; {{Luke 19:38|Luke 19:38}}; {{John 12:13|John 12:13}}). 

Jesus quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem ({{Matthew 23:39|Matthew 23:39}}; {{Luke 13:35|Luke 13:35}}).

Wise people are happy. They have integrity (see {{Psalm 84:11|Psalm 84:11}}) and follow God's guidance. They obey God's teachings and seek them with complete devotion (see {{Psalm 27:7|Psalm 27:7}}; {{Psalm 119:10|119:10}}, {{Psalm 119:45|45}}, {{Psalm 119:94|94}}, {{Psalm 119:155|155}}). They reject all evil forms. Compare {{Psalm 1:1-2|Psalm 1:1–2}}.

*Aleph* (א) is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 is written as an acrostic poem. Each section has eight verses, and every verse in that section begins with the same Hebrew letter. The first section begins with *Aleph*.

God, the author of these instructions, commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

Psalm 119 talks about the Mount Sinai covenant as a blessing for God’s people. It praises God for how wonderful his laws are. These are the laws recorded in the Law of Moses. Obeying them leads to wisdom, joy and life.

The poem is divided into 22 sections. Each section has eight verses. At the beginning of each section there is a word in the Hebrew language. These are the names of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 is an alphabet poem.

This psalm blends wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. It often uses eight Hebrew words translated as: 

- “Instructions” 

- “law” 

- “words” 

- “commandments”

- “statutes”

- “judgments”

- “promises” 

- “precepts“

These words encourage love for and obedience to God's instructions in the Scriptures (see {{2 Timothy 3:14-17|2 Timothy 3:14–17}}). A deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
To keep God’s commandments means to guard them by obeying them.

- A young person often acts foolishly ({{Proverbs 22:15|Proverbs 22:15}}) and can easily make mistakes that ruin their life ({{Proverbs 7:6-23|Proverbs 7:6–23}}). However, youth is the best time to build self-discipline and seek wisdom (see {{Psalm 34:11|Psalm 34:11}}; {{Proverbs 1:4|Proverbs 1:4}}). 

- *keep his way pure*: This means avoiding corruption by evil and sin and developing the integrity described in {{Psalm 15:1-5|Psalm 15}}.

*Beth* (ב) is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It makes the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist is determined to stay pure and encourages gaining wisdom through God's principles ({{Psalm 119:9|Psalm 119:9}}) and instructions ({{Psalm 119:10-16|119:10–16}}).
The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not stray.
God's wisdom is more valuable than any wealth people desire ({{Psalm 119:72|Psalm 119:72}}, {{Psalm 119:127|127}}; {{Proverbs 3:14-15|Proverbs 3:14–15}}).
The path of wisdom involves thinking deeply about God's teachings (see {{Psalm 119:1|Psalm 119:1}}, {{Psalm 119:3|3}}). Wise people consider the meaning of God's word.

The psalmist wants to live a life full of praise and obedience to please the Lord ({{Psalm 118:17|Psalms 118:17}}; {{Psalm 119:25|119:25}}, {{Psalm 119:77|77}}, {{Psalm 119:116|116}}, {{Psalm 119:144|144}}, {{Psalm 119:175|175}}). Only the Lord can remove his enemies and help him understand the wonderful truths in God's teachings.

*Gimel *(ג) is the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

Like a stranger in a hostile land, God's servant needs God's guidance.
The arrogant are probably those who mock the psalmist (Psalm {{Psalm 119:22-23|119:22–23}}).
Those who meditate on God’s instructions receive wise advice from them.

*Daleth *(ד) is the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The poet feels deep pain and sadness but asks the Lord to give him strength. He wants to follow the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s discipline ({{Psalm 118:17-18|Psalms 118:17–18}}; {{Psalm 119:67|119:67}}, {{Psalm 119:71|71}}, {{Psalm 119:75|75}}), but his instruction renews the weary soul (see {{Psalm 119:12|119:12}}).

- *path of deceit*: Self-deception comes from sinful human nature ({{Jeremiah 17:9|Jeremiah 17:9}}). It leads to foolishness. 

- Access to God’s word is a privilege, not a right.

*He *(ה) is the fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
The love for money can lead to sin (compare {{Exodus 18:21|Exodus 18:21}}; {{1 Timothy 3:1-5|1 Timothy 3:1–5}}; {{1 Timothy 6:10|6:10}}).
The psalmist asks for protection from enemies who speak harshly (see {{Psalm 42:10|Psalms 42:10}}; {{Psalm 44:16|44:16}}; {{Psalm 89:50-51|89:50–51}}; {{Psalm 102:8|102:8}}).

*Waw* (ו) is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his love and salvation.
The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
The psalmist finds joy in God's word despite experiencing pain ({{Psalm 119:92|Psalm 119:92}}, {{Psalm 119:143|143}}).

*Zayin *(ז) is the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist asks God to remember his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
*judgments of old*: This refers to God’s just rulings or decisions (his laws). These are found in the Torah, the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

*Heth *(ח) is the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist seeks God’s favor and loving devotion. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
Wicked people try to lead him into sin, but the psalmist remembers God's word and stays strong (see {{Psalm 119:16|Psalm 119:16}}).
God's goodness fills the earth. The entire creation shows evidence of his goodness (see {{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}}; {{Isaiah 11:9|11:9}}).

- *Good judgment and knowledge *come from wisdom ({{Psalm 111:10|Psalm 111:10}}). 

- The psalmist admits he used to wander like a lost sheep ({{Psalm 119:176|Psalm 119:176}}). 

- *now I keep your word*: See {{Psalm 119:25-29|Psalm 119:25–29}}. 

- *You are good, and You do what is good*: God's character is perfect ({{Psalm 97:2|Psalm 97:2}}; {{James 1:17|James 1:17}}; {{1 John 1:5|1 John 1:5}}).

*Teth *(ט) is the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist admits his sin and gratefully accepts the Lord's discipline.
As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.

*Yodh *(י) is the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.

*Kaph *(כ) is the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist feels exhausted from waiting for the Lord, but he still hopes for God's future rescue.
God's word is trustworthy. This contrasts with the lies of the enemies who hunt the psalmist without reason (see {{Psalm 119:78|Psalm 119:78}}).

*Lamedh *(ל) is the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
The wicked planned to kill the psalmist, but they faced destruction themselves ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).
*I have seen a limit to all perfection*: Humans cannot fully understand God's ways (see {{Ecclesiastes 3:11|Ecclesiastes 3:11}}).
*make me wiser*: God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.

*Mem *(מ) is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far better than the best that human teachers can offer.

- Wisdom is better than the finest food ({{Psalm 19:10|Psalm 19:10}}; {{Psalm 81:16|81:16}}). 

- The psalmist had already turned away from the false promises of foolishness (see {{Psalm 119:18|Psalm 119:18}}, {{Psalm 119:78|78}}, {{Psalm 119:86|86}}, {{Psalm 119:163|163}}).

The Lord’s word is like a lamp. It offers perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness ({{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalm 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 119:130|119:130}}). This light also gives life ({{Proverbs 6:23|Proverbs 6:23}}).

*Nun *(נ) is the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist's deep commitment to God's word comes from within ({{Psalm 119:112|Psalm 119:112}}) and directs his actions.

- *freewill offerings of my mouth*: This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (compare {{Psalm 50:23|Psalm 50:23}}).

- The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
The godly hate the wicked and their actions ({{Psalm 5:4-6|Psalm 5:4–6}}; compare {{Ezekiel 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11}}).

*Samekh *(ס) is the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.

*Ayin *(ע) is the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The servant of the Lord struggles to endure the evil around him. He confidently asks the Lord to rescue him right away!
Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives discernment will he understand it.

*Pe *(פ) is the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.

*Tsadhe *(צ) is the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
The psalmist feels angry (compare {{Psalm 69:9|Psalm 69:9}}) because he sees wicked people ignoring God's word.
The psalmist feels very troubled by those who oppress him (see {{Psalm 119:143|Psalm 119:143}}; compare {{Isaiah 53:1-12|Isaiah 53}}).
*I rise* and *anticipate* translate the same Hebrew verb.

*Qoph* (ק) is the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Even when God seems distant, he is actually close.
*Coming to attack me* (or *draw near*) is a Hebrew wordplay on *You are near*. The wicked stay far from God's instructions, but the psalmist stays close, so he does not need to fear.
Resh (ר): This request for life appears throughout {{Psalm 119:1-176|Psalm 119}}, but it is focused in this stanza.

- *my heart fears … I rejoice*: Fear, trembling, and joy show the psalmist’s devotion to God. 

- God’s word is a treasure (*great spoil*). 

- In the Old Testament, the number seven represents wholeness.

*Shin *(ש) is the twenty-first letter of the alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.

*Taw *(ת) is the twenty-second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God's servant asks the Lord for help one last time. He still feels like a lost sheep.
God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his lost sheep ({{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}; {{Luke 15:4-6|Luke 15:4–6}}).
The psalmist is surrounded by liars, so he makes his lament to the Lord, the only one who can help him.

This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.

These short and memorable songs were sung by pilgrims as they traveled to Jerusalem for the national festivals held three times each year ({{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}). The title of these psalms includes a Hebrew word that can mean “steps” or “stairs.” Some scholars understand it to mean “going up to Jerusalem.” These psalms, often called the Songs of Ascents, lead the listener on a journey to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel through history.

- The psalmist speaks with the liars around him. He feels confident that the Lord will judge them. 

- The Divine Warrior (see {{Psalm 7:12-13|Psalms 7:12–13}}; {{Psalm 11:4-6|11:4–6}}) will attack the liars with sharp arrows and burning coals.

Meshech was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. Kedar was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both places. 

Meshech was known for its slave trade ({{Ezekiel 27:13|Ezekiel 27:13}}; see also {{Exodus 21:16|Exodus 21:16}}), and Kedar was known for its warriors ({{Isaiah 21:16-17|Isaiah 21:16–17}}). These places represented the rebellious and violent land where the psalmist suffered.
The psalmist feels the pain of being alone, isolated, and in constant conflict.

The mountains were known for idol worship ({{Deuteronomy 12:2|Deuteronomy 12:2}}), and Israel was drawn to the hilltop shrines ({{Hosea 4:13|Hosea 4:13}}). This verse can be seen as a rhetorical question expecting a "no" answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot save anyone. 

Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength ({{Psalm 95:4|Psalm 95:4}}). In that case, the question would be taken literally (*From where does my help come?*), with the answer in the next verse.
The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.
God watches over his own, even and especially when they face many troubles ({{Psalm 12:5|Psalms 12:5}}, {{Psalm 12:7|7}}; {{Psalm 69:29|69:29}}; {{Psalm 91:14|91:14}}; {{Psalm 146:9|146:9}}).

- The Maker of heaven and earth ({{Psalm 121:2|Psalm 121:2}}) protects Israel. 

- God stands with Israel, offering support and care to the faithful (see {{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalm 16:7–8}}). 

- Both the sun and the moon were worshiped as gods in the ancient Near East. But God limits their power. They are part of creation and also praise the Lord ({{Psalm 148:3|Psalm 148:3}}).
The central sanctuary was *the house of the LORD*. This phrase first referred to the tabernacle ({{Exodus 23:19|Exodus 23:19}}; {{Exodus 34:26|34:26}}).

Jerusalem is presented here as the city of God, the city of David, and the center of faith. A group of pilgrims joyfully arrives in the city ({{Psalm 122:1-2|Psalm 122:1–2}}). The psalmist praises Jerusalem ({{Psalm 122:3-5|Psalm 122:3–5}}) and prays for the city’s peace ({{Psalm 122:6-9|122:6–9}}).
Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being inside the gates of the city ({{Psalm 9:14|Psalms 9:14}}; {{Psalm 87:2|87:2}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 118:19|118:19}}).
In the time of David and Solomon, people knew Jerusalem as a safe place ({{1 Kings 10:6-7|1 Kings 10:6–7}}).
Jerusalem can represent God’s heavenly dwelling place. David became the model for the rulers God chooses.

- Each person in Israel belonged to a tribe, and all tribes belonged to the Lord. 

- Giving thanks means presenting an offering acceptable to the Lord ({{Psalm 50:14|Psalms 50:14}}, {{Psalm 50:23|23}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 118:19|118:19}}). 

- *as a testimony for Israel*: See {{Exodus 23:17|Exodus 23:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}.
*the thrones of judgment stand*: In the time of David and Solomon ({{1 Kings 3:28|1 Kings 3:28}}), Jerusalem was known for wisdom and justice. It will be like that again ({{Isaiah 9:7|Isaiah 9:7}}).
Prayers for the peace of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

This lament about the psalmist's humble position shows strong trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 123:1-2|Psalm 123:1–2}}). The psalmist prays for God's favor on the community because evil surrounds them ({{Psalm 123:3-4|Psalm 123:3–4}}). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem ({{Psalm 122:1-9|Psalm 122}}) to God's throne in heaven.
The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the Lord was indeed on their side.
This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
*the raging waters*: The enemies could have defeated the Israelites and destroyed them if the Lord had not supported his people (compare {{Psalm 69:15|Psalm 69:15}}; {{Jeremiah 46:8|Jeremiah 46:8}}).

The enemies of God's people were like lions or bears that tear prey with their teeth (see {{Psalm 57:4|Psalm 57:4}}; {{Proverbs 28:15|Proverbs 28:15}}). The Lord shut their mouths ({{Daniel 6:22|Daniel 6:22}}).
The psalmist expresses the community's trust in the Lord's protection ({{Psalm 125:1-2|Psalm 125:1–2}}) and prays for peace ({{Psalm 125:3-5|125:3–5}}).
*surrounds*: God guards and protects like a wall of fire ({{Zechariah 2:5|Zechariah 2:5}}).
The godly may be tempted to abandon God’s ways because of pressure from others or from the surrounding culture.
People who do not follow the "straight paths" are foolish ({{Proverbs 2:12-15|Proverbs 2:12–15}}). God gives his goodness to the godly (see {{Psalm 122:6-9|Psalm 122:6–9}}).

The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt ({{Psalm 114:1|Psalm 114:1}}). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into laughter and showed the Lord’s character to the nations ({{Psalm 9:11|Psalm 9:11}}; {{Psalm 64:9|64:9}}; {{Isaiah 12:4|Isaiah 12:4}}).
This psalm celebrates Israel's return from exile ({{Psalm 126:1-3|Psalm 126:1–3}}). The psalmist then prays that God will fully restore the people ({{Psalm 126:4-6|Psalm 126:4–6}}).

- The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the garden of Eden ({{Isaiah 51:3|Isaiah 51:3}}; {{Ezekiel 47:1-23|Ezekiel 47}}). However, the reality was far from paradise. Here, the restoration community prays for complete redemption (see {{Haggai 2:19|Haggai 2:19}}). 

- *like streams in the Negev*: Seasonal rains filled the dry riverbeds (*wadis*), making the land green again. The prayer seeks a similar change in Israel’s fortunes, fulfilling the imagery of the "Second Exodus" in Isaiah (see "The Promise of a Second Exodus" Theme Note). 

- *carrying sheaves of grain*: This harvest represents God's complete restoration.

- *Unless*: These conditional statements emphasize that the Lord is the one who protects the city (compare {{Psalm 124:1-2|Psalm 124:1–2}}). 

- Human effort achieves nothing unless the Lord blesses it (see {{Psalm 44:3|Psalm 44:3}}). 

- *you rise early and stay up late*: This phrase describes people who work constantly and live with pressure and competition.

- Those whom God loves can rest and sleep in peace ({{Psalm 3:5|Psalm 3:5}}; {{Psalm 4:8|4:8}}).

Blessings and protection come from God. Without his presence, success is not possible ({{Psalm 127:1-2|Psalm 127:1–2}}). This is especially true for children, who are gifts from God ({{Psalm 127:3-5|Psalm 127:3–5}}).

Children are one of God’s blessings. In Hebrew, the word for children (*banim*) sounds like the word for builders (*bonim*; {{Psalm 127:1|Psalm 127:1}}). This wordplay shows that having children helps build a family.

*Like arrows*: The image compares children to arrows in a warrior’s hand. Children strengthen and support the family and help defend its honor when others accuse or oppose them (compare {{Psalm 120:4|Psalms 120:4}}; {{Psalm 7:12-13|7:12–13}}).
*eating the fruit of your labor*: This means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.

The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness ({{Psalm 128:1-2|Psalm 128:1–2}}). The Lord is with them (see {{Psalm 127:1-2|Psalm 127:1–2}}), strengthens their family life ({{Psalm 128:3-4|128:3–4}}), and blesses them for generations ({{Psalm 128:5-6|128:5–6}}).

Children are like strong young olive trees because they are full of potential. Olive oil symbolizes God's blessing ({{Psalm 104:15|Psalm 104:15}}; {{Numbers 18:12|Numbers 18:12}}; {{Jeremiah 31:12|Jeremiah 31:12}}; {{Haggai 2:19|Haggai 2:19}}).

- God will continually bless those who fear him ({{Psalm 133:3|Psalm 133:3}}) from his dwelling in Zion ({{Psalm 20:2|20:2}}; {{Psalm 50:2|50:2}}; {{Psalm 110:2|110:2}}), no matter where they live. 

- *children's children*: God's blessings continue through generations for those who are faithful ({{Psalm 79:12-13|Psalms 79:12–13}}; {{Psalm 89:1|89:1}}; {{Psalm 100:4-5|100:4–5}}; {{Psalm 103:17-19|103:17–19}}).
Israel’s earliest years as a nation took place while the people were living in Egypt.

The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble ({{Psalm 129:1-2|Psalm 129:1–2}}) and redemption ({{Psalm 129:3-4|129:3–4}}). He ends with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly ({{Psalm 129:5-6|Psalm 129:5–6}}).
*The LORD is righteous*: He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
Grass on a rooftop had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was ignored by the harvester when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

A cry from the depths comes from a place of deep distress (compare {{Psalm 69:2|Psalm 69:2}}, {{Psalm 69:14|14}}; {{Isaiah 51:10|Isaiah 51:10}}; {{Ezekiel 27:34|Ezekiel 27:34}}). Feeling weak, the psalmist prays for God's favor.

Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy ({{Psalm 130:1-3|Psalm 130:1–3}}) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 130:4-6|Psalm 130:4–6}}), trusting that the Lord will rescue in his own time and way. With this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord ({{Psalm 130:7-8|Psalm 130:7–8}}).
The psalmist knows that his sins make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.

Israel is encouraged to hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 9:18|Psalms 9:18}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}; {{Psalm 131:3|131:3}}) because the Lord pays the high price for redemption and removes the sin that separates humans from him (see also {{Psalm 111:9|Psalm 111:9}}; {{Exodus 6:6-8|Exodus 6:6–8}}; {{2 Samuel 7:23-24|2 Samuel 7:23–24}}; {{Isaiah 43:1-4|Isaiah 43:1–4}}; {{Titus 2:14|Titus 2:14}}; {{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}; {{1 Peter 1:18|1 Peter 1:18}}).

- The *heart* represents the entire person (see {{Psalm 27:8|Psalm 27:8}}). 

- God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life ({{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}). 

- The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.
Out of his contentment in the Lord, the psalmist invites Israel to seek their rest in God ({{Psalm 131:3|Psalm 131:3}}).

- The psalmist has calmed and quieted himself. He has given up his ambitions and pride ({{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}). 

- *like a weaned child*: The psalmist compares himself to a contented child who rests quietly with its mother.

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s faithfulness to David. When David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem ({{Psalm 132:1-5|Psalm 132:1–5}}), the Lord agreed and made Jerusalem his earthly home ({{Psalm 132:6-10|132:6–10}}). God’s choice of Jerusalem also shows his choice: 

- of David's family line ({{Psalm 132:11-13|Psalm 132:11–13}}),

- of Zion ({{Psalm 132:14-17|Psalm 132:14–17}}), and

- of the priesthood ({{Psalm 132:9|Psalm 132:9}}, {{Psalm 132:16|16}}).

- *Ephrathah* is another name for Bethlehem ({{Genesis 35:19|Genesis 35:19}}; {{Genesis 48:7|48:7}}). 

- *Jaar* is the singular form of the plural *Jearim*. The ark was at Kiriath-jearim for 20 years in Samuel’s time ({{1 Samuel 7:1-2|1 Samuel 7:1–2}}).
These verses recall David moving the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem ({{2 Samuel 6:1-15|2 Samuel 6:1–15}}) and the Lord's promise to David ({{2 Samuel 7:4-16|2 Samuel 7:4–16}}).
These verses are a quotation from Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple ({{2 Chronicles 6:41-42|2 Chronicles 6:41–42}}).
The priests were to show righteousness by the way they live ({{Psalm 132:16|Psalm 132:16}}; {{Malachi 2:6|Malachi 2:6}}).

*The LORD swore an oath to David *({{2 Samuel 7:4-16|2 Samuel 7:4–16}}): God's promise is unconditional, but the covenant depends on conditions (*If … then*). Those who break God's covenant should expect God's judgment as discipline (see {{Psalm 89:30-37|Psalm 89:30–37}}).
The psalmist remembers how God chose Jerusalem and appointed the priests.

*anointed one*: God chose and established this ruler (see {{Psalm 1:1-8:9|Psalms 1–8}}) to always provide light for the Lord’s people. This light would shine continuously (see {{1 Kings 11:36|1 Kings 11:36}}; {{2 Kings 8:19|2 Kings 8:19}}; compare {{John 8:12|John 8:12}}; {{Revelation 21:23-24|Revelation 21:23–24}}).
The enemies will feel shame, while the king will be honored ({{Psalm 132:9|Psalm 132:9}}, {{Psalm 132:16|16}}).
Brothers are connected by family, by work, or by loyalty. In this psalm, *brothers* means all members of the community, including men and women, who live in unity.
The psalmist speaks about the joy of relationships dedicated to God.
In this wisdom psalm (see {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}}), peaceful and harmonious relationships show that God is present.

- The *fine oil *was used to appoint and set apart Aaron for his role as priest (see {{Exodus 29:7|Exodus 29:7}}). 

- *head … beard … collar of his robes*: The oil set Aaron apart completely for God’s service.

- The *dew* represents the richness of God’s blessings (his goodness and care). In Jerusalem, this moisture comes from winds off the Mediterranean Sea. Mount Hermon, which has snow on its peak, is known for its abundant moisture.

- A *blessing* is God’s life-giving power. It shows his provision (care for needs) and protection ({{Psalm 5:12|Psalm 5:12}}; {{Psalm 41:2|41:2}}). It also comes from his presence ({{Psalm 21:6|21:6}}; {{Psalm 67:1|67:1}}). In the end, all nations will receive God’s blessing ({{Psalm 67:1-7|Psalms 67}}; {{Psalm 72:17|72:17}}). Zion is the central place of God's blessing ({{Psalm 134:3|Psalms 134:3}}; {{Psalm 147:13|147:13}}). 

- God gives everlasting life to people.
Those who *serve by night *were the priests and Levites (see also {{Psalm 135:2|Psalm 135:2}}).
In the last of the pilgrims’ songs ({{Psalm 120:1-134:3|Psalms 120–134}}), the travelers ask the temple workers to praise the Lord. In return, they will receive a long-awaited blessing.
God is the Creator and the Lord of history, the “Maker of heaven and earth” ({{Psalm 134:3|Psalm 134:3}}). He deserves praise because, unlike idols, he saves his people.
The names *Jacob* and *Israel* represent all twelve tribes. The Lord loves his chosen people. They are his treasure among all the world's kingdoms ({{Exodus 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5–6}}).
The Lord is greater than any real or imagined supernatural being (see {{Psalm 95:3-5|Psalms 95:3–5}}; {{Psalm 115:4-8|115:4–8}}).

- God has complete authority and power over the whole created order. God does whatever pleases him.

- The phrase *in the heavens and on the earth* refers to all of creation.

The psalmist tells of God’s complete power and authority over the weather ({{Psalm 29:1-11|Psalms 29}}; {{Psalm 77:17-18|77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 78:26|78:26}}; {{Psalm 104:4|104:4}}; {{Psalm 147:8-9|147:8–9}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}).

- In the tenth and final plague against Egypt, God destroyed the firstborn of each family.

- The* signs and wonders* refer to the ten plagues (see {{Exodus 7:1-11:10|Exodus 7–11}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:34|Deuteronomy 4:34}}; {{Nehemiah 9:10|Nehemiah 9:10}}).
The Lord had complete authority and power over the exodus and the conquest of the promised land.
God’s name and character are very different from idols.

Idols lead people to think wrongly because they are only things humans make. They cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe ({{Isaiah 41:22-24|Isaiah 41:22–24}}; {{Isaiah 44:9|44:9}}, {{Isaiah 44:18|18}}; {{Romans 1:21-23|Romans 1:21–23}}).
This entire section is repeated in {{Psalm 115:4-11|Psalm 115:4–11}}.
The groups mentioned here formed the covenant community (see {{Psalm 115:9-11|Psalm 115:9–11}}).
The psalmist calls the community to praise the Lord, who is good and full of love. He is the true Lord over all people. Verse 1 echoes the poetic line in {{2 Chronicles 5:13|2 Chronicles 5:13}}.

This is the last of the Great Hallel psalms ({{Psalm 120:1-136:26|Psalms 120–136}}). It uniquely repeats the phrase *His loving devotion endures forever* in every verse. 

The hymn begins and ends with a call to praise ({{Psalm 136:1-3|Psalm 136:1–3}}, {{Psalm 136:26|26}}). It declares the Lord as the Creator of everything and the Redeemer of Israel, both in ancient times ({{Psalm 136:10-22|Psalm 136:10–22}}) and in the recent past ({{Psalm 136:23-24|136:23–24}}).
The psalmist tells the early history of Israel's redemption.
The psalmist tells the recent story of Israel's redemption, but does not specify the details.
The Lord provides for all of his creatures.

The phrase *God of heaven* is a name for the Lord used during and after the exile (when many Israelites were taken from their land). It appears in:

- Ezra ({{Ezra 1:2|Ezra 1:2}}; {{Ezra 5:11|5:11}}, {{Ezra 5:12|12}}; {{Ezra 6:9|6:9}}, {{Ezra 6:10|10}}; {{Ezra 7:12|7:12}}), 

- Nehemiah ({{Nehemiah 1:5|Nehemiah 1:5}}; {{Nehemiah 2:4|2:4}}, {{Nehemiah 2:20|20}}), and

- Daniel ({{Daniel 2:18|Daniel 2:18}}, {{Daniel 2:19|19}}, {{Daniel 2:37|37}}, {{Daniel 2:44|44}}).

In Psalm 137 people complain to God. They lament and tell him how sad and angry they are. They are sad and angry about unfair things that are happening. Babylonian armies had taken control of the southern kingdom. They had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. They had taken many Jews as prisoners and forced them to live in Babylon.

The speakers of this psalm were some of those Jews forced to live in exile. They were very sad. The Babylonians made fun of them. Psalm 89 talked about this too. That psalm also complained to God about the mean things said by other nations. It accused God of breaking down Jerusalem’s walls. It accused God of breaking his covenant with David. This was because God didn’t protect the king from David’s family line or his city. That city was Jerusalem.

The speakers of Psalm 137 never wanted to forget Jerusalem. God had promised to put his name in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 6:6). This means that people knew that God was present with them there. If they forgot Jerusalem, it would be like forgetting all about God.

The speakers of Psalm 137 prayed to God about those who destroyed Jerusalem. They reminded God about how the Edomites had celebrated that terrible event. They wanted God to remember the sins of the Edomites and the Babylonians. The Jews believed that God would take action as Judge and bring judgement. They wanted him to bring judgement against those who had hurt them.

In response to the pain of exile ({{Psalm 137:1-4|Psalm 137:1–4}}), the psalmist decides to remember Jerusalem, even though the memories cause him pain ({{Psalm 137:4-6|137:4–6}}). He also speaks a strong prayer asking God to bring justice on his enemies ({{Psalm 137:7-9|Psalm 137:7–9}}).

Because the music of Jerusalem was connected to the joy of life in the promised land, the exile took away any reason to sing joyful songs. The Babylonians asked the Judeans to sing and dance for them, but the people were so full of grief that they could not do it.

The songs about the Lord celebrate his power and goodness, but his people were now filled with doubt and questions. They hung their harps in the trees, which may show that their joy had come to an end under God’s judgment ({{Deuteronomy 21:23|Deuteronomy 21:23}}).
The psalmist pledges his loyalty to Jerusalem, the city at the center of God’s reign and the location of fellowship with him.

- The poet saw how the Edomites betrayed the people of Judah, so he calls on God to judge Edom. The long conflict between Edom and Judah reached its worst point near the end of Judah’s history. At that time, the Edomites handed the Judeans over to the Babylonians ({{Obadiah 10-11|Obadiah 1:10–11}}) and celebrated Jerusalem's fall. 

- This prayer asking God to bring justice uses strong language and can be shocking.
The Lord receives praise before the gods of the nations.
In this wisdom psalm, the Lord is presented as the God of gods. He rescued his people and has a perfect plan for them as individuals. The nations will join Israel in glorifying God.

In this final group of psalms of David, psalms of praise and wisdom ({{Psalm 138:1-139:24|Psalms 138–139}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) form a frame around five psalms of lament ({{Psalm 140:1-144:15|Psalms 140–144}}).
As the Lord's glory fills the earth, people must willingly submit to him. Every king (compare {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}) will join in praise when they learn the Lord's ways of truth and love.
God is holy and great, far beyond human understanding (see {{Psalm 99:2|Psalms 99:2}}; {{Psalm 113:4|113:4}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}).
The exalted God cares for the humble ({{Psalm 138:6|Psalm 138:6}}), especially his servant, the psalmist ({{Psalm 138:7-8|138:7–8}}).
The psalmist trusts in the Lord's perfect plans and prays for God's continued involvement. The psalmist sees himself as part of God’s plans (see {{Psalm 9:10|Psalms 9:10}}; {{Psalm 139:14|139:14}}).
The Lord knows the psalmist well. God has examined him closely, in a thorough examination that can be painful at times ({{Job 7:17-19|Job 7:17–19}}).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist opens every part of his life to God. He invites God to examine his thoughts, actions, and words. Even though life is difficult, he wants to grow in wisdom so that he does not share in the judgment of the wicked ({{Psalm 141:5|Psalm 141:5}}; {{Psalm 142:3|142:3}}; {{Psalm 143:8|143:8}}, {{Psalm 143:10|10}}; {{Psalm 144:3-4|144:3–4}}). 

The psalmist also knows that he cannot escape from the Lord. His stress fades as he remembers that God has cared for him with love, even before he was born ({{Psalm 139:13-18|Psalm 139:13–18}}). He ends by asking God to keep examining him and to guide him on the path of wisdom ({{Psalm 139:23-24|Psalm 139:23–24}}).
The phrase *when I sit and when I rise* refers to everyday activities (compare {{Deuteronomy 6:6-9|Deuteronomy 6:6–9}}).
The Lord's all-knowing and all-powerful nature provides comfort to the godly, but it troubles the wicked ({{Psalm 2:3|Psalm 2:3}}).
The Lord’s wonderful understanding lies beyond the psalmist’s ability to comprehend (see {{Judges 13:18|Judges 13:18}}).
The psalmist shows wonder at God being everywhere at all times.
*if I make my bed in Sheol*: God has complete access to all he has created, even the most hidden or hard-to-reach places.

- *rise on the wings of the dawn*: This poetic expression describes traveling eastward, as far as the sunrise, if that were possible.

- *the farthest sea*: This expression takes the traveler in the opposite direction, far to the west.

- *my inmost being*: The delicate inner parts of the body include a person's very being. 

- Even when hidden in his mother’s womb, the psalmist was guided by the Lord.
*How precious to me are Your thoughts*: God’s careful examination shows his loving care. Life with the Lord brings blessings that are beyond words.

The psalmist’s sense of awe leads him to consider the wicked and to reflect on himself. The Lord, as the examiner of all people, judges the wicked for their destructive acts and speech. So, the psalmist prays that he will not be among them.
*Do I note hate those who hate You*: Rejecting evil shows wisdom (see {{Psalm 1:1|Psalms 1:1}}; {{Psalm 5:4-6|5:4–6}}).
As the psalmist prays about the wicked, he also reflects on himself. He does not assume that he is righteous. This prayer has been spoken again and again by God’s people over many generations.
The path of wisdom leads to eternal life (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}; {{Proverbs 4:18|Proverbs 4:18}}; {{Proverbs 6:23|6:23}}).
The psalmist prays for the Lord to rescue him from wicked people.

In this personal lament, the psalmist describes God's enemies and their evil plans. He prays for the Lord's protection and rescue, trusting in God's strength and justice. He predicts that fire will judge the evil ({{Psalm 140:9-11|Psalm 140:9–11}}) and that he will be proven right and live in the Lord's presence ({{Psalm 140:13|140:13}}).
*snakes … vipers*: These creatures portray the wicked as very corrupt people (see {{Proverbs 23:32|Proverbs 23:32}}; {{Isaiah 14:29|Isaiah 14:29}}; {{Romans 3:13|Romans 3:13}}).
The psalmist prays for God's protection (see {{Psalm 121:1-8|Psalm 121}}), asking the Lord to keep him safe from the wicked's many plans.

*O GOD the Lord*: This title comes from combining the name *Yahweh* with the title *Adonai* (which means Master). See also {{Psalm 68:20|Psalms 68:20}}; {{Psalm 69:6|69:6}}; {{Psalm 71:16|71:16}}; {{Psalm 73:28|73:28}}; {{Psalm 109:21|109:21}}; {{Psalm 141:8|141:8}}.
The psalmist prays for God’s judgment on the wicked.

The psalmist asks for *burning coals* to fall on his enemies and for them to be thrown* into the miry pits*, so that they cannot attack again. This language hints at the New Testament teachings on hell (see {{Matthew 5:22|Matthew 5:22}}, {{Matthew 5:29-30|29–30}}; {{Matthew 10:28|10:28}}; {{Matthew 18:9|18:9}}; {{Mark 9:43-47|Mark 9:43–47}}; {{Luke 12:5|Luke 12:5}}; {{James 3:6|James 3:6}}; {{2 Peter 2:4|2 Peter 2:4}}).

- The psalmist urgently prays for rescue. He does not have incense or an evening offering ({{Exodus 29:38-39|Exodus 29:38–39}}), but his prayers and devotion represent those elements (see {{Isaiah 1:13|Isaiah 1:13}}; {{Revelation 5:8|Revelation 5:8}}). 

- *uplifted hands*: This is a posture of prayer ({{Psalm 28:2|Psalms 28:2}}; {{Psalm 88:9|88:9}}; {{Psalm 143:6|143:6}}; {{Exodus 9:29|Exodus 9:29}}; {{1 Timothy 2:8|1 Timothy 2:8}}).
The psalmist prays for rescue and for wisdom. He also looks ahead to the end of evil. The idea that people receive what they deserve ({{Psalm 141:10|Psalm 141:10}}) holds the psalm together.

- Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. People might say or think things that lead to a harmful path ({{Proverbs 13:3|Proverbs 13:3}}; {{Proverbs 21:23|21:23}}). 

- Wisdom accepts correction from godly people (see {{Proverbs 3:11|Proverbs 3:11}}; {{Proverbs 9:8|9:8}}; {{Proverbs 15:31|15:31}}; {{Proverbs 19:25|19:25}}).
Although overwhelmed by his persecutors ({{Psalm 142:6|Psalm 142:6}}), the psalmist seeks wisdom from the Lord.
*when he was in the cave*: Compare {{Psalm 57:1|Psalm 57:1}}.
He feels trapped and stressed, similar to being in prison (see {{Psalm 107:10|Psalm 107:10}}).

The psalmist feels deep despair (see {{Psalm 77:3|Psalm 77:3}}), and the Lord helps him in his distress. The psalmist trusts in the Lord's wisdom (see {{Psalm 139:1-24|Psalm 139}}) but mourns being trapped by evil people ({{Psalm 5:9-10|5:9–10}}; {{Psalm 140:5|140:5}}; {{Psalm 141:9|141:9}}; {{Psalm 142:3|142:3}}).
Even when alone, the psalmist trusts the Lord, who is his life (see {{Psalm 9:9|Psalms 9:9}}; {{Psalm 16:5|16:5}}; {{Psalm 27:13|27:13}}).
Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.
The psalmist faces severe persecution, so he cries to the Lord, and the Lord will rescue him.
The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.

In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant trouble from his enemies, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers what God has done in the past and longs for God to renew his love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that God’s instruction leads to life.
Everyone has sinned and is guilty before God ({{Romans 3:20-24|Romans 3:20–24}}).
*My spirit grows faint within me*: The psalmist admits his desperation as his life seems to slip away under cruel and powerful enemies.
Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness ({{Psalm 42:4|Psalms 42:4}}; {{Psalm 63:6|63:6}}; {{Psalm 77:3|77:3}}, {{Psalm 77:6|6}}; {{Psalm 119:55|119:55}}).
The psalmist’s thirst is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see {{Psalm 42:1-2|Psalm 42:1–2}}).

The psalmist experiences depression. He describes himself as close to death from sorrow ({{Psalm 31:10|Psalms 31:10}}; {{Psalm 119:87|119:87}}). He feels worn out ({{Psalm 39:10|Psalms 39:10}}; {{Psalm 71:9|71:9}}; {{Psalm 119:81|119:81}}). He is weak from longing ({{Psalm 84:2|Psalm 84:2}}). He feels overwhelmed by the burdens of life ({{Psalm 90:7|Psalm 90:7}}, {{Psalm 90:9|9}}).
The psalmist asks the Lord to renew his love.

- The psalmist prays for wisdom (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 25:4-6|25:4–6}}; {{Psalm 138:1-8|138}}; {{Psalm 143:10|143:10}}). 

- *Your good Spirit*: The Spirit brings God's goodness (see {{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).
*revive*: Here, it means to bring someone out of despair and restore them to life ({{Psalm 80:19|Psalms 80:19}}; {{Psalm 85:6|85:6}}; {{Psalm 138:7|138:7}}).
The psalm ends with a prayer for God to show that the psalmist is in the right and to restore his life.
*my Rock … my steadfast love … my deliverer … my shield*: The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 144:3-4|Psalm 144:3–4}}). The psalmist asks for God's help and anticipates victory ({{Psalm 144:5-11|Psalm 144:5–11}}). 

A new song ({{Psalm 144:9-10|Psalm 144:9–10}}) and a prayer for rescue ({{Psalm 144:11|144:11}}) introduce the theme of the Lord’s blessings through his care and protection ({{Psalm 144:12-15|Psalm 144:12–15}}).

*what is man*: The same question in {{Psalm 8:4-6|Psalm 8:4–6}} leads to the answer that humans are only mortal (they do not live forever), yet God gives them honor and responsibility to rule. 

The psalmist focuses on how brief and fragile human life is. He describes it as temporary and passing quickly (see {{Psalm 90:3|Psalms 90:3}}, {{Psalm 90:7-10|7–10}}; {{Psalm 102:11|102:11}}; {{Psalm 109:23|109:23}}; {{Psalm 146:4|146:4}}).
The psalmist asks God to act against his enemies (compare {{Psalm 18:7-19|Psalm 18:7–19}}).
The psalmist compares sons and daughters to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.

This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of {{Psalm 140:1-144:15|Psalms 140–144}}to a close. It describes God’s provision (care for needs) and protection (keeping people safe; see {{Psalm 127:1-5|Psalm 127}}), not only for the psalmist but also for his children and for all who follow God.
*no going into captivity, and no cry of lament*: These images show peace and safety.
The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see {{Psalm 47:2|Psalm 47:2}}).

This psalm of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David ({{Psalm 138:1-145:21|Psalms 138–145}}). Praise continues in the last five psalms ({{Psalm 146:1-150:6|Psalms 146–150}}). 

This psalm celebrates the Lord as the King of all ({{Psalm 145:1-3|Psalm 145:1–3}}, {{Psalm 145:10-13|10–13}}). God's actions show his royal qualities ({{Psalm 145:4-7|Psalm 145:4–7}}). He cares for all creatures ({{Psalm 145:14-17|Psalm 145:14–17}}) and for those who fear him ({{Psalm 145:18-20|145:18–20}}).

This litany (a repeated form of praise, often with the same line said again and again) celebrates God’s character and his mighty deeds. Each generation will continue to tell others about God’s power ({{Psalm 22:30|Psalm 22:30}}).
God consistently demonstrates his character toward all his creation (see {{Psalm 136:25|Psalm 136:25}}).
These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.
The Lord cares for his creatures.

The Lord cares for those who love him and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him ({{Psalm 5:11|Psalm 5:11}}). They seek him as their only true Savior ({{Psalm 40:16|Psalms 40:16}}; {{Psalm 70:4|70:4}}). They will experience a good future ({{Psalm 69:36|Psalm 69:36}}) and enjoy the peace that God gives ({{Psalm 119:165|119:165}}).

The call to praise ({{Psalm 146:1-2|Psalm 146:1–2}}) leads to a warning against foolishness and false confidence ({{Psalm 146:3-4|146:3–4}}). The psalm ends with a blessing for everyone who places their hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 146:5-7|Psalm 146:5–7}}).

The book of Psalms ends with five poems of praise. These psalms praise God for being the King who rules for ever over everything and everyone. They praise him for being the Maker of everything that exists. They praise him for taking care of every part of creation.

This includes caring for the stars, the weather, the land, plants and animals. It includes making sure that justice is done for needy people.
